# Exact scope

The construction is for every excellent local germ, after reduction, with a nonempty intrinsic centred ray boundary when the local reduction has positive dimension. Sections use arbitrary proper primary ideals. Nonminimal prime supports and infinite function values are retained. Zero-dimensional local reduction gives the empty boundary. For nonreduced germs this is a semivaluation theory of the reduction; nilpotent intersection multiplicities are not supplied.

The independent geometric core uses actual primary blowups of the reduced germ, actual negative effective finite real Cartier presentations, and degree >=0 on every contracted proper integral curve. Common product-ideal blowups identify presentations. There is no assertion that this system is cofinal in all proper birational models, no nonnormal Weil-coefficient substitute for Cartier effectivity, and no arbitrary-characteristic resolution assertion. The uniform and actual decreasing completions are justified by the proved comparison C_geom=C_ideal and D_geom=D_ideal; core positivity is geometric before that comparison.

P is the finite REAL positive ideal cone; Q=-P; C is its finite continuous uniform closure; D consists of actual decreasing C-nets with bottom allowed. N is the normalization-RAW compatible cone. Q subset N subset C, and both uniform closures equal C. The nonisolated cusp separates N and C from Q. No raw equality is asserted.

Primary-gauge changes are the exact homogeneous cocycle u_b(v/v(b))=u_a(v)/v(b), with bounded positive denominator. Completion is an all-semivaluation homeomorphism with exact primary contraction. Normalization branches are local normal centres above the marked point, not merely minimal components. Finite conductor value gives a singleton fibre; infinite value gives exactly the conductor quotient identification. The infinity stratum is closed and its finite complement open. Both C and D descend exactly iff constant on all fibres, including mixedzero and partialbottom. The same class-level pullback/descent result holds for every reduced finite injection over an excellent reduced local target. This supplies the cone rules asked in P12.2, not all geometric operators of P12.6.

Full BFJ specialization is proved on ALL semivaluations at a smooth affine closed germ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. C is exactly its finite continuous subclass; D is its full canonically retracted formal psh class with identically bottom adjoined. Smooth DVR and empty dimension zero are direct. Source domains are not enlarged to positive-characteristic singular SNC settings.

The cone is not identified with literal classical or CLD logarithmic radial extensions. The mixedzero nodal profile (-1,0) belongs to this boundary cone and remains excluded by the stated radial compatibility obstruction. Global projective trivially valued energy constructions are not claimed to solve this local target.

P12.3 obstacle envelopes, P12.4 bounded mixed Monge--Ampere products, P12.5 energy and P12.6 geometric envelope/product/operator functoriality are separate. They are not constructed here and their omission is not a P12.2 gap. This manuscript is a complete-solution candidate for ORIGINAL P12.2 only, requiring subsequent independent whole-original review.

## ENTIRE original-problem.txt

P12.3 (T4): An independently geometric singular envelope theory
Construct obstacle envelopes for the independently geometric singular psh cone, establish
their positivity and the appropriate regularity, and compare them with the complete ideal-
psh envelope already known on reduced-curve links.

ENTIRE ORIGINAL FAMILY DOSSIER
6     A geometric local theory on singular germs
Active items: P12.2, P12.3, P12.4, P12.5, P12.6. Status: Open in the residual scope.

6.1   Atomic targets
P12.2 (T4): An independently geometric singular valuative psh cone
On the intrinsic normalized boundary of an excellent singular or nonnormal germ, construct
a valuative psh class with independent geometric meaning and the correct smooth-germ spe-
cialization. Identify its relation to the existing ideal-generated cone. Deﬁning another order-
theoretic completion does not by itself supply that identiﬁcation.

P12.3 (T4): An independently geometric singular envelope theory
Construct obstacle envelopes for the independently geometric singular psh cone, establish
their positivity and the appropriate regularity, and compare them with the complete ideal-
psh envelope already known on reduced-curve links.

P12.4 (T5): Model-independent bounded singular-local products
Construct bounded mixed Monge–Ampère products on singular and nonnormal normalized
local boundaries, with model independence, the correct intersection comparison, locality and
continuity. The existing compact boundary construction alone supplies no such product.

P12.5 (T5): Finite energy on singular local boundaries
Construct an energy functional, ﬁnite-energy class, and its Monge–Ampère calculus for excel-
lent singular and nonnormal germs. Specify reference data, changes of primary gauge, and
the relation between bounded approximation and ﬁnite-energy limits.

P12.6 (T4): Geometric ﬁnite-map functoriality and conductor descent
Establish compatibility of independently geometric singular psh cones, envelopes and Monge–
Ampère products with ﬁnite maps, normalization and conductor descent. Finite restric-
tion, ideal-cone extrema, normal-domain norm traces, ﬁnite-ﬂat determinant traces and their
tower/gauge rules are known. They do not identify the geometric operators; an unrestricted
continuous degree trace is obstructed.

6.2   What constitutes a solution
The requested geometric cone, envelopes, bounded products, ﬁnite energy and map compat-
ibility are separate targets. Prove their smooth-germ specialization, primary-gauge changes
and normalization/conductor rules. Do not identify an ideal-generated order completion with
a geometric pluripotential theory without an additional comparison theorem.

6.3   Full statement and detailed state of the art
Finite-map progress is now available in Book Section 70.2: continuous positive trace over
normal targets without ﬂatness, ﬁber extrema for arbitrary ﬁnite maps onto their exact im-
ages, and the exact conductor criterion for continuous descent. The ideal-generated cones
are explicit; their identiﬁcation with a geometric singular psh class and compatibility with
envelopes and Monge–Ampère products are not claimed. This settles the valuative transfer
layer of P12.6 and narrows its remaining geometric target.

Problem 6.1. Extend the normalized local theory of Book Chapter 70 from smooth complex
germs to excellent singular and nonnormal germs. On the normalized boundary of Book
Section 70.1.1, construct, when possible, psh functions, envelopes, bounded products, ﬁnite
energy, and ﬁnite-map functoriality.
    The normalizing-boundary part is resolved in arbitrary dimension. Book Theorem 70.1.2
gives the intrinsic centered ray space and its nonempty compact sections for all m-primary
ideals, with exact change (Book 70.7a). Book Theorem 70.1.3 presents each section as a
quotient of the separated normalization branches. Fibers are singletons where the conductor
has ﬁnite value; on its inﬁnite-value stratum, equality of restrictions to the conductor quo-
tient is the precise identiﬁcation rule. Nonprimary ideals deﬁne the partial sections (Book
70.7e), which can be noncompact. Nilpotents are invisible to these semivaluations, and a zero-
dimensional local reduction has empty centered cone. This settles P12.1, while P12.2–P12.6
retain their separate psh, envelope, product, energy and ﬁnite-map targets. It does not assert
an intersection theory or resolution in positive characteristic.
    In dimension one, this construction reduces to a ﬁnite branch set. By Book Theorem 70.1.4,
the link normalized by an m-primary ideal a is the ﬁnite discrete set of normalization branches
q above the closed point, with point

                                         ordq / ordq (a).

Changing the primary ideal rescales this same branch set by the exact cocycle (Book Chap-
ter 70, †). In particular, branches cannot be indexed only by irreducible components: the irre-
ducible node in Book Example 70.1.4 has one minimal prime and two normalization branches.
    There is also an exact link-level ﬁnite-map formula. Book Proposition 70.1.2 applies to
an arbitrary ﬁnite local homomorphism of reduced Nagata curve germs, without injectivity.
When a source branch has ramiﬁcation index e over a target branch, both its order and the
order of the extended ideal aS acquire the factor e, so normalization cancels it. The resulting
restriction maps are compatible with composition and change of primary ideal. They need
not be surjective; this remains a link-level result.
    There is now also an exact conductor-controlled ideal-level range. Book Proposition 70.1.3
shows that every suﬃciently deep integral vector of branch orders is realized by one downstairs
nonzerodivisor generating an m-primary ideal. Consequently Book Theorem 70.1.5 identiﬁes
the principal-ideal proﬁles with the strictly negative rational orthant, their uniform closure
with all nonpositive functions on the ﬁnite link, and their raw obstacle envelope with min{φ, 0}.
The monotone boundary is sharp: all nonpositive proﬁles admit increasing approximation
from below, whereas a proﬁle with a zero branch coordinate cannot be a decreasing limit of
primary-ideal proﬁles. These conclusions concern only the explicitly deﬁned ideal-function
family.
    There is now also a complete order-theoretic calculus for the book-local ideal-closure can-
didate. By Book Theorem 70.1.6, its continuous ideal-psh class is every ﬁnite nonpositive
function on the branch link, and its decreasing completion is every extended nonpositive func-
tion. Equivalently, it is the intrinsic cone of nonpositive degree-one homogeneous functions
on the unnormalized branch-valuation rays. Changing the primary ideal merely changes the
cross-section and obeys an exact cocycle; ﬁnite local maps pull the class back, preserve prin-
cipal models, and commute with the envelope min{φ, 0}. Their pullback image is exactly the
ﬁber-constant subclass; pullback is injective precisely for a surjective branch map and sur-
jective precisely for an injective branch map, while surjective branch maps act isometrically
on the continuous class. On the completed lattices, ﬁberwise supremum and inﬁmum give
explicit left and right adjoints to pullback, with −∞ and zero as the two empty-ﬁber conven-
tions; the resulting source-side composites are the least ﬁber-constant majorant and greatest
ﬁber-constant minorant, so their ﬁxed points are exactly the functions descending through

analytic function; scaled logarithms and a decreasing limit then give all remaining slopes.
For the converse, a zero branch forces a nonnegative nodal value by upper semicontinuity;
any simultaneously negative branch then contradicts its closed-disc Shilov maximum prin-
ciple. Hence the mixed-zero ideal proﬁle (−1, 0) is excluded, while every proﬁle with all
coordinates strictly negative or −∞ does extend. The conductor realizes the required branch-
wise monomials by single downstairs analytic functions, so this supplies the exact branch-
compatibility rule throughout the stated disc-normalized curve range. The ordinary multinode
theorem Book Theorem 70.1.10 records the explicit coordinate-ring instance. At the oppo-
site extreme, the unibranch cusp in Book Example 70.1.9 has conductor t2 Khti, and its cone
{0} ∪ [−∞, 0) = [−∞, 0] contains every nonpositive radial proﬁle; the mixed-zero obstruction
is therefore genuinely multibranch. The result does not decide whether a diﬀerent boundary-
trace comparison exists, or treat a singular germ outside this normalization-and-conductor
range.
    There is a genuine, but diﬀerent, global boundary case. Over an algebraically closed
ﬁeld of characteristic zero, the global trivially-valued framework used in [BJ23, §2] treats an
integral projective variety without initially assuming normality: it supplies a global psh class,
its ﬁnite-energy space and energy, and a Monge–Ampère operator with dense ﬁnite-energy
image. Exact surjectivity there is equivalent to the envelope property, which that source
records in the smooth case. This global construction neither selects a normalized link for an
excellent local germ nor supplies the curve-local conductor realization above, local bounded
products, or the required local ﬁnite-map formula. It therefore does not discharge any part
of Problem 6.1.
    The remaining programme tests higher-dimensional normal crossings, quotient singulari-
ties, and purely inseparable universal homeomorphisms. Any claim of independence of psh
or intersection constructions from boundary choices must respect the established radial com-
parison and conductor quotient. Relative b-divisors can be deﬁned on suitable model sys-
tems, but beyond the normalized boundary and, in dimension one, the branch link, its ideal-
psh candidate and envelope, its arbitrary ﬁnite-map pullback, its branch-surjective generic
trace and conductor descent, its ﬁnite conditional-expectation calculus, its ﬁnite-ﬂat canoni-
cal norm pushforward, and the principal-ideal range above, the independently geometric psh
and intersection-theoretic package is presently open.
    Two older local-volume questions should not be carried forward as open. For the
Boucksom–de Fernex–Favre local volume, Yuchen Zhang proves a positive dimension-
dependent lower bound for every nonzero volume of an isolated Gorenstein singularity and

                                               62

constructs a non- Q-Gorenstein isolated singularity of volume zero that admits no boundary
making the pair log canonical [Zha14]. Thus the ﬁrst conjectural direction is conﬁrmed and
the second implication is disproved. These results delimit the singular theory above; they are
resolved history, not additional problems.

\section{Canonical ideals: reconstruction on the entire boundary}
\label{sec:canonical}
\textit{Support: the entire qualified G331 only. None of the current408 or historical notes is a correctness premise.}

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be excellent local. Semivaluations kill nilpotents, so throughout this section replace $R$ by $R_{\rm red}$. If this reduction has dimension zero its centred boundary is empty and all envelopes mean its unique empty function. Otherwise fix a proper $\mathfrak m$-primary ideal $\mathfrak a$ and the compact, nonempty section $X=V_{\mathfrak a}(R)$. Every prime support strictly below $\mathfrak m$ is retained. G331 supplies the independent geometric core: actual negative effective finite real Cartier presentations on directed actual primary blowups, with degree nonnegative on every contracted proper integral curve. Its uniform class $C$ and actual decreasing-net class $D$ equal the corresponding ideal classes. We use this qualified comparison, its rational-profile density, finite maxima, full-fibre positive descent, and its exact published smooth specialization. No envelope theorem is part of that grant.

For a finite continuous signed obstacle $f:X\to\mathbb R$ define
\[
 A_0=R,\qquad A_m=\{g\in R:\ v(g)+mf(v)\ge0\text{ for all }v\in X\}\quad(m\ge1),
 \qquad h_m=-v(A_m)/m.
\]
This definition uses no fraction field of $R$ and is meaningful also when $v(g)=+\infty$. Set $c=\max(0,-\min_X f)$. Any positive integer $N\ge mc$ gives $\mathfrak a^N\subset A_m$. The ultrametric inequality proves addition closure and nonnegative values on $R$ prove multiplication closure. If $f$ is negative at one point, no unit lies in any $A_m$, so every $A_m$ is proper primary. If $f\ge0$, every $A_m=R$. Thus $h_m$ is always a finite continuous unit-or-primary profile, is below $f$, and has actual geometric positivity by G331. In the proper case its presentation is $-E_{A_m}/m$ on the actual blowup of $A_m$; the negative exceptional bundle is relatively ample.

Multiplying the defining inequalities gives $A_mA_n\subset A_{m+n}$. Each $A_m$ is integrally closed as an ideal. Indeed, if $g$ satisfies a monic degree-$q$ equation with coefficient of index $i$ in $A_m^i$, then at a semivaluation where $v(g)<v(A_m)$ the leading term has uniquely least finite value. This contradicts the equation. All ideal values here are finite because $A_m$ contains a primary power. Infinite $v(g)$ imposes no difficulty.

Define only a raw function, without a positivity assertion,
\[
 p(f)=\sup\{u\in D:u\le f\}.
\]
We prove
\[
 p(f)=\sup\{u\in C:u\le f\}=\sup_{m\ge1}h_m.
 \tag{1}
\]
A rational unit-or-primary competitor $-v(I)/r\le f$ has $I\subset A_r$, and hence is below $h_r$. A $C$ competitor can be approximated uniformly by rational profiles and then shifted down by a rational negative $\mathfrak a$-constant. Such a shift is again a rational primary profile, by multiplication of ideals after clearing denominators. Sending the approximation error to zero proves the $C$ assertion. If $u=\inf_i g_i\le f$ in an actual decreasing $C$-net, the open sets $\{g_i<f+\epsilon\}$ cover $X$. Directedness and compactness select one index valid everywhere. The function $g_i-\epsilon\in C$ is a competitor and $u\le\sup_m h_m+\epsilon$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This step uses continuity of $f$, not continuity of $u$; bottom and partial poles are permitted. The reverse inequalities follow because each $h_m$ is itself a $D$ competitor.

Put $M_1=\|v(A_1)\|_\infty$ and $H_N=\max_{1\le r\le N}h_r\in C$. Write $m=kr+s$, $0\le s<r$. The inclusion $A_r^kA_1^s\subset A_m$, together with $h_r\le0$, gives
\[
 h_m\ge \frac{kr}{m}h_r-\frac{s}{m}M_1
 \ge h_r-\frac{rM_1}{m},\qquad
 H_N-\frac{NM_1}{m}\le h_m\le p(f).
 \tag{2}
\]
These estimates hold on every support, even when generator values are infinite. In particular the full degree sequence converges pointwise to $p(f)$. The function $p(f)$ is finite, nonpositive and lower semicontinuous, bounded below by $h_1$.

The following exact criterion is not a solution of general continuity:
\[
 p(f)\text{ continuous}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_N\to p(f)\text{ uniformly}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_m\to p(f)\text{ uniformly}. \tag{3}
\]
For the forward implication the increasing strict error-test open sets for $H_N$ cover compact $X$, so one $N$ works uniformly. Equation (2) then gives uniform convergence of the full sequence. Conversely a uniform limit lies in the closed geometric class $C$, so is continuous and is the greatest $D$ minorant by (1). We do not declare an upper semicontinuous regularization positive.

The raw envelope is monotone and satisfies
\[
 \|p(f)-p(g)\|_\infty\le\|f-g\|_\infty. \tag{4}
\]
If $f\le g+\epsilon$, any $D$ minorant $u$ of $f$ has $u-\epsilon\in D$ below $g$. The shift belongs to $D$ by adding a fixed negative primary profile to its defining decreasing net. Supremizing proves the one-sided inequality; reversing $f,g$ proves (4). Consequently uniform approximation by obstacles whose envelopes are already in $C$ proves a $C$ envelope for the limit. This is an implication, not a general density assertion.

For completeness we independently reconstruct the finite-generation reduction. Suppose $\mathcal A=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}A_mt^m$ is generated by homogeneous $g_it^{d_i}$, $d_i>0$. Let $L$ be a common multiple of the degrees, $D_0=\max d_i$, and $J=(g_i^{L/d_i})_i$. On each support some generator has finite value: otherwise the degree-one ideal $A_1$ would have infinite value. Every degree-$m$ expression has value at least $m\min_i v(g_i)/d_i$. Moreover $J\subset A_L$, so
\[
 h_m\le -v(J)/L\le h_L\le p(f).
\]
The middle profile is therefore $p(f)=h_L$, and it is also $\max_{r\le D_0}h_r$ by using a generator attaining the finite minimum. The radical of the generator coefficient ideal contains $A_1$, so $J$ is primary in the proper case. Equation (2) gives
\[
 0\le p(f)-h_m\le D_0M_1/m. \tag{5}
\]
The unit case is immediate.

Conversely, if $p(f)=-v(J)/q$ for a proper primary $J$ and positive integer $q$, then the definition and (1) imply
\[
 A_m=\{g:v(g)\ge (m/q)v(J)\text{ on all }X\}
     =\{g:g^q\in\overline{J^m}\}. \tag{6}
\]
For the second equality apply the centred rank-one DVR integral-closure criterion to each minimal-component quotient and then the all-minimal-component criterion (Swanson--Huneke 6.8.3--4 and 1.1.5). Every such quotient has positive dimension: a zero-dimensional minimal component of a local reduced ring would make its maximal ideal minimal and the whole ring zero-dimensional. The images of $J$ and $\mathfrak a$ are primary, and each centred DVR normalizes into $X$. Monic ideal-integrality equations give the reverse inequalities on all other supports as well, by the same uniquely least finite term argument. These are applications of the complete immediate published units, read afresh; their deeper valuation-domination foundations are disclosed in the ledger.

Set $B=R[Jt^q]$. Primary $J$ contains a regular element by finite prime avoidance. Thus $B$ is reduced excellent and its total quotient ring is $\prod_j K_j(t^q)$, with $K_j=\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p_j)$. Its finite extension $\prod_j K_j(t)$ may be inseparable. The standard excellent/Nagata finite-normalization property makes the integral closure of $B$ in that extension finite over $B$. An equation for $g^q$ over $J^m$, multiplied by powers of $t^{mq}$, makes $g^qt^{mq}$ integral over $B$, and then $gt^m$ integral by its $q$th-power equation. Hence $B\subset\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal A$ is a $B$-submodule of that finite normalization. Noetherianity makes it finite over $B$, hence finitely generated over $R$. The same statement for the zero envelope is $\mathcal A=R[t]$. A finite maximum of canonical profiles is a rational unit-or-primary profile, by ideal sums after clearing denominators. We have proved equivalence of finite generation, rational primary attainment, and finite canonical-max attainment, without assuming any of them generally.

For a signed integral exceptional Cartier obstacle $f_D$ on an actual primary blowup of a normal $R$, let $Y$ be its finite normalization, with the pulled-back divisor and its canonical rational trivialization. There is an exact model computation
\[
 A_m(f_D)=H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y(mD))\cap R. \tag{6a}
\]
Testing the all-boundary inequalities at the finitely many height-one exceptional orders gives the section inequalities there; at other height-one primes $D$ is zero and $g\in R$ is already regular. Normal height-one intersection proves that $g$ is a section. Conversely a section pulls back to the valuation ring of $\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)$ at every semivaluation support. The generic point is outside the closed exceptional fibre, so the invertible bundle has its canonical nonzero trivialization there. If its local generator is $b$, then the section has $v(g)-v(b)\ge0$, and $v(b)=-mf_D(v)$. This yields the canonical inequality on every support, with infinite $v(g)$ automatic. Properness gives the valued centre; no total quotient field is mapped through a nonminimal support. For a rational divisor use denominator multiples. The finite generation of this particular section-intersection algebra is a hypothesis to establish in any application, not a theorem for arbitrary signed model obstacles.

For another primary gauge $\mathfrak b$, put $d(v)=v(\mathfrak b)>0$ and $T(v)=v/d(v)$. If $f_{\mathfrak b}(Tv)=f_{\mathfrak a}(v)/d(v)$, then
\[
 (Tv)(g)+mf_{\mathfrak b}(Tv)=(v(g)+mf_{\mathfrak a}(v))/d(v).
\]
The canonical ideals and graded algebra are literally unchanged. Profiles and raw envelopes divide by $d$; substitution gives the three-gauge cocycle. Uniform errors divide by the positive minimum of $d$. For the finite normalization $S$ of $R$, surjective restriction gives $A_m^R=A_m^S\cap R$. This includes every conductor-infinite quotient fibre; it does not assert that contraction preserves finite generation. If the source geometric envelope exists and is constant on every normalization fibre, G331's positive descent supplies the downstairs envelope: it is below $f$ and dominates every pulled-back downstairs competitor. Compatibility of the obstacle alone is not sufficient.

If a decreasing directed family of continuous obstacles has envelopes $H_i\in C$, then $H=\inf_iH_i\in D$ is the envelope of their infimum: every minorant of the infimum is below every $H_i$, and $H$ is below every obstacle. This uses an actual decreasing net and no flattening. For excellent reduced curves the finite normalization centres are DVRs. This diagnoses the limitation of (5), rather than an envelope failure.

\section{Smooth continuous envelopes from the complete BFJ model estimate}
\label{sec:smooth}
\textit{Support: G331 and earlier own n1 (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}). The BFJ envelope estimate is a new published application, not an envelope grant imported from G331.}

\[
 W=\sup\{Z:Z\text{ nef},\ Z\le Z(F)\}.
\]
This is a finite nef Weil divisor: restrict the competitors by replacing them with their maximum with the barrier $-M$; maxima preserve nefness and the obstacle bound. \]
The inequality $H\le F$ holds on all supports. Put $B_m=L^\infty(mW)$ in the completed ring, using BFJ~3.15. By 3.17,

\]

\section{Arbitrary continuous obstacles on finite smooth quotient germs}
\label{sec:quotient}
\textit{Support: the entire qualified G331 and earlier own n1,n2. This is new scoped original-residual progress, not a theorem for every excellent normal germ.}

Suppose $S$ is a positive-dimensional smooth affine closed-germ local domain over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, and a finite group $G$ acts faithfully by local automorphisms. Assume $R=S^G$ is excellent Noetherian and $S$ is finite over $R$; these hypotheses hold for the algebraic quotient example below. The ring $R$ is a normal local domain: an element of $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ integral over $R$ is integral over $S$, hence belongs to the normal ring $S$, and, being invariant, belongs to $R$. Fix a proper primary $\mathfrak a\subset R$, put $b=\mathfrak aS$, and let
\[
 \rho:V_b(S)\longrightarrow V_{\mathfrak a}(R)
\]
be restriction. This map is continuous surjective by G331, including semivaluations with nonminimal supports. Both the obstacle and the normalizing source ideal $b$ are invariant.

We need the entire fibres, not just field valuations. Let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(S)$. Then $L^G=K$: if $s/t\in L^G$, multiply its denominator by the finite product of its $G$-translates; that product lies in $R$, and the resulting invariant numerator lies in $R$. Here is the needed fixed-field argument, so no unpublished fibre-transitivity theorem is assumed. Distinct automorphisms $\sigma_i$ are linearly independent as $L$-valued functions on $L$: in a relation with the fewest nonzero coefficients, evaluate at $ax$ and subtract $\sigma_j(a)$ times the relation at $x$. Choosing $a$ on which two distinct automorphisms differ produces a shorter nonzero relation, a contradiction; a one-term relation is impossible by evaluating at $1$. Consequently the evaluation columns $(\sigma_i(x))_i$ span $L^d$, for otherwise a nonzero annihilating row would give such a relation. Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ with invertible evaluation matrix. For arbitrary $x\in L$, solve
\[
 \sigma_i(x)=\sum_j c_j\sigma_i(x_j)\quad\text{for every }\sigma_i\in G.
\]
Applying any $\tau\in G$ permutes the rows, so uniqueness forces $\tau(c_j)=c_j$. Hence $c_j\in K$, and the identity row writes $x=\sum_jc_jx_j$. The invertible matrix also proves the $x_j$ are $K$-linearly independent. Thus $[L:K]=d$. For each $x$, the product over its distinct orbit elements of $T-\sigma(x)$ is a separable polynomial with invariant coefficients. Its minimal polynomial over $K$ divides it and splits in $L$. This proves $L/K$ is Galois, with precisely $G$ as its automorphism group. Also $S$ is the integral closure of $R$ in $L$, since any element integral over $R$ is integral over $S$ and lies in $S$ by normality.

Use now the full qualified G331 normal-target coefficient-norm trace theorem, including its proof of full fibre support on all semivaluations. For any $w\in\rho^{-1}(v)$ one may take the splitting field $L$ and the lift $w$ itself on its finite integral closure $S$. There is no inseparable multiplicity in characteristic zero. That theorem says the canonical trace measure is
\[
 \mu_v=\sum_{\sigma\in G}\delta_{w\circ\sigma},\qquad
 \operatorname{supp}\mu_v=\rho^{-1}(v). \tag{9}
\]
Thus each restriction fibre is exactly the $G$-orbit of any one of its points, with repeated group points counted in the measure. This use of G331 is essential: its coefficient identity is proved using valued quotient fraction fields after killing supports. We do not apply Galois extension theory to an original fraction field through a nonzero semivaluation support. Formula (9) retains all those supports and proves the needed full-fibre orbit assertion without deleting a singular stratum.

For every finite continuous signed obstacle $f$ on $V_{\mathfrak a}(R)$ set $F=f\circ\rho$. By n2 its greatest source geometric minorant $H_S=P_S(F)$ belongs to the continuous class $C_S$. Pullback by each automorphism preserves $C_S,D_S$ and $F$. By uniqueness of the greatest minorant, $H_S\circ\sigma=H_S$. Formula (9) makes $H_S$ constant on every restriction fibre. G331's positive continuous descent therefore yields a unique $H_R\in C_R$ with $\rho^*H_R=H_S$.

Surjectivity gives $H_R\le f$. If $u\in D_R$ and $u\le f$, its positive pullback lies in $D_S$ below $F$, so $\rho^*u\le H_S=\rho^*H_R$. Surjectivity again gives $u\le H_R$. Consequently
\[
 P_R(f)=H_R\in C_R,\qquad \rho^*P_R(f)=P_S(f\circ\rho), \tag{10}
\]
for every such $f$. This is actual geometric positivity and continuity, not positivity ascribed to an upper semicontinuous regularization. It applies to arbitrary continuous obstacles, including obstacles that are not model functions and without any canonical finite-generation hypothesis.

There is an explicit sequence of downstairs actual primary Cartier profiles. Let $B_m=A_m^S(F)$. These ideals are $G$-stable: replacing $w$ by $w\circ\sigma$ in their defining all-support inequalities proves this directly. Their profiles $h_m^S=-w(B_m)/m$ are therefore orbit constant. Define $J_m=\mathcal N_{L/K}(B_m)$, the coefficient norm ideal of G331. To spell out the construction, choose finite $R$-module generators $s_i$ of $B_m$, form
\[
 N_{L(T)/K(T)}\Big(\sum_i T_i s_i\Big)
 =\prod_{\sigma\in G}\Big(\sum_i T_i\sigma(s_i)\Big),
\]
and let $J_m$ be its coefficient ideal in $R$. Coefficients are integral over normal $R$ and lie in $K$, hence lie in $R$. G331 proves independence of generators and the all-support identity
\[
 v(J_m)=\sum_{\sigma\in G}(w\circ\sigma)(B_m)=d\,w(B_m). \tag{11}
\]
It also proves the ideal contains a primary power: $B_m$ contains $\mathfrak a^NS$, and pure-variable coefficients for base generators contain their $d$th powers. If the envelope is nonzero, $B_m$ is proper and (11) makes $J_m$ proper primary; the unit case gives the zero profile. Hence
\[
 \kappa_m=-v(J_m)/(dm),\qquad \rho^*\kappa_m=h_m^S,
\]
are actual geometric primary profiles below $f$ and converge uniformly to $P_R(f)$. This follows from n2's smooth continuity and n1's canonical uniform criterion; the source-to-target restriction is surjective, so the sup norms agree. The construction involves no finite flatness or determinant norm on an arbitrary finite module. It uses only the granted normal-target coefficient norm. The canonical ideals downstairs are also exactly $A_m^R(f)=B_m\cap R$, by the same all-support restriction argument as n1; we do not infer finite generation from this contraction.

For every signed real Cartier model obstacle on an actual primary model over $R$, a stronger bound is available. G331's exact evaluation formula for an integral exceptional Cartier divisor expresses it as a finite signed sum of primary ideal values with a fixed primary section correction; real finite presentations give real finite sums. Pulling these ideals to $S$ and using the smooth common principalization makes the maximal-ideal-gauge source obstacle a function determined on one BFJ dual complex. In n2's notation let $M,C$ be its fixed model constants and set
\[
 e=CM/\min_{\nu\in V_{\mathfrak m_S}(S)}\nu(b).
\]
The denominator is positive and bounded by primaryness. The exact gauge transport turns (8) into
\[
 0\le P_R(f)-\kappa_m\le e/m \quad\text{on all }V_{\mathfrak a}(R). \tag{12}
\]
In particular $J_m\subset A_{dm}^R(f)$ and $h_{dm}^R\ge\kappa_m$. To bound the \emph{full} downstairs canonical sequence, for $k\ge d$ put $m=\lfloor k/d\rfloor$ and $r=dm$, so $0\le k-r<d$. Grading with $(A_1^R)^{k-r}$ and nonpositivity gives
\[
 h_k^R\ge h_r^R-dM_1^R/k.
\]
Combining with (12), and using $m\ge k/(2d)$ for $k\ge2d$, gives
\[
 0\le P_R(f)-h_k^R
 \le \frac{e}{\lfloor k/d\rfloor}+\frac{dM_1^R}{k}
 \le\frac{2de+dM_1^R}{k}\qquad(k\ge2d). \tag{13}
\]
Every ideal used in (12)--(13) is unit or genuine primary in every degree. The constants depend on this obstacle and smooth model; the graded algebra need not be finitely generated. We assert no new finite-generation example or general excellent-germ bound. The primary correction is fixed for the obstacle, and all infinite generator values are accommodated by its finite primary-ideal values.

Here is an actual normal nonisolated higher-dimensional domain in the new theorem. For $r\ge1$, take
\[
 S=k[x,y,z_1,\ldots,z_r]_{(x,y,z_1,\ldots,z_r)},\quad
 G=\{1,\sigma\},\quad \sigma(x,y,z)=(-x,-y,z).
\]
The invariant monomials have even total $x,y$ degree and are generated by $a=x^2,b=xy,c=y^2,z_i$. Thus
\[

\]
The only relation is $ac=b^2$: monomials reduced by this relation have distinct images, and the image has the displayed dimension. The extension is finite, since $x,y$ satisfy their quadratic equations; localizing the invariant ring at the origin gives exactly the indicated local cover. To check localization of invariants explicitly, multiply any local denominator by its orbit product; the product is an invariant unit at the origin, and an invariant fraction then has invariant numerator. The cover's unique point above the origin is the origin. The rings are excellent finite-type local rings. Normality follows from the invariant argument already given. The dimension is $r+2$, and the singular locus is $(a,b,c)$, of dimension $r$: off it a derivative of $ac-b^2$ is a unit, whereas on it the local quadratic equation has no linear term and embedding dimension exceeds dimension by one. This is a normal nonisolated germ, not a nonnormal crossing example.

For a concrete continuous signed obstacle with cancellation sensitivity take $r=1$, $\mathfrak m=(a,b,c,z)$,
\[
 I=(a+b,b+c,z)+\mathfrak m^2,\qquad

\]
Both ideals are proper primary, so (14) is continuous and finite on every support. This defines a valuation after the injective substitution; its restriction gives $\mathfrak m$ value two. The sums $a+b=x(x+y)$ and $b+c=y(x+y)$ have weight three, so after normalization $v(I)=3/2$, while $v(J)=1$. A monomial valuation with $(x,y,z)$ weights $(1,1,6)$ gives the same values on $a,b,c,z$ but $v(I)=1$, $v(J)=1$. Thus the respective obstacles are $1/4+\sin(1)/100>0$ and $-1/4+\sin(1)/100<0$. They detect cancellation despite identical coordinate weights. The envelope of (14) is constructed by the $J_m$ profiles above and is continuous geometric; no closed formula or claim about finite generation for this example is made. Formula (10) applies to every other continuous signed obstacle on this germ as well, independently of any finite contact certificate.

Equations (10)--(13) obey the exact primary-gauge cocycle of n1; the canonical ideals are unchanged by gauge transport. Normalization/conductor compatibility always means EVERY fibre, including the infinite-value quotient stratum. Nilpotents reduce away, zero-dimensional reduction has empty boundary, the BFJ domain is exactly the published smooth affine CLOSED/algebraically closed/characteristic-zero domain, and the literal multibranch radial class stays distinct. \begin{abstract}
We reconstruct the canonical obstacle filtration on the entire boundary of an
excellent reduced local germ, retaining every support and every primary gauge.
At the exact published smooth hypotheses, the full BFJ model-envelope estimate
implies uniform primary approximation without finite generation; obstacle
density then gives every continuous signed obstacle. Using the qualified
G331 full-fibre coefficient trace, we prove continuous geometric envelopes for
all continuous obstacles on finite smooth invariant quotients. Signed real
Cartier model obstacles satisfy an explicit full-degree uniform error estimate.
Actual normal nonisolated quotient germs are included. The general excellent
normal/imperfect/mixed-characteristic residual and the entire inherited
historical proof audit remain open. All claims are unverified mathematical
drafts. ROOT handles compilation, publication and acceptance.

\section{Canonical ideals: reconstruction on the entire boundary}
\label{sec:canonical}
\textit{Support: the entire qualified G331 only. None of the current408 or historical notes is a correctness premise.}

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be excellent local. Semivaluations kill nilpotents, so throughout this section replace $R$ by $R_{\rm red}$. If this reduction has dimension zero its centred boundary is empty and all envelopes mean its unique empty function. Otherwise fix a proper $\mathfrak m$-primary ideal $\mathfrak a$ and the compact, nonempty section $X=V_{\mathfrak a}(R)$. Every prime support strictly below $\mathfrak m$ is retained. G331 supplies the independent geometric core: actual negative effective finite real Cartier presentations on directed actual primary blowups, with degree nonnegative on every contracted proper integral curve. Its uniform class $C$ and actual decreasing-net class $D$ equal the corresponding ideal classes. We use this qualified comparison, its rational-profile density, finite maxima, full-fibre positive descent, and its exact published smooth specialization. No envelope theorem is part of that grant.

For a finite continuous signed obstacle $f:X\to\mathbb R$ define
\[
 A_0=R,\qquad A_m=\{g\in R:\ v(g)+mf(v)\ge0\text{ for all }v\in X\}\quad(m\ge1),
 \qquad h_m=-v(A_m)/m.
\]
This definition uses no fraction field of $R$ and is meaningful also when $v(g)=+\infty$. Set $c=\max(0,-\min_X f)$. Any positive integer $N\ge mc$ gives $\mathfrak a^N\subset A_m$. The ultrametric inequality proves addition closure and nonnegative values on $R$ prove multiplication closure. If $f$ is negative at one point, no unit lies in any $A_m$, so every $A_m$ is proper primary. If $f\ge0$, every $A_m=R$. Thus $h_m$ is always a finite continuous unit-or-primary profile, is below $f$, and has actual geometric positivity by G331. In the proper case its presentation is $-E_{A_m}/m$ on the actual blowup of $A_m$; the negative exceptional bundle is relatively ample.

Multiplying the defining inequalities gives $A_mA_n\subset A_{m+n}$. Each $A_m$ is integrally closed as an ideal. Indeed, if $g$ satisfies a monic degree-$q$ equation with coefficient of index $i$ in $A_m^i$, then at a semivaluation where $v(g)<v(A_m)$ the leading term has uniquely least finite value. This contradicts the equation. All ideal values here are finite because $A_m$ contains a primary power. Infinite $v(g)$ imposes no difficulty.

Define only a raw function, without a positivity assertion,
\[
 p(f)=\sup\{u\in D:u\le f\}.
\]
We prove
\[
 p(f)=\sup\{u\in C:u\le f\}=\sup_{m\ge1}h_m.
 \tag{1}
\]
A rational unit-or-primary competitor $-v(I)/r\le f$ has $I\subset A_r$, and hence is below $h_r$. A $C$ competitor can be approximated uniformly by rational profiles and then shifted down by a rational negative $\mathfrak a$-constant. Such a shift is again a rational primary profile, by multiplication of ideals after clearing denominators. Sending the approximation error to zero proves the $C$ assertion. If $u=\inf_i g_i\le f$ in an actual decreasing $C$-net, the open sets $\{g_i<f+\epsilon\}$ cover $X$. Directedness and compactness select one index valid everywhere. The function $g_i-\epsilon\in C$ is a competitor and $u\le\sup_m h_m+\epsilon$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This step uses continuity of $f$, not continuity of $u$; bottom and partial poles are permitted. The reverse inequalities follow because each $h_m$ is itself a $D$ competitor.

Put $M_1=\|v(A_1)\|_\infty$ and $H_N=\max_{1\le r\le N}h_r\in C$. Write $m=kr+s$, $0\le s<r$. The inclusion $A_r^kA_1^s\subset A_m$, together with $h_r\le0$, gives
\[
 h_m\ge \frac{kr}{m}h_r-\frac{s}{m}M_1
 \ge h_r-\frac{rM_1}{m},\qquad
 H_N-\frac{NM_1}{m}\le h_m\le p(f).
 \tag{2}
\]
These estimates hold on every support, even when generator values are infinite. In particular the full degree sequence converges pointwise to $p(f)$. The function $p(f)$ is finite, nonpositive and lower semicontinuous, bounded below by $h_1$.

The following exact criterion is not a solution of general continuity:
\[
 p(f)\text{ continuous}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_N\to p(f)\text{ uniformly}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_m\to p(f)\text{ uniformly}. \tag{3}
\]
For the forward implication the increasing strict error-test open sets for $H_N$ cover compact $X$, so one $N$ works uniformly. Equation (2) then gives uniform convergence of the full sequence. Conversely a uniform limit lies in the closed geometric class $C$, so is continuous and is the greatest $D$ minorant by (1). We do not declare an upper semicontinuous regularization positive.

The raw envelope is monotone and satisfies
\[
 \|p(f)-p(g)\|_\infty\le\|f-g\|_\infty. \tag{4}
\]
If $f\le g+\epsilon$, any $D$ minorant $u$ of $f$ has $u-\epsilon\in D$ below $g$. The shift belongs to $D$ by adding a fixed negative primary profile to its defining decreasing net. Supremizing proves the one-sided inequality; reversing $f,g$ proves (4). Consequently uniform approximation by obstacles whose envelopes are already in $C$ proves a $C$ envelope for the limit. This is an implication, not a general density assertion.

For completeness we independently reconstruct the finite-generation reduction. Suppose $\mathcal A=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}A_mt^m$ is generated by homogeneous $g_it^{d_i}$, $d_i>0$. Let $L$ be a common multiple of the degrees, $D_0=\max d_i$, and $J=(g_i^{L/d_i})_i$. On each support some generator has finite value: otherwise the degree-one ideal $A_1$ would have infinite value. Every degree-$m$ expression has value at least $m\min_i v(g_i)/d_i$. Moreover $J\subset A_L$, so
\[
 h_m\le -v(J)/L\le h_L\le p(f).
\]
The middle profile is therefore $p(f)=h_L$, and it is also $\max_{r\le D_0}h_r$ by using a generator attaining the finite minimum. The radical of the generator coefficient ideal contains $A_1$, so $J$ is primary in the proper case. Equation (2) gives
\[
 0\le p(f)-h_m\le D_0M_1/m. \tag{5}
\]
The unit case is immediate.

Conversely, if $p(f)=-v(J)/q$ for a proper primary $J$ and positive integer $q$, then the definition and (1) imply
\[
 A_m=\{g:v(g)\ge (m/q)v(J)\text{ on all }X\}
     =\{g:g^q\in\overline{J^m}\}. \tag{6}
\]
For the second equality apply the centred rank-one DVR integral-closure criterion to each minimal-component quotient and then the all-minimal-component criterion (Swanson--Huneke 6.8.3--4 and 1.1.5). Every such quotient has positive dimension: a zero-dimensional minimal component of a local reduced ring would make its maximal ideal minimal and the whole ring zero-dimensional. The images of $J$ and $\mathfrak a$ are primary, and each centred DVR normalizes into $X$. Monic ideal-integrality equations give the reverse inequalities on all other supports as well, by the same uniquely least finite term argument. These are applications of the complete immediate published units, read afresh; their deeper valuation-domination foundations are disclosed in the ledger.

Set $B=R[Jt^q]$. Primary $J$ contains a regular element by finite prime avoidance. Thus $B$ is reduced excellent and its total quotient ring is $\prod_j K_j(t^q)$, with $K_j=\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p_j)$. Its finite extension $\prod_j K_j(t)$ may be inseparable. The standard excellent/Nagata finite-normalization property makes the integral closure of $B$ in that extension finite over $B$. An equation for $g^q$ over $J^m$, multiplied by powers of $t^{mq}$, makes $g^qt^{mq}$ integral over $B$, and then $gt^m$ integral by its $q$th-power equation. Hence $B\subset\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal A$ is a $B$-submodule of that finite normalization. Noetherianity makes it finite over $B$, hence finitely generated over $R$. The same statement for the zero envelope is $\mathcal A=R[t]$. A finite maximum of canonical profiles is a rational unit-or-primary profile, by ideal sums after clearing denominators. We have proved equivalence of finite generation, rational primary attainment, and finite canonical-max attainment, without assuming any of them generally.

For a signed integral exceptional Cartier obstacle $f_D$ on an actual primary blowup of a normal $R$, let $Y$ be its finite normalization, with the pulled-back divisor and its canonical rational trivialization. There is an exact model computation
\[
 A_m(f_D)=H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y(mD))\cap R. \tag{6a}
\]
Testing the all-boundary inequalities at the finitely many height-one exceptional orders gives the section inequalities there; at other height-one primes $D$ is zero and $g\in R$ is already regular. Normal height-one intersection proves that $g$ is a section. Conversely a section pulls back to the valuation ring of $\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)$ at every semivaluation support. The generic point is outside the closed exceptional fibre, so the invertible bundle has its canonical nonzero trivialization there. If its local generator is $b$, then the section has $v(g)-v(b)\ge0$, and $v(b)=-mf_D(v)$. This yields the canonical inequality on every support, with infinite $v(g)$ automatic. Properness gives the valued centre; no total quotient field is mapped through a nonminimal support. For a rational divisor use denominator multiples. The finite generation of this particular section-intersection algebra is a hypothesis to establish in any application, not a theorem for arbitrary signed model obstacles.

For another primary gauge $\mathfrak b$, put $d(v)=v(\mathfrak b)>0$ and $T(v)=v/d(v)$. If $f_{\mathfrak b}(Tv)=f_{\mathfrak a}(v)/d(v)$, then
\[
 (Tv)(g)+mf_{\mathfrak b}(Tv)=(v(g)+mf_{\mathfrak a}(v))/d(v).
\]
The canonical ideals and graded algebra are literally unchanged. Profiles and raw envelopes divide by $d$; substitution gives the three-gauge cocycle. Uniform errors divide by the positive minimum of $d$. For the finite normalization $S$ of $R$, surjective restriction gives $A_m^R=A_m^S\cap R$. This includes every conductor-infinite quotient fibre; it does not assert that contraction preserves finite generation. If the source geometric envelope exists and is constant on every normalization fibre, G331's positive descent supplies the downstairs envelope: it is below $f$ and dominates every pulled-back downstairs competitor. Compatibility of the obstacle alone is not sufficient.

If a decreasing directed family of continuous obstacles has envelopes $H_i\in C$, then $H=\inf_iH_i\in D$ is the envelope of their infimum: every minorant of the infimum is below every $H_i$, and $H$ is below every obstacle. This uses an actual decreasing net and no flattening. For excellent reduced curves the finite normalization centres are DVRs. A regular conductor element has finite order on each, so all boundary fibres are singleton. The independent geometric DVR core has every finite nonpositive real slope, with no contracted curves. Positive descent yields the entire nonpositive finite orthant; decreasing truncations yield the extended orthant. Consequently $P(f)=\min(f,0)$ geometrically, at every branch. The literal classical/CLD multibranch radial class still excludes mixed-zero profiles and is not identified with this boundary class.

On a DVR, $f=-\alpha$ with $\alpha>0$ irrational gives $A_m=(x^{\lceil m\alpha\rceil})$ and the continuous real Cartier envelope $-\alpha$. Finite homogeneous generators would force a rational minimum order/degree ratio, contradicting the limiting slope $\alpha$. Thus finite generation is not necessary for continuity. This diagnoses the limitation of (5), rather than an envelope failure.


\section{Smooth continuous envelopes from the complete BFJ model estimate}
\label{sec:smooth}
\textit{Support: G331 and earlier own n1 (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}). The BFJ envelope estimate is a new published application, not an envelope grant imported from G331.}

In this section only, $S$ is the local ring at a smooth closed point of an affine variety over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field. We first use its maximal-ideal gauge. Dimension at least two is the exact BFJ setting; the DVR and empty cases were treated directly in n1. Completion and primary contraction are those of G331 and transport functions on every semivaluation, not merely fraction-field valuations.

We apply Boucksom--Favre--Jonsson, \emph{Valuations and plurisubharmonic singularities}, Proposition~3.18, including its entire immediate proof and Lemma~3.22, together with its stated function version Remark~3.21. Definitions~3.15--3.17 and the immediate preceding multiplier-ideal units were read in full. The setting, retractions, closed-simplex continuity and all-retraction extension are precisely the published ones. Smooth principalization and usual multiplier-ideal subadditivity are named deeper foundations; they are not extended to singular or positive-characteristic germs. The reading ledger gives the complete windows and the boundary of this source audit.

Let $F$ be a finite continuous function determined on a single BFJ dual complex: $F=F\circ r_{\pi_0}$. A signed real linear combination of primary ideal values has this property on a common principalization (BFJ~1.14), and these functions are uniformly dense (1.15, also G331's independently proved lattice density). Set $M=\max(0,-\min F)$. The constant $-M$ is a nef primary real profile below $F$.

Consider the weak nef Weil envelope
\[
 W=\sup\{Z:Z\text{ nef},\ Z\le Z(F)\}.
\]
This is a finite nef Weil divisor: restrict the competitors by replacing them with their maximum with the barrier $-M$; maxima preserve nefness and the obstacle bound. They form a directed family with finite coefficient bounds $-M\le Z\le0$. Their componentwise limit lies in the weakly closed nef cone. Thus $-M\le W\le0$ and $W\le Z(F)$. This is the published Definition~3.17 construction, with its bounds made explicit.

By BFJ~3.11 let $H$ be its formal psh function, extended to every semivaluation by
\[
 H(v)=\inf_{\pi}H(r_\pi v).
\]
The inequality $H\le F$ holds on all supports. On every closed simplex it follows from the coefficient inequality and density of its divisorial rational points, using the actual closed-simplex continuity theorem. For $\pi\ge\pi_0$, $r_{\pi_0}r_\pi=r_{\pi_0}$, hence $F(r_\pi v)=F(v)$. Taking the infimum over that cofinal family gives $H(v)\le F(v)$. Also $H\ge-M$ everywhere. Every nonbottom $u\in D$ below $F$ is, by the full qualified smooth comparison in G331, a BFJ formal psh function with nef coefficients below $Z(F)$. Those coefficients are below $W$, and their all-retraction extensions are below $H$. The bottom function is harmless. Thus $H=p_S(F)$ as a raw function, and $H$ is already an actual $D$ envelope. Its continuity is still to be proved.

Put $B_m=L^\infty(mW)$ in the completed ring, using BFJ~3.15. By 3.17,
\[
 L^\infty(mW)=L^\infty(mZ(F)). \tag{7}
\]
These ideals contain the primary power $\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\lceil mM\rceil}$, with a positive power chosen when necessary. In the nonzero-envelope case they are proper. After exact primary contraction they are exactly the canonical ideals of n1 for $F$.

Here is a complete check of the latter assertion on all supports. The canonical inequality implies the coefficient tests at every divisorial point. Conversely let a formal $g$ pass those coefficient tests, and choose $N\ge mM$, $N>0$. The primary-or-unit ideal $(g)+\widehat{\mathfrak m}^N$ has divisorial profile
\[
 \log|(g)+\widehat{\mathfrak m}^N|=\max(\log|g|,-N)\le mF.
\]
Its profile is a BFJ all-retraction extension and a continuous geometric ideal profile. As in the preceding paragraph, the divisorial inequality extends through the closed simplices and all refinements of $\pi_0$ to every support. Since $v(g)\ge v((g)+\widehat{\mathfrak m}^N)$, it gives $v(g)+mF(v)\ge0$ everywhere, including infinite $v(g)$. The completion homeomorphism of G331 then contracts $B_m$ precisely to $A_m^S(F)$. This argument does not map the original fraction field through a nonminimal support and does not divide an infinite value.

If $W=0$, then $0\le F$ on the dense divisorial points and hence on the whole space, and the envelope and all profiles are zero. Otherwise BFJ~3.14 gives strict negativity of $H$, uniformly bounded above by a negative constant. On the fixed compact dual complex, thinness $A$ is bounded and $H$ is continuous and strictly negative. Choose a finite constant $C>0$ as in Proposition~3.18; its proof allows $C$ with $A\le-CW$ on this single complex. It uses thinness only there, not on the entire boundary.

Write $W_t=t^{-1}Z(L^\infty(tW))$ for positive real $t$. The published inequality 3.18(iii) says
\[
 W_t\le W\le (1-C/t)W_{t-C}\qquad(t>C).
\] At $t=m+C$ this implies
\[
 (1+C/m)W\le W_m\le W.
\]
Every displayed coefficient inequality extends to all semivaluations by closed-simplex continuity and the infimum over all retractions. The extension of $W_m$ is exactly $h_m=-v(A_m^S(F))/m$. Since $-M\le H\le0$, we obtain the uniform, all-support estimate
\[
 0\le H-h_m\le CM/m\qquad(m\ge1). \tag{8}
\]
Thus $H$ is a uniform limit of actual positive primary Cartier profiles and belongs to the continuous independently geometric class $C$. No finite generation of the canonical algebra was used. This is an obstacle-dependent primary approximation obtained from a smooth-model estimate, with every infinity-support endpoint included. It does not use a singular Jacobian correction.

Now let $F$ be any finite continuous signed obstacle on the smooth boundary. Choose signed primary model functions $F_j\to F$ uniformly by the complete density statement. Their envelopes $H_j\in C$ exist by (8). The raw Lipschitz estimate (4) makes $H_j$ uniformly Cauchy and identifies its limit with $p_S(F)$. Uniform closedness of the independently geometric class proves that $p_S(F)\in C$ and is the greatest $D$ minorant. This establishes arbitrary continuous-obstacle regularity at the precise published smooth hypotheses, rather than assuming it as an extra G331 grant.

All primary gauges follow the exact homogeneous transport of n1. If $\nu$ has maximal-ideal normalization and $b$ is another primary gauge, then $w=\nu/\nu(b)$ and $F_{\mathfrak m}(\nu)=\nu(b)F_b(w)$. For a signed primary model obstacle, $F_{\mathfrak m}$ is still a signed real primary model function. Estimate (8) in the $b$ gauge divides by $\nu(b)$, whose positive minimum is finite on the compact section. For arbitrary continuous obstacles the same transport preserves continuity and the greatest-minorant property. None of these statements applies BFJ to a smooth formal germ outside its algebraic closed-point domain: completion transport supplies precisely the already granted function identification, not an enlarged source theorem.


\section{Arbitrary continuous obstacles on finite smooth quotient germs}
\label{sec:quotient}
\textit{Support: the entire qualified G331 and earlier own n1,n2. This is new scoped original-residual progress, not a theorem for every excellent normal germ.}

Suppose $S$ is a positive-dimensional smooth affine closed-germ local domain over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, and a finite group $G$ acts faithfully by local automorphisms. Assume $R=S^G$ is excellent Noetherian and $S$ is finite over $R$; these hypotheses hold for the algebraic quotient example below. The ring $R$ is a normal local domain: an element of $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ integral over $R$ is integral over $S$, hence belongs to the normal ring $S$, and, being invariant, belongs to $R$. Fix a proper primary $\mathfrak a\subset R$, put $b=\mathfrak aS$, and let
\[
 \rho:V_b(S)\longrightarrow V_{\mathfrak a}(R)
\]
be restriction. This map is continuous surjective by G331, including semivaluations with nonminimal supports. Both the obstacle and the normalizing source ideal $b$ are invariant.

We need the entire fibres, not just field valuations. Let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(S)$. Then $L^G=K$: if $s/t\in L^G$, multiply its denominator by the finite product of its $G$-translates; that product lies in $R$, and the resulting invariant numerator lies in $R$. Here is the needed fixed-field argument, so no unpublished fibre-transitivity theorem is assumed. Distinct automorphisms $\sigma_i$ are linearly independent as $L$-valued functions on $L$: in a relation with the fewest nonzero coefficients, evaluate at $ax$ and subtract $\sigma_j(a)$ times the relation at $x$. Choosing $a$ on which two distinct automorphisms differ produces a shorter nonzero relation, a contradiction; a one-term relation is impossible by evaluating at $1$. Consequently the evaluation columns $(\sigma_i(x))_i$ span $L^d$, for otherwise a nonzero annihilating row would give such a relation. Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ with invertible evaluation matrix. For arbitrary $x\in L$, solve
\[
 \sigma_i(x)=\sum_j c_j\sigma_i(x_j)\quad\text{for every }\sigma_i\in G.
\]
Applying any $\tau\in G$ permutes the rows, so uniqueness forces $\tau(c_j)=c_j$. Hence $c_j\in K$, and the identity row writes $x=\sum_jc_jx_j$. The invertible matrix also proves the $x_j$ are $K$-linearly independent. Thus $[L:K]=d$. For each $x$, the product over its distinct orbit elements of $T-\sigma(x)$ is a separable polynomial with invariant coefficients. Its minimal polynomial over $K$ divides it and splits in $L$. This proves $L/K$ is Galois, with precisely $G$ as its automorphism group. Also $S$ is the integral closure of $R$ in $L$, since any element integral over $R$ is integral over $S$ and lies in $S$ by normality.

Use now the full qualified G331 normal-target coefficient-norm trace theorem, including its proof of full fibre support on all semivaluations. For any $w\in\rho^{-1}(v)$ one may take the splitting field $L$ and the lift $w$ itself on its finite integral closure $S$. There is no inseparable multiplicity in characteristic zero. That theorem says the canonical trace measure is
\[
 \mu_v=\sum_{\sigma\in G}\delta_{w\circ\sigma},\qquad
 \operatorname{supp}\mu_v=\rho^{-1}(v). \tag{9}
\]
Thus each restriction fibre is exactly the $G$-orbit of any one of its points, with repeated group points counted in the measure. This use of G331 is essential: its coefficient identity is proved using valued quotient fraction fields after killing supports. We do not apply Galois extension theory to an original fraction field through a nonzero semivaluation support. Formula (9) retains all those supports and proves the needed full-fibre orbit assertion without deleting a singular stratum.

For every finite continuous signed obstacle $f$ on $V_{\mathfrak a}(R)$ set $F=f\circ\rho$. By n2 its greatest source geometric minorant $H_S=P_S(F)$ belongs to the continuous class $C_S$. Pullback by each automorphism preserves $C_S,D_S$ and $F$. By uniqueness of the greatest minorant, $H_S\circ\sigma=H_S$. Formula (9) makes $H_S$ constant on every restriction fibre. G331's positive continuous descent therefore yields a unique $H_R\in C_R$ with $\rho^*H_R=H_S$.

Surjectivity gives $H_R\le f$. If $u\in D_R$ and $u\le f$, its positive pullback lies in $D_S$ below $F$, so $\rho^*u\le H_S=\rho^*H_R$. Surjectivity again gives $u\le H_R$. Consequently
\[
 P_R(f)=H_R\in C_R,\qquad \rho^*P_R(f)=P_S(f\circ\rho), \tag{10}
\]
for every such $f$. This is actual geometric positivity and continuity, not positivity ascribed to an upper semicontinuous regularization. It applies to arbitrary continuous obstacles, including obstacles that are not model functions and without any canonical finite-generation hypothesis.

There is an explicit sequence of downstairs actual primary Cartier profiles. Let $B_m=A_m^S(F)$. These ideals are $G$-stable: replacing $w$ by $w\circ\sigma$ in their defining all-support inequalities proves this directly. Their profiles $h_m^S=-w(B_m)/m$ are therefore orbit constant. Define $J_m=\mathcal N_{L/K}(B_m)$, the coefficient norm ideal of G331. To spell out the construction, choose finite $R$-module generators $s_i$ of $B_m$, form
\[
 N_{L(T)/K(T)}\Big(\sum_i T_i s_i\Big)
 =\prod_{\sigma\in G}\Big(\sum_i T_i\sigma(s_i)\Big),
\]
and let $J_m$ be its coefficient ideal in $R$. Coefficients are integral over normal $R$ and lie in $K$, hence lie in $R$. G331 proves independence of generators and the all-support identity
\[
 v(J_m)=\sum_{\sigma\in G}(w\circ\sigma)(B_m)=d\,w(B_m). \tag{11}
\]
It also proves the ideal contains a primary power: $B_m$ contains $\mathfrak a^NS$, and pure-variable coefficients for base generators contain their $d$th powers. If the envelope is nonzero, $B_m$ is proper and (11) makes $J_m$ proper primary; the unit case gives the zero profile. Hence
\[
 \kappa_m=-v(J_m)/(dm),\qquad \rho^*\kappa_m=h_m^S,
\]
are actual geometric primary profiles below $f$ and converge uniformly to $P_R(f)$. This follows from n2's smooth continuity and n1's canonical uniform criterion; the source-to-target restriction is surjective, so the sup norms agree. The construction involves no finite flatness or determinant norm on an arbitrary finite module. It uses only the granted normal-target coefficient norm. The canonical ideals downstairs are also exactly $A_m^R(f)=B_m\cap R$, by the same all-support restriction argument as n1; we do not infer finite generation from this contraction.

For every signed real Cartier model obstacle on an actual primary model over $R$, a stronger bound is available. G331's exact evaluation formula for an integral exceptional Cartier divisor expresses it as a finite signed sum of primary ideal values with a fixed primary section correction; real finite presentations give real finite sums. Pulling these ideals to $S$ and using the smooth common principalization makes the maximal-ideal-gauge source obstacle a function determined on one BFJ dual complex. In n2's notation let $M,C$ be its fixed model constants and set
\[
 e=CM/\min_{\nu\in V_{\mathfrak m_S}(S)}\nu(b).
\]
The denominator is positive and bounded by primaryness. The exact gauge transport turns (8) into
\[
 0\le P_R(f)-\kappa_m\le e/m \quad\text{on all }V_{\mathfrak a}(R). \tag{12}
\]
In particular $J_m\subset A_{dm}^R(f)$ and $h_{dm}^R\ge\kappa_m$. To bound the \emph{full} downstairs canonical sequence, for $k\ge d$ put $m=\lfloor k/d\rfloor$ and $r=dm$, so $0\le k-r<d$. Grading with $(A_1^R)^{k-r}$ and nonpositivity gives
\[
 h_k^R\ge h_r^R-dM_1^R/k.
\]
Combining with (12), and using $m\ge k/(2d)$ for $k\ge2d$, gives
\[
 0\le P_R(f)-h_k^R
 \le \frac{e}{\lfloor k/d\rfloor}+\frac{dM_1^R}{k}
 \le\frac{2de+dM_1^R}{k}\qquad(k\ge2d). \tag{13}
\]
Every ideal used in (12)--(13) is unit or genuine primary in every degree. The constants depend on this obstacle and smooth model; the graded algebra need not be finitely generated. We assert no new finite-generation example or general excellent-germ bound. The primary correction is fixed for the obstacle, and all infinite generator values are accommodated by its finite primary-ideal values.

\[

\]
The invariant monomials have even total $x,y$ degree and are generated by $a=x^2,b=xy,c=y^2,z_i$. Thus

\]
The only relation is $ac=b^2$: monomials reduced by this relation have distinct images, and the image has the displayed dimension. The extension is finite, since $x,y$ satisfy their quadratic equations; localizing the invariant ring at the origin gives exactly the indicated local cover. To check localization of invariants explicitly, multiply any local denominator by its orbit product; the product is an invariant unit at the origin, and an invariant fraction then has invariant numerator. The cover's unique point above the origin is the origin. The rings are excellent finite-type local rings. Normality follows from the invariant argument already given. The dimension is $r+2$, and the singular locus is $(a,b,c)$, of dimension $r$: off it a derivative of $ac-b^2$ is a unit, whereas on it the local quadratic equation has no linear term and embedding dimension exceeds dimension by one. \]
Both ideals are proper primary, so (14) is continuous and finite on every support. \section*{Main theorem and proof map}
Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be excellent local and replace it by its reduction.
For every proper primary $\mathfrak a$, let $V_{\mathfrak a}$ be the compact
section of centred real semivaluations with $v(\mathfrak a)=1$, retaining every
prime support. Define $Q$ by finite nonnegative real sums of negative
unit-or-primary ideal values, $C$ by uniform closure, and $D$ by actual infima
of nonempty decreasing $C$-nets, with bottom allowed.

On actual primary blowups, take actual negative effective finite real Cartier
presentations having nonnegative degree on every contracted proper integral
curve. Their evaluations define $M_{\rm geom}$ independently of ideal
positivity. Then
\[
 Q\subset M_{\rm geom}\subset C,\qquad
 C_{\rm geom}=C,\qquad D_{\rm geom}=D.
\]
For every reduced finite injection, the pullback image of either completed
class is precisely its full-fibre-constant subclass. Normalization fibres are
singletons at finite conductor value and precisely conductor-quotient fibres
at infinite value. Primary changes obey the exact homogeneous cocycle.
At a smooth affine closed germ over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero
field, $C$ is exactly the finite continuous BFJ subclass and $D$ is the full
BFJ all-semivaluation extension with the identically bottom function adjoined.
Smooth DVR and empty dimension zero are direct.

give full algebraic descent; n7 discharges the exact published geometric inputs;

\section{n1. Boundary, finite lifting, conductor fibres, and completion}
\textit{Earlier local supports: none.}

All rings below are commutative. For a Noetherian local ring \((R,\mathfrak m)\), a centred real semivaluation is a map to \([0,+\infty]\) satisfying \(v(0)=+\infty\), \(v(1)=0\), multiplicativity, the ultrametric inequality, and \(0<v(\mathfrak m)<+\infty\). Its support \(v^{-1}(+\infty)\) is a prime strictly below \(\mathfrak m\); no minimal-support restriction is imposed. Ideal values are minima over finite generating sets. Relations between generating sets prove independence and
\[
v(IJ)=v(I)+v(J),\qquad v(I+J)=\min\{v(I),v(J)\}.
\]
Units have value zero. A proper primary ideal always means primary for the marked maximal ideal.

Fix a proper primary ideal \(\mathfrak a\). The section \(V_{\mathfrak a}(R)=\{v:v(\mathfrak a)=1\}\) is compact Hausdorff. Indeed semivaluation axioms and \(v(\mathfrak m)=1\) are closed conditions in the compact product \([0,+\infty]^R\); addition, minimum and the order relation have the required continuity/closedness. Choose \(\mathfrak m^r\subset\mathfrak a\subset\mathfrak m^s\), with \(r\ge s\ge1\). Then \(s v(\mathfrak m)\le v(\mathfrak a)\le r v(\mathfrak m)\). Rescaling identifies the two sections. Every primary ideal value is finite positive continuous and bounded there. For another primary ideal \(\mathfrak b\),
\[
H_{\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b}(v)=v/v(\mathfrak b),\qquad
u_{\mathfrak b}(H_{\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b}v)=u_{\mathfrak a}(v)/v(\mathfrak b).
\]
The denominator and its inverse are bounded. Substitution proves the inverse and the exact three-gauge cocycle. The centred cone is the product of its section and the positive radial coordinate \(v(\mathfrak a)\); hence these sections represent its intrinsic ray quotient. Nonprimary proper ideals give only their open finite-value domain, which can be noncompact. Units and zero ideals have no level-one section.

Nilpotents have infinite value. Comparing \(f+n\) and \((f+n)-n\) proves that reduction preserves every semivaluation and ideal gauge. A zero-dimensional reduced local ring is a field and has empty centred boundary. For a positive-dimensional excellent reduced local ring, a penultimate prime of a saturated chain to the maximal ideal gives a one-dimensional excellent domain quotient. Its finite normalization has a local DVR factor, whose order pulls back and normalizes into the section. This proves nonemptiness. Ordinary background used throughout is lying over, prime avoidance, finite Artinian decompositions, and the quotient/finite-type-localization stability, Nagata finiteness and universal catenarity consequences of excellence. None is used to assert resolution in arbitrary characteristic.

Every finite integral injection \(R\hookrightarrow B\), with \(B\) reduced and nonzero, gives a continuous surjective restriction \(V_{\mathfrak aB}(B)\to V_{\mathfrak a}(R)\). Here a finite algebra has the finite union of its closed-centre sections above \(\mathfrak m\). To lift \(v\) with support \(\mathfrak p\), choose a prime \(P\) of \(B\) above \(\mathfrak p\) and form the finite field extension \(\operatorname{Frac}(B/P)/\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)\). Extend the valuation ring by taking the integral closure, a prime over its maximal ideal, and a dominating valuation ring. The domination assertion follows from Zorn: in a maximal dominating local subring, either adjoining \(x\) or \(x^{-1}\) leaves the maximal ideal proper. If \(1=\sum a_i x^{-i}\) with all \(a_i\) in that ideal, multiplying by a power and dividing by \(1-a_0\) makes \(x\) integral, so lying over makes the ideal proper after adjoining \(x\). Localizing contradicts maximality unless one of the two elements already belongs. Intersection with the old field is the original valuation ring: an element outside it has inverse in its maximal ideal. An algebraic equation for any new nonzero field element has two least-valued terms; thus an integer multiple of its value is in the old value group. Dividing this old real value by the integer gives a well-defined order-preserving real embedding, using common multiples. Integral elements have nonnegative value by the least-term test for a monic equation. Compose with \(B\to B/P\), assigning \(P\) infinite value. This construction first kills the support; it never extends a nonzero-support semivaluation to the original fraction field. Compactness makes restriction a quotient map.

Let \(S\) be the finite normalization of an excellent reduced \(R\), and \(\mathfrak c=(R:S)\). Clearing denominators of finitely many generators of \(S\) gives a regular conductor element. The conductor is an ideal of both rings and
\[
R=S\times_{S/\mathfrak c}(R/\mathfrak c).
\]
An element of \(S\) whose residue comes from \(R\) differs from an element of \(R\) by an element of \(\mathfrak c\), proving this identity. The normalization boundary is the finite disjoint union of local normal centres above \(\mathfrak m\). Idempotents choose a minimal component; localization at its centre changes no values of denominators. Chinese remainder elements separating the finitely many centres, and their complements, have open positive-value loci selecting these pieces. The pieces are therefore clopen. Branches mean these local centres, not merely minimal primes.

If \(v(\mathfrak c)<+\infty\), choose \(c\in\mathfrak c\) of finite value. Every lift satisfies \(w(s)=v(cs)-v(c)\), so it is unique. The subtracted number is finite. If \(v(\mathfrak c)=+\infty\), all lifts kill the conductor, and equality after restriction \(S/\mathfrak c\to R/\mathfrak c\) is exactly their identification. This infinity stratum is closed; its finite complement is open, without a closedness claim. A fibre-constant continuous function descends continuously by the compact quotient. A fibre-constant extended nonpositive upper semicontinuous function descends upper semicontinuously: its closed superlevel sets have compact, hence closed, images. These assertions alone supply no positivity descent.

Completion preserves the entire boundary for every Noetherian local ring. For \(F\in\widehat R\), choose representatives \(F_N\) modulo \(\mathfrak m^N\), and put \(d=v(\mathfrak m)>0\). Differences have value at least \(Nd\). If some \(v(F_N)<Nd\), later values stabilize; otherwise they tend to infinity. Define \(\widehat v(F)\) by this limit. It is independent of representatives and satisfies
\[
\min\{\widehat v(F),Nd\}=\min\{v(F_N),Nd\}.
\]
Applying this to sums and products proves all axioms and uniqueness, including infinite values; completed units have unit representatives. Compose with \(q(t)=t/(1+t)\), \(q(+\infty)=1\). The displayed continuous truncations have uniform error at most \((1+N/r)^{-1}\), because \(d\ge1/r\). Thus completed evaluation is continuous and completion restriction is a homeomorphism. Every completed primary \(J\) contains \(\widehat{\mathfrak m}^N\). Representatives modulo that power of its generators belong to \(J\cap R\) and, with the boundary power, generate \(J\). Hence \(J=(J\cap R)\widehat R\). The quotient isomorphism also proves contraction of an extended primary ideal recovers it. Unit-or-primary profiles and their uniform and decreasing classes therefore agree under completion. No equivalence of geometric model categories is asserted.

This is a mathematical argument with the stated ordinary background. Swanson--Huneke 6.4.1--2 were read in full and agree with the domination proof. Artifact n1.md is authoritative and is reproduced in argument.md and the paper. Rerun: python audit\_inputs.py; python build\_delivery.py. Execution does not verify the mathematics.

\section{n2. Exact algebraic applications and their qualifications}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1.}

Use n1 for boundary conventions. The following are ordinary published theorem applications at their stated hypotheses, with their immediate units checked from the bound primary data. This is not an independent reconstruction of all historical proofs.

Swanson--Huneke is the current author PDF created July 2024, not asserted byte-identical to the 2006 printing. Its complete 6.8.1--4 statements and proofs give the following consequence. Let \(E\) be Noetherian semilocal, \(J\) contain a boundary power, and \(Q\) be a finite ideal. If every normalized centred semivaluation satisfies \(w(Q)\ge w(J)\), and \(Q\) has zero image on every zero-dimensional minimal component where \(J\) is nonunit, then
\[
Q\subset\overline J.
\]
Apply 6.8.4 on each positive-dimensional local domain component, normalizing each centred rank-one DVR by the boundary ideal. Apply 6.8.3 to all minimal components. On zero-dimensional components there are no boundary points; the extra zero-image condition is needed. In all uses below \(Q=K(\mathfrak aE)^L\), with \(L>0\), so this condition holds. Unit components of \(J\) impose no condition. For nonreduced \(E\), lift the componentwise monic equations, multiply them over the finitely many minimal primes, then raise to a power to kill the nilpotent error. The resulting equation is monic with degree-i coefficients in \(J^i\). This is the finite-minimal-prime argument of 1.1.5, also read completely. PDF inspection of printed page 140 confirmed the integral-closure bars omitted in the text extraction.

The common exponent needed later has a short direct proof. Each \(qt\), \(q\in Q\), is integral over \(E[Jt]\) with its homogeneous ideal-integrality equation. Thus \(E[(J+Q)t]\) is finite graded over \(E[Jt]\). Choose homogeneous module generators of degrees at most \(h\). Its degree \(N+h\) terms have coefficients in \(J^{N+h-d}\subset J^N\). Consequently
\[
Q^{N+h}\subset (J+Q)^{N+h}\subset J^N\quad(N\ge1).
\]
This works for nonreduced rings and assumes no finiteness of the full normalized Rees algebra. The complete 1.2.3--5 reduction chain was checked too; printed page 6 confirms the criterion uses integral closure.

For an excellent local domain \(A\) of positive dimension and a nonzero proper primary ideal, 10.2.2, including its proof ending at 10.2.3, constructs finitely many Rees DVRs centred at the closed point. The full 10.4.3 proof gives their residue transcendence degree \(\dim A-1\) when \(A\) is formally equidimensional. Excellence supplies universal catenarity, and the full B.5.1 statement/proof identifies this with local formal equidimensionality for Noetherian domains. B.3.2 and its immediate context give, for a finite-type birational domain \(B\) over excellent local domain \(A\), and \(P\cap A=\mathfrak m\),
\[
\dim B_P+\operatorname{trdeg}_{A/\mathfrak m}\kappa(P)=\dim A.
\]
The book describes B.3.2's proof as a modification of an earlier dimension argument. Its recursive historical dependencies, including Mori--Nagata and Ratliff, are disclosed rather than claimed independently read.

Stacks 0C23, full immediate HTML lemma/proof, states that normal Noetherian local rings with normal formal fibres have normal completion; excellence suffices. Its proof refers to Algebra 10.163.8, not recursively read. A normal local completed ring is a domain. Thus an excellent normal local domain is analytically irreducible and analytically unramified. This is not claimed for an arbitrary nonnormal domain.

Exact Rond--Spivakovsky arXiv 1404.4885v1, complete pages 1--2 definitions and statements 1.3, 1.4 and 1.7, yields an order bound at precisely this analytic domain. For a centred divisorial valuation \(\nu\) and the finitely many maximal-ideal Rees valuations \(\nu_j\), 1.3 gives \(\nu(f)\le c_j\nu_j(f)\). Set \(C_0=\max_j c_j\nu_j(\mathfrak m)\). Statements 1.4 and 1.7 imply
\[
\nu(f)\le C_0\min_j\frac{\nu_j(f)}{\nu_j(\mathfrak m)}
=C_0\overline{\operatorname{ord}}_{\mathfrak m}(f)
\le C_0(\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak m}(f)+K).
\]
For nonzero nonunits the order is at least one and finite by Krull intersection, giving \(\nu(f)\le C_0(1+K)\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak m}(f)\). Units have both values zero and are handled separately. The literal strict Remark 1.6 fails on units and is not used. Swanson's full Rees-valuations Section 5 was read; its 5.2 is stated for complete domains. The general-domain application here uses exact Rond--Spivakovsky 1.3. Original Rees 1989 and the historical Izumi proofs have not been independently read. Published applications with these disclosed dependencies are allowed by the task; metadata and old reading receipts are not grants.
