\section{n3. Uniform criterion, exact transports, decreasing obstacles, and a necessary limitation}

Support: entire qualified G331 and earlier own n1,n2. The geometric classes and all qualifications remain those of G331.

For every finite continuous obstacle f, n2 gives an unconditional canonical pointwise limit p(f)=lim h\_m, not yet an attained positive envelope. Its continuity is equivalent to uniform convergence of h\_m, and equivalent to uniform convergence of H\_N=max\_\{r<=N\}h\_r. Indeed, if p is continuous, the increasing continuous H\_N converge to it; their strict error-test open sets cover compact X, so one N works uniformly. Given epsilon and such N, n2's residue estimate bounds p-h\_m by epsilon+NM\_1/m. Conversely uniform convergence puts p in the uniformly closed C by G331, so p is continuous and the greatest geometric envelope. This criterion states the missing regularity plainly; it does not prove it for arbitrary f.

Raw envelopes obey a one-sided obstacle shift estimate without any regularity hypothesis. If f<=g+epsilon, every u<=f in D has u-epsilon<=g in D, because a negative constant is an actual primary profile. Therefore p(f)<=p(g)+epsilon. If ||f-g||<=epsilon, then ||p(f)-p(g)||<=epsilon, since both raw envelopes are finite. This transfers any proved uniform approximation by obstacles having continuous geometric envelopes: their envelopes are uniformly Cauchy and converge in C to p(f). It does not establish density of finitely generated obstacles.

There is also an actual decreasing construction that permits infinitely determined and unbounded obstacles. Let f\_i be a nonempty decreasing directed family of continuous obstacles, each satisfying the finite-generation condition of n2, and set f=inf\_i f\_i. Their geometric envelopes H\_i lie in C and decrease by monotonicity. The ACTUAL decreasing C-net has infimum H in D by G331's definition; no net flattening is used. Since H<=f and every D competitor u<=f satisfies u<=H\_i at every index, H is the greatest geometric envelope of f. It is upper semicontinuous and nonpositive, with bottom and partial poles retained. The assertion is conditional on the individual finite-generation hypotheses and the specified decreasing family; it does not approximate an arbitrary obstacle by such a family. If f\_i converge uniformly to a finite continuous f, the shift estimate additionally gives uniform convergence of H\_i and a continuous C envelope.

Primary changes preserve the canonical construction exactly, not just after comparison. For another primary b, d(v)=v(b)>0 is bounded continuous on X\_a, T(v)=v/d(v), and f\_b(Tv)=f\_a(v)/d(v). Then



\[
(Tv)(g)+m f_b(Tv)=(v(g)+m f_a(v))/d(v).
\]



Hence A\_m(f\_a)=A\_m(f\_b) as ideals and their graded algebras are identical. The raw envelopes, the h\_m, and any constructed H transport by division by d. Substituting twice gives the exact three-gauge cocycle. The uniform error in n2 becomes at most D\_0 M\_1/(m min d); equivalently use the value norm of A\_1 in the new gauge. No gauge-dependent redefinition of positivity is made.

For finite normalization S of R and a downstairs obstacle f, define the source ideals using f composed with restriction on the entire semilocal normalization boundary. Boundary surjectivity and equality of restricted values give the exact identity A\_m\textasciicircum{}R=A\_m\textasciicircum{}S intersect R. At finite conductor value the fibre is singleton; at infinite conductor value it is the full quotient relation through S/c -> R/c. Both are in this identity. It does not imply finite generation of one algebra from that of the other by mere contraction.

If geometric source envelopes exist and their tuple is constant on EVERY normalization fibre, G331's positive D descent gives a downstairs h. It is below f by surjectivity. Pullback of any downstairs competitor is dominated by the source envelopes, so u<=h. Thus h is the downstairs envelope. This is the exact conditional normalization rule. Neither source positivity nor full-fibre compatibility is inferred just from the fact that the obstacle descends. For a decreasing family whose source envelopes are each fibre-compatible, the infimum remains fibre-compatible and the same argument applies to the actual decreasing limits.

On an excellent reduced curve the normalization is a finite set of DVR local centres, and a regular conductor element has finite order at every centre. Thus the boundary fibres are singleton. A DVR has one ray, and the closed point is an actual effective Cartier divisor with no contracted curves to test. All finite nonpositive branch coordinates are independently geometric; semilocal gluing and G331 positive descent give C equal to the full finite nonpositive orthant. For an extended vector u, the vectors max(u,-j) decrease in C to u, so D is the full extended nonpositive orthant. Its geometric obstacle envelope is exactly min(f,0), matching the ideal envelope through the independent geometric comparison. Irrational coordinates cause no obstruction.

For n1's explicit conifold obstacles, n2's converse computes the entire canonical filtration, not just its limit: A\_m(f\_delta)=integral-closure(J\textasciicircum{}m), independently of delta>=0. Its algebra is the finite normalized Rees algebra. Integral dependence makes v(A\_1)=v(J) on every support; in the m-gauge its norm is four, since J contains powers with exponents at most four of every maximal generator, and the singular-supported z-order realizes four. Thus any homogeneous generator degree bound D\_0 for that particular normalized Rees algebra yields the all-support error 4D\_0/m. No numerical generator-degree bound for this ring was computed in the finite arithmetic diagnostic.

For n1's mixed-characteristic obstacles there is an even sharper exact computation. The order valuation nu has F\_delta(nu)=-1, so g in A\_m must have ord\_n(g)>=m and hence belong to n\textasciicircum{}m. Conversely membership in n\textasciicircum{}m gives v(g)>=m on every support, and F\_delta>=-1 makes the defining obstacle inequality hold. Therefore A\_m(F\_delta)=n\textasciicircum{}m at EVERY degree, independently of delta>=0, and h\_m=-1 exactly with zero error. These are actual fixed-obstacle canonical-algebra applications on the nonisolated cancellation-sensitive examples, not computations of general arbitrary model-obstacle algebras.

In fact finite generation in n2 is NOT necessary for continuous-envelope regularity. On the smooth DVR R=k[[x]], normalized by (x), take the singleton obstacle f=-alpha for a positive irrational alpha. Its geometric envelope is -alpha. Its canonical ideals are (x\textasciicircum{}\{ceil(m alpha)\}). If their algebra were generated by finitely many homogeneous elements of degrees d\_i, the minimum generator ratios ord\_x(g\_i)/d\_i would be rational; n2's elementary generator argument would make the asymptotic order slope that rational number. But ceil(m alpha)/m tends to alpha, a contradiction. Hence this algebra is not finitely generated although the envelope is continuous and already in the geometric core as a real Cartier divisor. Non-finite-generation is therefore not a CE counterexample, even in dimension one. Likewise the historical failure of a universal primary correction is not an obstruction to this fixed-obstacle construction.

At the exact published smooth affine CLOSED germ over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, G331 identifies this same C/D class with BFJ's all-semivaluation class, with bottom adjoined. A greatest minorant proved here is consequently the BFJ envelope in that same class; the published domain is not enlarged. Nilpotents reduce away, and zero-dimensional local reduction has the unique empty boundary function. Literal classical/CLD radial classes keep their multibranch mixed-zero exclusion; this construction does not identify them with the valuative class. \section*{Main theorem and proof map}
Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be excellent local and replace it by its reduction.
For every proper primary $\mathfrak a$, let $V_{\mathfrak a}$ be the compact
section of centred real semivaluations with $v(\mathfrak a)=1$, retaining every
prime support. Define $Q$ by finite nonnegative real sums of negative
unit-or-primary ideal values, $C$ by uniform closure, and $D$ by actual infima
of nonempty decreasing $C$-nets, with bottom allowed.

On actual primary blowups, take actual negative effective finite real Cartier
presentations having nonnegative degree on every contracted proper integral
curve. Their evaluations define $M_{\rm geom}$ independently of ideal
positivity. Then
\[
 Q\subset M_{\rm geom}\subset C,\qquad
 C_{\rm geom}=C,\qquad D_{\rm geom}=D.
\]
For every reduced finite injection, the pullback image of either completed
class is precisely its full-fibre-constant subclass. Normalization fibres are
singletons at finite conductor value and precisely conductor-quotient fibres
at infinite value. Primary changes obey the exact homogeneous cocycle.
At a smooth affine closed germ over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero
field, $C$ is exactly the finite continuous BFJ subclass and $D$ is the full
BFJ all-semivaluation extension with the identically bottom function adjoined.
Smooth DVR and empty dimension zero are direct.

The proofs are the numbered local chain below: n1 gives the boundary; n2--n6
give full algebraic descent; n7 discharges the exact published geometric inputs;
n8 constructs and compares the independent cone; n9 gives full BFJ recovery;
n10--n11 preserve raw-cone and radial distinctions; n12 records the exact
original-target decision. Each support list contains only earlier local IDs.
Source applications are ordinary published applications, with disclosed
recursive historical dependencies, and no supplied draft is an accepted premise.
Separate envelopes, products, energy and their geometric operator theory are
the P12.3--P12.6 targets. They are not claimed here.
\section{n1. Boundary, finite lifting, conductor fibres, and completion}
\textit{Earlier local supports: none.}

All rings below are commutative. For a Noetherian local ring \((R,\mathfrak m)\), a centred real semivaluation is a map to \([0,+\infty]\) 
satisfying \(v(0)=+\infty\), \(v(1)=0\), multiplicativity, the ultrametric inequality, and \(0<v(\mathfrak m)<+\infty\). Its support 
\(v^{-1}(+\infty)\) is a prime strictly below \(\mathfrak m\); no minimal-support restriction is imposed. Ideal values are minima over 
finite generating sets. Relations between generating sets prove independence and
\[
v(IJ)=v(I)+v(J),\qquad v(I+J)=\min\{v(I),v(J)\}.
\]
Units have value zero. A proper primary ideal always means primary for the marked maximal ideal.

Fix a proper primary ideal \(\mathfrak a\). The section \(V_{\mathfrak a}(R)=\{v:v(\mathfrak a)=1\}\) is compact Hausdorff. Indeed 
semivaluation axioms and \(v(\mathfrak m)=1\) are closed conditions in the compact product \([0,+\infty]^R\); addition, minimum and the 
order relation have the required continuity/closedness. Choose \(\mathfrak m^r\subset\mathfrak a\subset\mathfrak m^s\), with \(r\ge s\ge1\).
 Then \(s v(\mathfrak m)\le v(\mathfrak a)\le r v(\mathfrak m)\). Rescaling identifies the two sections. Every primary ideal value is finite
 positive continuous and bounded there. For another primary ideal \(\mathfrak b\),
\[
H_{\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b}(v)=v/v(\mathfrak b),\qquad
u_{\mathfrak b}(H_{\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b}v)=u_{\mathfrak a}(v)/v(\mathfrak b).
\]
The denominator and its inverse are bounded. Substitution proves the inverse and the exact three-gauge cocycle. The centred cone is the 
product of its section and the positive radial coordinate \(v(\mathfrak a)\); hence these sections represent its intrinsic ray quotient. 
Nonprimary proper ideals give only their open finite-value domain, which can be noncompact. Units and zero ideals have no level-one section.

Nilpotents have infinite value. Comparing \(f+n\) and \((f+n)-n\) proves that reduction preserves every semivaluation and ideal gauge. A 
zero-dimensional reduced local ring is a field and has empty centred boundary. For a positive-dimensional excellent reduced local ring, a 
penultimate prime of a saturated chain to the maximal ideal gives a one-dimensional excellent domain quotient. Its finite normalization has 
a local DVR factor, whose order pulls back and normalizes into the section. This proves nonemptiness. Ordinary background used throughout is
 lying over, prime avoidance, finite Artinian decompositions, and the quotient/finite-type-localization stability, Nagata finiteness and 
universal catenarity consequences of excellence. None is used to assert resolution in arbitrary characteristic.

Every finite integral injection \(R\hookrightarrow B\), with \(B\) reduced and nonzero, gives a continuous surjective restriction 
\(V_{\mathfrak aB}(B)\to V_{\mathfrak a}(R)\). Here a finite algebra has the finite union of its closed-centre sections above \(\mathfrak 
m\). To lift \(v\) with support \(\mathfrak p\), choose a prime \(P\) of \(B\) above \(\mathfrak p\) and form the finite field extension 
\(\operatorname{Frac}(B/P)/\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)\). Extend the valuation ring by taking the integral closure, a prime over its 
maximal ideal, and a dominating valuation ring. The domination assertion follows from Zorn: in a maximal dominating local subring, either 
adjoining \(x\) or \(x^{-1}\) leaves the maximal ideal proper. If \(1=\sum a_i x^{-i}\) with all \(a_i\) in that ideal, multiplying by a 
power and dividing by \(1-a_0\) makes \(x\) integral, so lying over makes the ideal proper after adjoining \(x\). Localizing contradicts 
maximality unless one of the two elements already belongs. Intersection with the old field is the original valuation ring: an element 
outside it has inverse in its maximal ideal. An algebraic equation for any new nonzero field element has two least-valued terms; thus an 
integer multiple of its value is in the old value group. Dividing this old real value by the integer gives a well-defined order-preserving 
real embedding, using common multiples. Integral elements have nonnegative value by the least-term test for a monic equation. Compose with 
\(B\to B/P\), assigning \(P\) infinite value. This construction first kills the support; it never extends a nonzero-support semivaluation to
 the original fraction field. Compactness makes restriction a quotient map.

Let \(S\) be the finite normalization of an excellent reduced \(R\), and \(\mathfrak c=(R:S)\). Clearing denominators of finitely many 
generators of \(S\) gives a regular conductor element. The conductor is an ideal of both rings and
\[
R=S\times_{S/\mathfrak c}(R/\mathfrak c).
\]
An element of \(S\) whose residue comes from \(R\) differs from an element of \(R\) by an element of \(\mathfrak c\), proving this identity.
 The normalization boundary is the finite disjoint union of local normal centres above \(\mathfrak m\). Idempotents choose a minimal 
component; localization at its centre changes no values of denominators. Chinese remainder elements separating the finitely many centres, 
and their complements, have open positive-value loci selecting these pieces. The pieces are therefore clopen. Branches mean these local 
centres, not merely minimal primes.

If \(v(\mathfrak c)<+\infty\), choose \(c\in\mathfrak c\) of finite value. Every lift satisfies \(w(s)=v(cs)-v(c)\), so it is unique. The 
subtracted number is finite. If \(v(\mathfrak c)=+\infty\), all lifts kill the conductor, and equality after restriction \(S/\mathfrak c\to 
R/\mathfrak c\) is exactly their identification. This infinity stratum is closed; its finite complement is open, without a closedness claim.
 A fibre-constant continuous function descends continuously by the compact quotient. A fibre-constant extended nonpositive upper 
semicontinuous function descends upper semicontinuously: its closed superlevel sets have compact, hence closed, images. These assertions 
alone supply no positivity descent.

Completion preserves the entire boundary for every Noetherian local ring. For \(F\in\widehat R\), choose representatives \(F_N\) modulo 
\(\mathfrak m^N\), and put \(d=v(\mathfrak m)>0\). Differences have value at least \(Nd\). If some \(v(F_N)<Nd\), later values stabilize; 
otherwise they tend to infinity. Define \(\widehat v(F)\) by this limit. It is independent of representatives and satisfies
\[
\min\{\widehat v(F),Nd\}=\min\{v(F_N),Nd\}.
\]
Applying this to sums and products proves all axioms and uniqueness, including infinite values; completed units have unit representatives. 
Compose with \(q(t)=t/(1+t)\), \(q(+\infty)=1\). The displayed continuous truncations have uniform error at most \((1+N/r)^{-1}\), because 
\(d\ge1/r\). Thus completed evaluation is continuous and completion restriction is a homeomorphism. Every completed primary \(J\) contains 
\(\widehat{\mathfrak m}^N\). Representatives modulo that power of its generators belong to \(J\cap R\) and, with the boundary power, 
generate \(J\). Hence \(J=(J\cap R)\widehat R\). The quotient isomorphism also proves contraction of an extended primary ideal recovers it. 
Unit-or-primary profiles and their uniform and decreasing classes therefore agree under completion. No equivalence of geometric model 
categories is asserted.

This is a mathematical argument with the stated ordinary background. Swanson--Huneke 6.4.1--2 were read in full and agree with the 
domination proof. Artifact n1.md is authoritative and is reproduced in argument.md and the paper. Rerun: python audit\_inputs.py; python 
build\_delivery.py. Execution does not verify the mathematics.

\section{n2. Exact algebraic applications and their qualifications}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1.}

Use n1 for boundary conventions. The following are ordinary published theorem applications at their stated hypotheses, with their immediate 
units checked from the bound primary data. This is not an independent reconstruction of all historical proofs.

Swanson--Huneke is the current author PDF created July 2024, not asserted byte-identical to the 2006 printing. Its complete 6.8.1--4 
statements and proofs give the following consequence. Let \(E\) be Noetherian semilocal, \(J\) contain a boundary power, and \(Q\) be a 
finite ideal. If every normalized centred semivaluation satisfies \(w(Q)\ge w(J)\), and \(Q\) has zero image on every zero-dimensional 
minimal component where \(J\) is nonunit, then
\[
Q\subset\overline J.
\]
Apply 6.8.4 on each positive-dimensional local domain component, normalizing each centred rank-one DVR by the boundary ideal. Apply 6.8.3 to
 all minimal components. On zero-dimensional components there are no boundary points; the extra zero-image condition is needed. In all uses 
below \(Q=K(\mathfrak aE)^L\), with \(L>0\), so this condition holds. Unit components of \(J\) impose no condition. For nonreduced \(E\), 
lift the componentwise monic equations, multiply them over the finitely many minimal primes, then raise to a power to kill the nilpotent 
error. The resulting equation is monic with degree-i coefficients in \(J^i\). This is the finite-minimal-prime argument of 1.1.5, also read 
completely. PDF inspection of printed page 140 confirmed the integral-closure bars omitted in the text extraction.

The common exponent needed later has a short direct proof. Each \(qt\), \(q\in Q\), is integral over \(E[Jt]\) with its homogeneous 
ideal-integrality equation. Thus \(E[(J+Q)t]\) is finite graded over \(E[Jt]\). Choose homogeneous module generators of degrees at most 
\(h\). Its degree \(N+h\) terms have coefficients in \(J^{N+h-d}\subset J^N\). Consequently
\[
Q^{N+h}\subset (J+Q)^{N+h}\subset J^N\quad(N\ge1).
\]
This works for nonreduced rings and assumes no finiteness of the full normalized Rees algebra. The complete 1.2.3--5 reduction chain was 
checked too; printed page 6 confirms the criterion uses integral closure.

For an excellent local domain \(A\) of positive dimension and a nonzero proper primary ideal, 10.2.2, including its proof ending at 10.2.3, 
constructs finitely many Rees DVRs centred at the closed point. The full 10.4.3 proof gives their residue transcendence degree \(\dim A-1\) 
when \(A\) is formally equidimensional. Excellence supplies universal catenarity, and the full B.5.1 statement/proof identifies this with 
local formal equidimensionality for Noetherian domains. B.3.2 and its immediate context give, for a finite-type birational domain \(B\) over
 excellent local domain \(A\), and \(P\cap A=\mathfrak m\),
\[
\dim B_P+\operatorname{trdeg}_{A/\mathfrak m}\kappa(P)=\dim A.
\]
The book describes B.3.2's proof as a modification of an earlier dimension argument. Its recursive historical dependencies, including 
Mori--Nagata and Ratliff, are disclosed rather than claimed independently read.

Stacks 0C23, full immediate HTML lemma/proof, states that normal Noetherian local rings with normal formal fibres have normal completion; 
excellence suffices. Its proof refers to Algebra 10.163.8, not recursively read. A normal local completed ring is a domain. Thus an 
excellent normal local domain is analytically irreducible and analytically unramified. This is not claimed for an arbitrary nonnormal 
domain.

Exact Rond--Spivakovsky arXiv 1404.4885v1, complete pages 1--2 definitions and statements 1.3, 1.4 and 1.7, yields an order bound at 
precisely this analytic domain. For a centred divisorial valuation \(\nu\) and the finitely many maximal-ideal Rees valuations \(\nu_j\), 
1.3 gives \(\nu(f)\le c_j\nu_j(f)\). Set \(C_0=\max_j c_j\nu_j(\mathfrak m)\). Statements 1.4 and 1.7 imply
\[
\nu(f)\le C_0\min_j\frac{\nu_j(f)}{\nu_j(\mathfrak m)}
=C_0\overline{\operatorname{ord}}_{\mathfrak m}(f)
\le C_0(\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak m}(f)+K).
\]
For nonzero nonunits the order is at least one and finite by Krull intersection, giving \(\nu(f)\le C_0(1+K)\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak 
m}(f)\). Units have both values zero and are handled separately. The literal strict Remark 1.6 fails on units and is not used. Swanson's 
full Rees-valuations Section 5 was read; its 5.2 is stated for complete domains. The general-domain application here uses exact 
Rond--Spivakovsky 1.3. Original Rees 1989 and the historical Izumi proofs have not been independently read. Published applications with 
these disclosed dependencies are allowed by the task; metadata and old reading receipts are not grants.

inspect\_primary.py; python audit\_inputs.py; python build\_delivery.py. No finite check certifies these published applications or the new

\section{n3. Exact cones, density, and normal-target traces}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1.}

Use n1's sections. Define \(P_R\) to be the raw finite nonnegative REAL combinations of gauges \(v(I)\), where \(I\) contains a power of the
 primary boundary ideal, with the unit ideal allowed. Put \(Q_R=-P_R\), let \(C_R\) be its uniform closure in finite continuous functions, 
and let \(D_R\) consist of infima of nonempty decreasing \(C_R\)-nets. Include zero and the identically minus-infinity bottom. A finite 
semilocal algebra uses the product classes over its closed centres. These agree with global semilocal ideal profiles: local primary ideals 
contract to ideals primary at their own centre and unit at the others, and tuples glue in a common Artinian boundary quotient. Denominators 
synchronize by powers. Rational profiles \(-v(I)/k\) are uniformly dense in \(C_R\): approximate finitely many real coefficients rationally 
and turn their sum into a product-ideal profile. The class \(C_R\) is a closed convex cone, stable under maxima by ideal sums. Its 
decreasing completion is upper semicontinuous and stable under addition, positive scaling and finite maxima by product directed sets. We do 
not assume increasing-limit closure, arbitrary-infimum closure, or flattening of nested nets.

The rational difference span of bounded gauges is a lattice: after a common denominator every expression is \((v(I)-v(J))/k\), and
\[
\min\{v(I)-v(J),v(K)-v(H)\}=v(IH+KJ)-v(JH).
\]
It contains rational constants since \(v(\mathfrak a)=1\), and separates points using \(v((f)+\mathfrak a^N)=\min\{v(f),N\}\), and 
centre-separating ideals in the semilocal case. Its UNIFORM closure is a real vector lattice. The compact lattice approximation proof makes 
this closure all real continuous functions: affine combinations of a separating function match a target at two points; rational 
approximations preserve strict local error tests. For a fixed first point take finitely many minima to bound the target from above 
throughout the space, while matching near that point; then finitely many maxima over first-point neighbourhoods give a uniform 
approximation. Negating interchanges the needed bounds. No integer ideal formula is asserted for an arbitrary finite irrational span.

Let \(A\) be excellent normal local domain and \(A\subset B\) a finite domain extension, with fraction fields \(K\subset L\), \(n=[L:K]\). 
For a \(B\)-ideal \(J\), choose finite \(A\)-module generators \(b_i\) and define \(\mathcal N(J)\) as the coefficient ideal of
\[
N_{L(T)/K(T)}\Big(\sum_i T_i b_i\Big)
=\prod_{\sigma:L\hookrightarrow M}\Big(\sum_i T_i\sigma(b_i)\Big)^q,
\qquad q\,|\Sigma|=n.
\]
Here \(M/K\) is a finite field containing all embedding images. The generic inseparable length \(q\) follows by decomposing 
\(L\otimes_K\overline K\) into its Artinian factors: determinant of multiplication on a length-q factor is its residue scalar to the power 
q. The coefficients are integral over \(A\) and belong to \(K\), hence belong to \(A\). Linear substitution in both directions when changing
 generators proves independence of this coefficient ideal. If \(J\supset\mathfrak a^N B\), add base generators \(x\) of \(\mathfrak a^N\) 
redundantly: the pure variable coefficient is \(x^n\). The coefficient ideal therefore contains a boundary power and is unit-or-primary.

Let \(E\) be the finite integral closure of \(A\) in \(M\). Lift any base semivaluation to \(E\) by n1, including nonzero support, and 
compose with the embeddings to obtain \(w_\sigma\) on \(B\). Minimum coefficient values of polynomials multiply. To prove this, quotient by 
the support, enter the valued quotient fraction field, divide each nonzero polynomial by a coefficient of smallest finite value, and reduce 
to nonzero residue polynomials. Their product is nonzero. A polynomial vanishing modulo support has infinite coefficient minimum and causes 
no difficulty. Applying this to the displayed norm polynomial gives on EVERY support
\[
v(\mathcal N(J))=q\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}w_\sigma(J).
\]
Boundary-power ideals make these sums finite. Define \(\mu_v=q\sum_\sigma\delta_{w_\sigma}\), of mass \(n\). Its integrals on all ideal 
gauges are fixed by the coefficient identity; the density just proved and equal mass make it independent of the lift on every continuous 
function, hence as a finite measure. Its support is the full restriction fibre. Indeed for any fibre point on \(B\), extend it to \(E\) by 
n1 with the identity embedding of \(B\). That point occurs with positive weight. Choice independence forces it into the support of every 
such measure. Thus the whole fibre is finite of cardinality at most \(n\). This proof uses generic inseparable lengths and quotient-support 
Gauss values; it does not assume a defectless ramification/residue-degree formula.

The trace \(TH(v)=\int H\,d\mu_v\) is positive, of norm \(n\), and continuous-valued. Continuity holds first on gauges by the coefficient 
identity, then on all continuous functions by uniform density and the mass bound. It preserves \(C\), mapping a rational negative profile to
 \(-v(\mathcal N(J))/k\). A finite positive sum commutes with decreasing nonpositive extended limits: if one summand goes to bottom so does 
the sum; otherwise directedness approximates all finite limits simultaneously. Consequently a fibre-constant \(D_B\)-function descends via 
\(T/n\) to an actual decreasing \(C_A\)-net, as does a fibre-constant \(C_B\)-function.

For any reduced finite injection into normal local \(A\), choose the minimal source components dominating \(A\), at least one of which 
exists over the generic point, and normalize them. Sum their traces divided by the sum of their generic degrees. At every base semivaluation
 all traced values equal the descended value by constancy on the FULL original fibre. Vertical components receive no fabricated generic 
degree, but remain constrained by that full constancy. This proves exact \(C,D\) descent for normal targets. Pullback of ideals and limits 
supplies the converse. Every lift has the same base primary-gauge denominator, so these assertions obey n1's gauge cocycle.

\section{n4. Bounded descent for every reduced excellent finite injection}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1, n2, n3.}

Using n1--n3, we prove
\[
f^*C_R=\{u\in C_B:u\text{ is constant on every restriction fibre}\}
\]
for every excellent reduced local \(R\) and nonzero reduced finite injection \(R\hookrightarrow B\). Pullback is an isometry. The theorem 
concerns the continuous UNIFORM cone, not the raw cone or a decreasing completion.

Induct on target dimension. Dimension zero has empty sections. Normal targets are n3. In dimension d, first prove normalization descent, 
using the arbitrary finite-injection theorem below dimension d; then prove arbitrary injections by normalization base change. Let \(S\) 
normalize \(R\), \(\mathfrak c\) be its conductor, \(C_0=R/\mathfrak c\), and \(E=S/\mathfrak c\). A regular conductor element gives \(\dim 
C_0<d\). The injection \(C_0\hookrightarrow E\) stays injective after reduction because nilpotence is detected in an injected subring. 
Restriction of primary gauges and uniform limits to the quotient section preserves the class. Thus for fibre-constant \(u\in C_S\), its 
continuous descent \(h\) from n1 has quotient restriction \(h_0\in C_{C_0}\) by induction. If the quotient section is empty, the conductor 
value is finite at every point and quotient estimates below are unnecessary.

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose rational profiles \(j=-w(J)/k\) and \(\kappa=-v(K)/k\) approximating \(u\) and \(h_0\) with error less than 
\(\varepsilon\). All ideals contain boundary powers. We can make \(J\) proper at every positive-dimensional centre: add an arbitrarily small
 negative boundary constant before rational approximation, or multiply a rational profile ideal by the boundary ideal with an arbitrarily 
large common denominator. Start with smaller errors to accommodate this correction. Synchronize denominators by ideal powers and enlarge k 
until \(1/k<\varepsilon\). On the entire quotient boundary,
\[
|w(K_E)-w(J_E)|<2k\varepsilon.
\]
Choose integer \(L\) with \(2k\varepsilon<L\le2k\varepsilon+1\). The ideal \(Q=K_E(\mathfrak aE)^L\) has \(w(Q)\ge w(J_E)\) everywhere. Its 
POSITIVE boundary factor kills its image on zero-dimensional minimal components. The exact n2 criterion therefore gives 
\(Q\subset\overline{J_E}\), on all minimal components and even a nonreduced quotient. The finite graded argument gives one \(h'\ge0\) with 
\(Q^{N+h'}\subset J_E^N\) for every N.

Put \(I_N=J^N\cap R\). It contains a boundary power and is proper, hence primary. The conductor fibre product in n1 gives the exact residue 
identity
\[
(I_N+\mathfrak c)/\mathfrak c=J_E^N\cap C_0.
\]
For the nontrivial inclusion, lift a residue in the right side to an element of \(J^N\). Since its residue comes from \(C_0\), that very 
element lies in \(R\), and hence in \(I_N\). Thus the image contains \(K^{N+h'}(\mathfrak aC_0)^{L(N+h')}\). At a conductor-infinite point 
its quotient semivaluation yields
\[
\frac{v(I_N)}{kN}\le(1+h'/N)\left(\frac{v(K)}k+\frac Lk\right).
\]
All terms here are finite. At a conductor-finite point the unique lift \(w\) and \(\mathfrak cJ^N\subset I_N\) yield instead
\[
\frac{w(J)}k\le\frac{v(I_N)}{kN}\le\frac{w(J)}k+\frac{v(\mathfrak c)}{kN}.
\]
The latter estimate is used ONLY at finite conductor value. On every point the lower bound from \(I_N\subset J^N\) gives 
\(v(I_N)/(kN)\ge-h-\varepsilon\). The limit upper bound is at most \(-h+4\varepsilon\): at infinity use \(-\kappa\le-h+\varepsilon\) and 
\(L/k<3\varepsilon\), and at finite conductor use \(-j\le-h+\varepsilon\).

The continuous functions \(b_n=v(I_{2^n})/(k2^n)\) decrease, since \(I_N^2\subset I_{2N}\). Their increasing strict-test open sets 
\(\{b_n+h<5\varepsilon\}\) cover the compact section. One n covers it entirely. Together with the common lower bound this proves 
\(\|-b_n-h\|_\infty<5\varepsilon\), and then \(h\in C_R\). These negative dyadic profiles INCREASE internally. They are not used as a 
decreasing regularization, and no increasing-limit closure is invoked.

For arbitrary \(R\hookrightarrow B\), form \(B'=(B\otimes_R S)_{\rm red}\). Base change of an integral surjective spectrum map is 
surjective, so its kernel in reduced \(S\) lies in every prime and is zero. Hence \(S\hookrightarrow B'\) is a finite injection. Pullback of
 \(u\) is fibre constant over each normal local centre of \(S\); equal restrictions there imply equal underlying restrictions to \(R\). N3 
descends it to \(C_S\), exactly the pullback of \(h\). Normalization descent just proved gives \(h\in C_R\), closing induction. Ideal 
extension gives pullback inclusion and surjectivity in n1 gives the isometry.

Define \(N_R\) as the continuous functions whose normalization pullbacks belong to the RAW local negative real ideal cones and are fibre 
compatible. We have only
\[
Q_R\subset N_R\subset C_R,\qquad
\overline{Q_R}^{\|\cdot\|_\infty}=\overline{N_R}^{\|\cdot\|_\infty}=C_R.
\]
No raw equality is inferred. All conductor-infinite quotient supports remain. Artifacts: n4.md and the paper. Rerun: python 
build\_delivery.py. The incompatible-ideal contraction shortcut is deliberately absent; n11 diagnoses it.

\section{n5. Unbounded strictly negative descent by insertion}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1, n2, n3, n4.}

Use n1--n4. A fibre-constant \(u\in D_B\) descends into \(D_R\) whenever its descent \(h\) is everywhere strictly negative, including 
partial minus-infinity and discontinuous unbounded functions. The descent is upper semicontinuous by n1, so on a nonempty compact section 
\(h\le-c\) for some finite \(c>0\). All-bottom is directly the limit of \(-N v(\mathfrak a)\); zero is separate. Normal targets follow from 
n3. Induct on dimension exactly as in n4: prove normalization from lower-dimensional finite-injection descent and then arbitrary injections 
by reduced normalization base change.

In the normalization step use \(S,\mathfrak c,C_0,E\) from n4. A decreasing representation of \(u\) restricts to the quotient, whose 
fibre-constant limit descends by induction to \(h_0\in D_{C_0}\). We prove an insertion lemma: for every finite continuous test \(F>h\) 
there is \(q\in C_R\) with \(h<q<F\). Choose a FINITE positive lower bound \(e\) for the lower semicontinuous gap \(F-h\), for example any 
number below half the minimum of 1 and its infimum. When that infimum is infinite, e remains finite; no infinity subtraction is performed.

From a decreasing continuous representation of \(u\), choose one term \(g\) satisfying \(u\le g<-c/2\) and \(g<F\circ\rho-e/2\). Each point 
eventually satisfies these strict continuous tests; their open sets and directedness give one common index by compactness. No uniform 
convergence to \(u\) is used. Choose \(0<b<1/2\) with \(b\|g\|<e/8\). The scaled term \((1-b)g\) is still below \(F-e/4\), and exceeds 
finite \(u\) by at least \(bc/2\). Uniform rational approximation with error less than \(\min(e/8,bc/4)\), further tightened to retain 
strict negativity, gives \(j=-w(J)/k\) and a fixed \(s>0\) such that
\[
u+s\le j<F\circ\rho-e/8.
\]
The first inequality is automatic at bottom. \(J\) is proper at all centres and contains a boundary power. Put \(M=\|j\|\).

We need a rational quotient profile \(\kappa=-v(K)/k\) with \(h_0\le\kappa\) and \(\kappa\circ\rho_E<j|_E+\delta\), for arbitrarily small 
\(\delta>0\). Here is the needed construction. Choose \(0<b_1<1/2\) with \(b_1M<s/4\), and a decreasing \(C_{C_0}\)-net \(g_i\) to \(h_0\). 
Since \(u_E\le j_E-s\), we have \((1-b_1)u_E<j_E-s/4\). Compactness on E selects one i with its scaled pullback below \(j_E-s/8\); 
simultaneously compactness on \(C_0\) selects \(g_i<-c/2\). Scaling therefore lifts it above \(h_0\) by a positive uniform gap at finite 
points. Rational approximation with error less than \(\min(b_1c/4,s/16)\) gives \(\kappa\) with the stated two bounds, even with a negative 
gap to \(j_E\). Synchronize denominators with J and enlarge k so \(1/k<\delta\). If the quotient boundary is empty omit this construction.

Choose integer \(L\) with \(k\delta<L\le k\delta+1\). On E the ideal \(Q=K_E(\mathfrak aE)^L\) dominates \(J_E\) in value. N2, including the
 zero-dimensional boundary factor, gives \(Q\subset\overline{J_E}\) and a common \(h'\) with \(Q^{N+h'}\subset J_E^N\). Contract 
\(I_N=J^N\cap R\). The exact residue identity of n4 gives at infinity-conductor points
\[
\liminf_N[-v(I_N)/(kN)]\ge\kappa-2\delta\ge h-2\delta.
\]
At finite-conductor points its finite-value estimate gives limit j, at least \(h+s\). The dyadic \(f_n=-v(I_{2^n})/(k2^n)\) increase, are 
finite continuous, and satisfy \(f_n\le j\) on every lift. Their strict open sets \(\{f_n>h-3\delta\}\) cover the compact section, including
 bottom points: these sets are open because h is upper semicontinuous. Select one n valid everywhere.

Choose \(\delta\) so small that \(\eta=3\delta/c<1/2\) and \(\eta M<e/16\), and put \(q=(1-\eta)f_n\in C_R\). At finite \(h\le-c\),
\[
q>(1-\eta)(h-3\delta)\ge h+\eta c-3\delta(1-\eta)=h+3\delta\eta>h.
\]
At bottom q is finite. Also \(q\le(1-\eta)j\le j+\eta M<F\). This proves insertion using real positive scaling, not adding a positive 
constant to the class.

Let \(\mathcal Q\) be all continuous \(C_R\)-functions strictly above h. Zero belongs. For two members apply insertion to their continuous 
minimum; the test need not itself be psh. This gives a member below both, so \(\mathcal Q\) is downward directed. At any v and finite 
\(t>h(v)\), upper semicontinuity and compact Hausdorff normality give a finite continuous F strictly above h with \(F(v)<t\): choose 
\(h(v)<\ell<t\), a neighbourhood where \(h<\ell\), and a Urysohn cutoff supported there, interpolating from \(\ell\) to a global strict 
upper bound outside. Insertion supplies \(q(v)<t\). Thus \(\inf\mathcal Q=h\), and reverse pointwise order is an ACTUAL decreasing 
\(C_R\)-net to h. This closes normalization and the finite-injection induction. Neither an increasing completion step nor a flattening 
theorem is needed.

Artifacts: n5.md and the paper. Rerun: python build\_delivery.py. This proof reconstructs strict-negative descent without accepting any 
supplied provenance label. Mixed-zero descent is next.

\section{n6. Divisorial density, normal zero dichotomy, and full completed descent}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1, n2, n3, n4, n5.}

Use n1--n5. We prove the full statement
\[
f^*D_R=\{u\in D_B:u\text{ is constant on every restriction fibre}\}
\]
for every nonzero reduced finite injection over an excellent reduced local ring. It includes allzero, allbottom, mixedzero, partialbottom, 
conductor-infinite, and nonminimal supports.

First prove divisorial density on an excellent local domain \(A\). A basic neighbourhood of v in its primary section imposes finitely many 
strict coordinate tests. Choose a generator \(a_0\) of \(\mathfrak a\) with \(v(a_0)=1\) and put all \(a_j/a_0\) in a finite-type birational
 subalgebra \(B_0\subset\operatorname{Frac}(A)\). For each finite positive tested coordinate f choose rational bounds \(p/q<v(f)<r/s\) 
within its required interval, and put \(f^q/a_0^p\) and \(a_0^r/f^s\) in \(B_0\). For an infinity coordinate use only a lower bound and its 
first ratio. Units and zero have fixed values. Every denominator has finite value, so even a nonzero-support v extends nonnegatively to this
 algebra. Its positive-value prime P contains \(a_0\) and every strict-test ratio and contracts to \(\mathfrak m\). Thus \((B_0)_P\) is 
excellent domain of positive dimension. A Rees DVR of its maximal ideal, furnished by n2, is positive on P and nonnegative on \(B_0\). Its 
valuation \(\nu\) has \(\nu(\mathfrak a)=\nu(a_0)>0\); dividing by this number satisfies all the original tests.

This DVR is divisorial over A itself. N2's birational dimension formula gives \(\dim(B_0)_P+\operatorname{trdeg}_{A/\mathfrak 
m}\kappa(P)=\dim A\). The Rees DVR has residue transcendence degree \(\dim(B_0)_P-1\) over \(\kappa(P)\). Transcendence degrees add to 
\(\dim A-1\). Its value group is discrete rank one and centre on A is the closed point. Thus it has precisely the divisorial definition in 
Rond--Spivakovsky. This establishes density on the actual all-support pointwise section without any singular SNC or characteristic-zero 
resolution argument.

Now assume A is normal. N2 gives, for each centred divisorial \(\nu\), a finite constant with \(\nu(f)\le C_\nu\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak
 m}(f)\) for nonzero nonunits; units are separately zero. Normalize \(\nu\) by \(\mathfrak a\). If \(\mathfrak m^r\subset\mathfrak a\), then
 every \(v_0\) in the section has \(v_0(\mathfrak m)\ge1/r\). Choosing a nonzero generator attaining a proper primary ideal's finite 
\(v_0\)-value yields \(\nu(I)\le C_\nu r v_0(I)\). For unit ideals it holds too. Therefore every finite real negative ideal combination, and
 its uniform limit \(g\in C_A\), satisfies
\[
g(\nu)\ge C_\nu r\,g(v_0).
\]
If \(g(v_0)=0\), nonpositivity forces g to vanish at all divisorial points; density and continuity force \(g=0\). If \(u=\inf_i g_i\in D_A\)
 has value zero anywhere, every nonpositive \(g_i\) is zero there and hence everywhere. Thus on a normal local branch every completed 
function is either identically zero or everywhere strictly negative, with bottom allowed. Compact upper semicontinuity bounds each negative 
branch above by a finite negative constant.

Let \(u\in D_S\) be normalization-fibre constant. Call its finitely many normal centres active if their functions are everywhere negative, 
including bottom centres. Active and inactive points cannot share a fibre. The tuple \(\sigma=-1\) on active centres, zero elsewhere, 
belongs to \(C_S\) by primary-gauge/unit gluing from n3 and is fibre constant. The independently proved bounded theorem n4 descends it WITH 
POSITIVITY to \(\sigma\in C_R\). Its active set \(T=\{\sigma=-1\}\) is clopen. The descent h of u equals zero off T and is at most \(-c\) on
 T for some finite \(c>0\). If T is empty the result is zero. If every active value is bottom, the decreasing sequence \(N\sigma\) already 
proves the result.

For the remaining cases, every \(u-\delta\), \(\delta>0\), is an everywhere negative fibre-constant \(D_S\)-function by n3's addition rule, 
so n5 gives \(h-\delta\in D_R\). We do NOT take their increasing limit. Instead take any finite continuous test \(F>h\) on compact T and a 
finite positive lower gap e. Choose \(0<\eta<1/2\) with \(\eta(\|F\|+e)<e/4\), and set \(\delta=\eta c/[2(1-\eta)]\). At finite h on T,
\[
(1-\eta)(h-\delta)=h+\eta(-h-c/2)>h.
\]
Since \(h\le F-e\), the same choice gives \((1-\eta)(h-\delta)<F-e/2\), also at bottom. A decreasing \(C_R\)-net \(g_i\) to \(h-\delta\) has
 one index satisfying \((1-\eta)g_i<F-e/4\) throughout T, by compact strict-test covers. Choose \(N>0\) with \(-N<\min_T F\). Then
\[
q=\max\{(1-\eta)g_i,N\sigma\}\in C_R
\]
is strictly between h and F on T and EXACTLY zero off T. Both terms are below F on T; the first dominates the strictly larger scaled target 
at finite h, and q is finite at bottom. Off T its second term is zero and its first nonpositive.

The set of these continuous majorants, exactly zero off T and strictly above h on T, contains zero and is downward directed by insertion 
with the continuous minimum of two tests. The Urysohn construction in n5, applied on T, makes its pointwise infimum exactly h. Reverse 
pointwise order therefore gives an actual decreasing \(C_R\)-net. This proves full normalization descent, including mixed finite/bottom and 
mixed-zero functions, without an increasing closure or unproved flattening.

For arbitrary \(R\hookrightarrow B\), pull back to \((B\otimes_R S)_{\rm red}\), injective over S by n4. N3's traces at each normal local 
centre descend the pulled-back fibre-constant function to \(D_S\); it is precisely h pulled back from R. Full normalization descent then 
gives \(h\in D_R\). Conversely ideal extension preserves uniform and decreasing limits. Every primary change follows n1. Empty 
zero-dimensional sections have just their unique empty function. Artifacts: n6.md and the paper. Rerun: python build\_delivery.py. These are
 mathematical draft proofs, not consequences of registration.

\section{n7. Discharge of the primary-source geometry and real perturbation}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1.}

Use n1 for rings and the boundary. We prove the three geometric inputs, using the exact published primary units recorded below. No supplied 
continuation label is a premise.

Let Y be the actual blowup of a proper primary ideal I on a POSITIVE-DIMENSIONAL reduced Noetherian local R. Dimension zero is the 
empty-boundary case of n1, treated separately. No minimal component of this positive-dimensional local reduced ring is zero-dimensional: 
that would make its maximal ideal a minimal prime and force dimension zero. The Rees algebra is a subalgebra of R[t], so is reduced. Its 
component primes are obtained from the minimal primes of R: projecting the Rees algebra to each component domain gives prime kernels with 
intersection zero; component-separating elements of R show these kernels are the minimal primes. Since I has nonzero image on each 
positive-dimensional component, every component of its blowup dominates a component of R. The standard f-chart is the degree-zero subring 
R[I/f] of R\_f. Multiplication by f is injective there and I becomes (f). Consequently I O\_Y is invertible with a regular local generator, 
defining an ACTUAL effective Cartier divisor E; O\_Y(-E) is the relatively ample tautological bundle. The morphism is projective and is an 
isomorphism away from the closed point. Relative and absolute ampleness agree over this affine base, by complete Stacks 29.38.4--5 (01VG).

G1: T=H\textasciicircum{}0(Y,O\_Y) is a finite R-module by complete Stacks 30.16.1 and 30.16.3 (0B5S). Restriction to all generic components
 embeds T in the total quotient ring of R, since Y is reduced and those components are dense. The inclusion R into T is injective. Global 
sections localize on the base: choose a finite affine cover of the separated Y; its pairwise intersections are affine, and 
H\textasciicircum{}0 is the kernel of the difference map between finite products of the affine section modules. Localization is exact and 
commutes with those finite products. Since Y is the identity off the closed point, (T/R)\_p=0 for p different from m. The finite module T/R 
is therefore killed by m\textasciicircum{}h for some h>=0. Fix ONCE on this model
\[
\mathfrak c_0=\mathfrak m^{h+1},\qquad \mathfrak c_0 T\subset\mathfrak m\subset R.
\]
The containment is as elements of R: m\textasciicircum{}h T lies in R and then one more factor m puts it in m. This primary correction is 
not the full normalization conductor.

G2: Complete Stacks 28.27.13(7) (01PR) gives eventual generation of F tensor A\textasciicircum{}k for any coherent F and ample A on the 
Noetherian scheme Y. Thus for each invertible L, A\textasciicircum{}\{k-1\} tensor L is generated for large k. Complete 28.27.5 says ample 
tensor generated invertible is ample, so A\textasciicircum{}k tensor L is ample. Complete 28.27.2 gives the ample power-root assertion. 
These are applicable to Y without normality or smoothness. Their proofs were read, including the affine-section criterion and the high-power
 generation equivalences; deeper referenced scheme-theoretic results are published background, not claimed independently reconstructed.

G3 first for integral bundles: restrict to the full projective closed fibre X over the residue field, which may be nonreduced. Corrected 
Keeler, math/0108068v5 Corollary 5.19, gives generation of A\textasciicircum{}m tensor N uniformly over ALL integral curve-nef N for m 
sufficiently large (a fixed A has a very ample power). Apply it with N\textasciicircum{}k and m=k-1. Thus G=A\textasciicircum{}\{k-1\} 
tensor N\textasciicircum{}k is generated, and
\[
(A\otimes N)^k=A\otimes G
\]
is ample by 28.27.5. Taking a power root shows A tensor N ample on X. Complete Stacks 30.21.4 (0D2N) extends fibre ampleness to relative 
ampleness on a neighbourhood of the closed point. Every open neighbourhood of the closed point in Spec of a local ring is the whole base. 
The argument therefore proves integral curve-nef plus ample on Y. It applies directly to the nonreduced fibre; reduction is unnecessary. If 
used, complete 30.17.5 (01XO) separately supplies nilpotent invariance of ampleness.

The Keeler correction is essential. The complete immediate 1.5 proof, its 4.9--4.10 regularity/generation inputs, and the complete 5.19 
derivation were read together with the ENTIRE appended 2018 erratum. False original 3.3 (geometric integrality without the needed change of 
ground field) is not used. E1.3 replaces it with a finite faithfully flat altered base after localization and smooth geometrically integral 
fibres over the new base. E2.4 transfers vanishing through that finite base; E2.5 repairs the induction proving 1.5. The erratum retains 1.5
 and hence 5.19 on arbitrary projective schemes over arbitrary commutative Noetherian rings. No normal, reduced, characteristic, or smooth 
hypothesis is introduced. Its historical de Jong alteration, EGA, Illusie, Kleiman and regularity dependencies are disclosed published 
background. We do not claim every historical edition has been independently read.

Here is the real-Cartier extension, proved explicitly. Write additive bundle notation in \(\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb 
R\). Call a real class real-ample when it is a finite positive real sum of integral ample classes. Rational curve-nef F plus integral ample 
A is real-ample: for rational t>=0, clearing a common denominator makes A+tF genuinely rational ample by the integral theorem just proved. 
For arbitrary real t, bracket t by two nonnegative rational parameters and take their convex combination. Hence A+tF is real-ample. If S=sum
 s\_j A\_j is real-ample, with s\_j>0 and s=sum s\_j, then
\[
S+F=\sum_j s_j(A_j+F/s)
\]
is real-ample for rational nef F.

Fix an integral ample H and integral classes L\_i spanning a real curve-nef D. G2 gives positive integers N\_i such that N\_i H+L\_i and 
N\_i H-L\_i are ample. On every contracted integral curve, their positive degrees imply |deg L\_i|<=N\_i deg H. For rational delta>0 choose 
rational D\_r in this finite span with error coefficients e\_i in D-D\_r satisfying sum N\_i|e\_i|<delta/4. Then F=D\_r+delta H/4 is 
rational curve-nef. The residual is explicitly real-ample:
\[
D+\delta H-F=(3\delta/4-\sum_i N_i|e_i|)H+
\sum_i |e_i|(N_iH+\operatorname{sign}(e_i)L_i).
\]
The H coefficient is positive; omit zero error terms. Therefore D+delta H=F+S is real-ample. For arbitrary real delta>0 first use a rational
 delta\_0 between zero and delta and add (delta-delta\_0)H. This establishes curve-nef real plus any positive ample perturbation.

We also need finite-span openness, not a finite-rank assertion about the whole Picard group. For an integral ample A and finitely many L\_i 
choose N\_i A +/- L\_i ample. If sum N\_i|e\_i|<1, the identity
\[
A+\sum_i e_iL_i=(1-\sum_i N_i|e_i|)A+
\sum_i|e_i|(N_iA+\operatorname{sign}(e_i)L_i)
\]
is an ample-generator expression. For a general real-ample S reserve one positive summand sA, apply this expression to perturbations of that
 summand, and retain the other summands. This proves openness on every finite-dimensional coefficient span, even when relations exist among 
its classes.

Finally a rational Cartier class that is real-ample is genuinely Q-ample. Let G be the subgroup of Pic(Y) generated by its finitely many 
integral constituents and the integral ample classes in a positive real expression. G is a finitely generated abelian group, with finite 
torsion; \(G\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R\) embeds in \(\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R\) because the REAL NUMBERS are flat
 over Z. This tensor coefficient field is not the local base ring R. In G modulo torsion, equality with the rational class is a finite 
rational linear system for the positive expression coefficients. A positive real solution is approximated by a positive rational solution in
 that rational affine solution space (row reduction over Q proves rational points dense). Clear denominators and then kill the finite 
torsion. A positive integer multiple of the rational class is a tensor product of positive powers of integral ample bundles, hence ample. 
This proves genuine Q-ampleness without asserting finite rank of Pic(Y) or a Neron--Severi group.

\section{n8. Independent geometric construction and unconditional comparison}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1, n3, n4, n5, n6, n7.}

Use n1, n3 and n7 for the construction and comparison, and n4--n6 for its descent rules. Assume the local reduction has positive dimension; 
dimension zero has the unique empty-boundary cone directly. Here is the geometric definition BEFORE its comparison to ideals. Admissible 
models are actual blowups Y\_I of proper primary ideals of the reduced excellent local germ. On such a model consider an exceptional real 
Cartier divisor
\[
D=-\sum_{j=1}^r d_j A_j,\qquad d_j\ge0,
\]
where every A\_j is an ACTUAL effective integral Cartier divisor supported on the closed fibre. Real Cartier divisors here lie in the 
integral Cartier divisor group tensored over Z with the REAL NUMBERS; their bundle classes lie in the corresponding real Picard group. 
Require deg\_C D>=0 for EVERY proper integral curve contracted to the closed point. This is line-bundle degree positivity, and actual 
Cartier effectivity; it is not effectivity of a list of nonnormal Weil coefficients. Neither ideal generation nor membership in a completed 
function cone defines the positivity test.

The model system is directed. Y\_\{IJ\} maps to both Y\_I and Y\_J. To justify this over a reduced ring, on Y\_\{IJ\} the product of the 
pulled-back ideals is invertible, locally (f) with f regular. Set J'=f\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}J in the total quotient sheaf. I J'=O, which 
expresses 1 as a finite sum of products. In a local ring one product ij' is a unit. For any x in I, xj' belongs to O, and x=(xj')/(ij') 
times i. Thus I is principal there, with a regular generator because ij' is a unit in the total quotient ring. J is its invertible inverse 
times (f). The universal property of the blowup gives the two maps. Pullback preserves actual effectivity. For a contracted integral curve 
its image is a point or an integral curve; in the latter case degree of a pulled-back bundle is its image degree times a positive field 
degree, and in the former case it is zero. Thus curve-nefness is preserved. Identifying data after a common pullback is legitimate.

E\_I is a Cartier order unit on Y\_I, not merely a numerical order unit. An integral exceptional Cartier F is trivial as a divisor off the 
closed fibre. The coherent modules (O(F)+O)/O and (O(-F)+O)/O, viewed in the total quotient sheaf, are supported on that fibre. On a finite 
affine cover a common power of I O kills them. Since I O=O(-E), this gives inclusions O(F-NE) subset O and O(-F-NE) subset O. An invertible 
subsheaf of O with a regular local generator defines an actual effective Cartier divisor. Therefore
\[
-NE\le F\le NE
\]
in actual Cartier order, for some integer N. For finite real sums this yields real order bounds too.

Define evaluation on ALL boundary points as follows. For v with support p, first pass to the valued field Frac(R/p). A generator f of I of 
least finite value gives the centre on the f-chart, because every a/f has nonnegative value. The centre is independent of this choice by the
 blowup universal property, or by the overlap units when two generators have the same least value. Pull O(F) back to the spectrum of this 
field's valuation ring. The support's generic point lies outside the exceptional fibre, so O(F) there has its canonical trivialization as O.
 This identifies the pulled-back invertible module with a rank-one lattice inside the quotient fraction field. If g is a generator of that 
lattice, set f\_F(v)=-v(g). Its image is nonzero by the generic trivialization. This is a pullback of an invertible bundle with generic 
trivialization; it does NOT assume a homomorphism from the total quotient ring of R to Frac(R/p). Different generators differ by units of 
the valuation ring and so have value zero. Extend linearly to real divisors. Evaluation is homogeneous on rays, additive, invariant under 
common pullback, and f\_E=v(I). The order-unit bounds make it finite and bounded on a primary section. This construction uses quotient 
fraction fields; it never loses a nonminimal support by trying to use a fraction field of R itself.

We now prove continuity and comparison, rather than stipulate them. For a negative rational relatively ample exceptional L, take arbitrarily
 large sufficiently divisible k for which O(kL) is generated. Its sections F\_k=H\textasciicircum{}0(Y,O(kL)) lie in the finite algebra T of
 n7 because O(kL) subset O. They are finite R-modules by 0B5S. With the FIXED primary ideal c\_0 of n7 set J\_k=c\_0 F\_k. It is an ideal of
 R: multiplication by R preserves sections, and c\_0 T subset m AS ELEMENTS OF R. It is proper. Away from m it is the unit ideal, because 
c\_0 is unit there and O(kL)=O there; localization of H\textasciicircum{}0 and generation give this assertion. Therefore J\_k is proper 
primary. At every valued centre, global generation says the images of the sections generate the local invertible module, and at least one 
coefficient is a unit. Thus
\[
-v(J_k)/k=f_L(v)-v(\mathfrak c_0)/k
\]
on ALL semivaluations. All terms are finite. Since c\_0 is primary, its value is uniformly bounded. Hence f\_L is a uniform limit of 
negative rational primary profiles, with an explicit error bound ||v(c\_0)||/k.

For an arbitrary integral exceptional F, G2 and the order-unit assertion let us choose N so L=F-NE is both actual negative and ample. Apply 
the preceding section construction for any generated divisible k. Its equality gives
\[
f_F=-v(J_k)/k+v(\mathfrak c_0)/k+Nv(I).
\]
Each ideal in this equality is primary. This proves continuity of every exceptional Cartier evaluation, without assuming continuity of 
nonnormal model coefficients. Real evaluations are finite sums, hence continuous. A negative actual effective divisor has nonpositive 
evaluation.

Let M\_geom be all evaluations of the independent negative curve-nef divisors defined above, including zero; set C\_geom to their uniform 
closure, and D\_geom to actual infima of nonempty decreasing C\_geom-nets, including bottom. We prove M\_geom subset C\_R. Write D=-sum d\_j
 A\_j. By n7, D-delta E is real-ample for every delta>0, since -E is ample. In the finite span of the A\_j and E, round ALL nonnegative 
coefficients UP to nearby rational numbers. Finite-span openness retains ampleness; the rounded divisor D' is actual negative and rational. 
It is genuinely Q-ample by the finite-subgroup argument in n7. Continuity and boundedness of the finitely many evaluations give 
||f\_D'-f\_D|| arbitrarily small as delta and rounding errors tend to zero. Apply the fixed-c\_0 section construction to D' and send 
divisible k to infinity. This proves f\_D in C\_R. The generated section profiles can be chosen below f\_D, but only uniform approximation 
is needed. No full-conductor value is divided by k.

Conversely every raw finite REAL negative ideal combination is geometric: pull the finitely many primary-ideal exceptional divisors to their
 common product blowup. Each -E\_i is a pullback of an ample bundle and is curve-nef; each E\_i is actually effective. The combination meets
 the definition and evaluates to the given profile. Unit terms evaluate to zero. Thus
\[
Q_R\subset M_{\rm geom}\subset C_R,\qquad
C_{\rm geom}=C_R,\qquad D_{\rm geom}=D_R.
\]
This is the additional geometric comparison theorem required by ORIGINAL P12.2. It is not a renaming of ideal positivity. Raw equality with 
Q\_R is not claimed.

The geometric meaning is relative Cartier degree positivity on the explicitly stated primary-model system, followed by uniform and 
decreasing completion. We make no cofinality assertion for arbitrary proper birational models, no singular SNC or positive-characteristic 
resolution assertion, and no replacement of actual effectivity by nonnormal Weil coefficients. Finite pullback can also be checked on cores:
 a base primary ideal extends to a boundary ideal on the finite semilocal source; its blowup maps to the base blowup, actual effectivity 
pulls back, and degrees have the point/positive-degree rule. The comparison and n1, n4--n6 prove the full gauge and conductor rules without 
needing a separate raw descent claim.

\section{n9. Full smooth BFJ specialization on all semivaluations}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1, n3, n8.}

Use n1, n3 and n8. The published BFJ application in this note is ONLY at the closed point of a smooth affine variety over an algebraically 
closed field of characteristic zero. Dimension at least two is treated by BFJ; dimensions one and zero are treated directly below. No 
characteristic-free singular resolution is inferred.

The complete used units of Boucksom--Favre--Jonsson, Valuations and plurisubharmonic singularities, were checked from the bound publication:
 the setting; semivaluations and primary profiles; simple modifications, simplices, and retractions in Sections 1.2--1.7; Definitions 2.1 
and 2.5, Proposition 2.2, and 2.7--2.8; 3.6--3.14; and the complete proofs of 3.9--3.10 through 3.18 and 3.22--3.25. The historical smooth 
resolution, usual multiplier ideal subadditivity, and smooth Izumi inputs remain disclosed published background. BFJ's nef Weil cone is its 
weak closed cone generated by formal-ideal divisors; its formal psh functions are finite and strongly continuous on quasi-monomials and have
 that nef coefficient divisor. They extend to ALL semivaluations by
\[
H_W(v)=\inf_\pi H_W(r_\pi v).
\]
Proposition 2.7 says H\_W<=H\_W composed with r\_pi; the composed functions decrease under refinement. The projective-limit statement 1.13 
applies to the all-support compact semivaluation space, not just fraction-field valuations.

Proposition 3.11 proves substantive continuity on each CLOSED simplex. Its proof uses multiplier profiles 
h\_k=(1/k)log|L\textasciicircum{}2(kW)| and the estimate |h\_k-H\_W|<=A/k on divisorial points. Thinness A is bounded on each closed 
simplex. The continuous multiplier profiles are consequently uniformly Cauchy there, and their limit supplies the continuous extension, 
including its faces. One must not substitute the false assertion that a finite convex function is automatically continuous at the boundary 
of a closed simplex.

Correct 3.13 as follows. For a nonzero formal psh g, define, for integers j>=1,
\[
B_j=L^2(2^j g)+\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\,4^j},\qquad
g_j=2^{-j}\log|B_j|=\max\{2^{-j}\log|L^2(2^jg)|,-2^j\}.
\]
The exponents were checked visually in the actual PDF on printed page 475. Subadditivity 3.10 gives the decreasing first term, and 3.9 gives
 convergence to g at every quasi-monomial. The truncation also decreases. The ideals contain a boundary power but early terms can be the 
unit ideal. Nonzero g has g(ord\_m)<0 by 3.14, and 3.9 at ord\_m makes the multiplier profile strictly negative there for all large j. Thus 
B\_j is EVENTUALLY proper primary; discard a finite prefix. For g=0 use the UNIT ideal, not a sequence of proper primary ideals decreasing 
to zero. The identically bottom function is not a finite formal psh function on quasi-monomials; add it separately by 
-N=-v(m\textasciicircum{}N).

The approximants decrease to g on ALL semivaluations. Given finite t>g(v), choose a retraction with g(r\_pi v)<t by the definition of the 
all-retraction infimum, even when g(v) is bottom. Then choose j with g\_j(r\_pi v)<t. The formal-psh inequalities give
\[
g(v)\le g_j(v)\le g_j(r_\pi v)<t.
\]
This proves full convergence; it is not merely divisorial or quasi-monomial convergence. N1 contracts each completed primary B\_j exactly to
 R, preserving the profile. The completed unit also contracts to the unit. Thus every BFJ function, with bottom adjoined, belongs to D\_R, 
and every finite continuous BFJ function belongs to C\_R by the compact decreasing-continuous uniform-convergence argument (Dini's 
open-cover proof).

Conversely any finite real primary profile is BFJ formal psh, since its coefficient divisor is nef and its evaluation is continuous on 
simplices; principalization and the published retractions give its canonical all-semivaluation extension. Let g be a uniform limit of such 
profiles. Its divisorial coefficients give a finite weak limit W in BFJ's closed nef cone. Proposition 3.11 gives H\_W. Uniform convergence 
on quasi-monomials shows g=H\_W there: they agree on dense divisorial points of each simplex and both are continuous there. Moreover the 
same uniform error estimate survives taking the infimum over ALL retractions. Thus g(v)=inf\_pi H\_W(r\_pi v) at every semivaluation. This 
proves C\_R is EXACTLY the finite continuous BFJ subclass.

Now let g=inf\_i g\_i be a decreasing C\_R-net. BFJ 3.14 gives g\_i(v)<=g\_i(ord\_m) at every v (first on quasi-monomials, then by 
retractions). If g(ord\_m) is bottom, g is bottom everywhere. Otherwise 3.14 also gives C(v)g\_i(ord\_m)<=g\_i(v) at every quasi-monomial v,
 so g is finite there. Its divisorial coefficients give a finite weak-nef W. On a simplex the decreasing limit g is finite convex. For any 
point x take its MINIMAL face; x lies in that face's relative interior, where finite convex functions are continuous. H\_W is continuous on 
the whole face by the actual 3.11 theorem. Their equality on the dense rational divisorial points of that relative interior proves equality 
at x. Vertices are already divisorial. This handles every face without asserting closed-simplex continuity from convexity alone.

Finally, extended infima commute over the Cartesian product of the net and ALL models:
\[
g(v)=\inf_i\inf_\pi g_i(r_\pi v)
=\inf_\pi\inf_i g_i(r_\pi v)
=\inf_\pi H_W(r_\pi v).
\]
No arbitrary decreasing-net flattening principle is used. Hence D\_R minus the identically bottom function is exactly the full BFJ formal 
psh class with its canonical extension to all semivaluations. D\_R is that class with bottom adjoined, and n8 gives the same statements for 
D\_geom and C\_geom.

For a smooth DVR every nonempty normalized boundary is a singleton. Primary ideals are powers of the parameter, so C is all finite 
nonpositive constants and D all extended nonpositive constants. The closed point itself is an effective Cartier divisor, and degree 
conditions on contracted curves are empty, giving the same independent geometric core. In dimension zero the centred boundary is empty and 
all statements mean its unique empty function. General primary gauges in the BFJ range follow n1's exact homogeneous cocycle, with bounded 
positive denominators preserving uniform and decreasing convergence. Completion homeomorphism and primary contraction apply without claiming
 equivalent model categories.

Artifacts: n9.md, reports/source-images/bfj-475.png, source-application-ledger.md. Rerun: python inspect\_primary.py; python 
build\_delivery.py. This specialization has precisely the published smooth affine algebraically closed characteristic-zero domain; it does 
not transfer singular SNC theory to arbitrary excellent germs.

\section{n10. Nonisolated cusp: separation from the entire finite-real raw cone}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1, n3, n4, n8.}

Use n1, n3, n4 and n8. Work in characteristic zero, with
\[
R=k[t^2,t^3,z]_{(t^2,t^3,z)},\quad S=k[t,z]_{(t,z)},\quad
\mathfrak a=(t^2,t^3,z),\quad \mathfrak c=t^2S.
\]
Indeed S is finite via t, is normal, and has the same fraction field. R consists of polynomials with no term of t-degree one, localized at 
the stated maximal ideal; multiplying by t shows its conductor is exactly t\textasciicircum{}2S. The quotient R/c is k[z] localized, and S/c
 is its square-zero t-thickening. Their all-semivaluation boundaries are the same singleton when nonempty. N1 therefore makes restriction 
V\_\{aS\}(S) to V\_a(R) a continuous bijection and hence a homeomorphism, including the support (t) upstairs. This is a two-dimensional 
nonisolated cusp, not just a finite curve link.

Write s=w(t), u=w(z), b=z+t and B=w(b); min(2s,u)=1. Allow s,u,B to be infinite whenever the normalization permits. The bounded continuous 
positive profile
\[
A(w)=w((b,t^2))=\min\{B,2s\}
\]
descends topologically. For k>=1 define actual downstairs ideals
\[
K_k=(b^k(z-kt),\ t^2b^k,\ t^{2k+2})\subset R.
\]
The first generator has zero t-linear coefficient: the two contributions k z\textasciicircum{}k and -k z\textasciicircum{}k cancel. The 
other two have t-degree at least two. Localizations do not change membership. The ideals are proper primary: the last generator puts 
t\textasciicircum{}2 and t\textasciicircum{}3 in the radical, and the first then puts z in it.

For EVERY normalized semivaluation, every generator has value at least kA. For the first this is kB+w(z-kt)>=kA, and the other two are 
immediate. The upper bound is a complete case analysis. If A=2s<=B, cancellation forces s=u=1 (different values would give B=min(s,u)<2s), 
and the last generator has value kA+2. If A=B<2s and s<=u, normalization gives s<=1, and the second generator has value kA+2s<=kA+2. If s>u,
 including s infinite, then u=1 and B=w(z-kt)=1; the first generator has value kA+1. The case u infinite belongs to the second case. Thus on
 ALL supports, including cancellation and infinite coordinates,
\[
0\le v(K_k)/k-A\le2/k.
\]
Hence -A lies in C\_R, and is a normalization-raw profile in N\_R. This analytic bound is a proof; a finite sample check is only a 
diagnostic.

We separate A from the ENTIRE finite REAL positive raw cone P\_R, not merely rational single-ideal profiles. Let w\_infty kill t and give z 
value one. Let w\_star be the monomial valuation in coordinates (t,b) with weights (1,2); then z=b-t has value one, so both valuations are 
in the same primary section. They give A(w\_infty)=1 and A(w\_star)=2.

For ANY proper primary downstairs ideal I, put d=w\_infty(I), a positive integer. Choose f in I attaining d; its local denominator is a unit
 at both valuations. Expand in k[[t,z]]: no coefficient of t-degree one occurs. Its degree-d homogeneous part has nonzero 
z\textasciicircum{}d coefficient and zero t z\textasciicircum{}\{d-1\} coefficient. In characteristic zero it cannot be a scalar multiple of
 b\textasciicircum{}d=(z+t)\textasciicircum{}d. After substituting z=b-t, it therefore contains a nonzero term 
t\textasciicircum{}\{d-j\}b\textasciicircum{}j with j<d. That monomial has w\_star-value d+j<=2d-1. Terms of other total degrees cannot 
cancel it, since the linear substitution preserves total degree. If other terms have still smaller value they only strengthen the bound. 
Consequently
\[
w_\star(I)<2w_\infty(I).
\]
Every nonzero finite real positive combination of proper primary gauges retains this strict inequality; unit terms are zero. But A has 
equality. Thus A is outside P\_R, and -A is outside Q\_R. We have proved N\_R is not Q\_R and C\_R is not Q\_R in this example. Their 
uniform closures still agree by n4. This does not assert raw geometric and ideal equality.

Finally, v(c)<infinity is an OPEN complement of the CLOSED infinity stratum, not generally closed. Monomial valuations w\_N(t)=N, w\_N(z)=1 
converge pointwise to w\_infty. Their conductor values are 2N, while w\_infty(c)=infinity. The quantities v(c)/N are therefore not uniform 
errors on the whole section. Neither descent nor comparison uses such an error globally; n4 uses quotient estimates at infinity, and n8 uses
 a fixed PRIMARY correction.

Artifacts: n10.md, exact\_checks.py, reports/exact-checks.json. Rerun: python exact\_checks.py; python build\_delivery.py. The script 
reports its exact finite input domain and does not replace the universal proof or the raw-cone separation argument.

\section{n11. Rejected shortcuts and the radial scope constraint}
\textit{Earlier local supports: n1, n2, n3, n4, n8, n10.}

Use n1--n4, n8 and n10. These are diagnostics, not extra hypotheses.

An incompatible-contraction shortcut is false even over a smooth normal surface. Inject A=k[x,y]\_(x,y) diagonally into A times A and take 
J=((x,y\textasciicircum{}2),(x\textasciicircum{}2,y)). Then I\_N=J\textasciicircum{}N intersect 
A=(x,y\textasciicircum{}2)\textasciicircum{}N intersect (x\textasciicircum{}2,y)\textasciicircum{}N. The m-order of both fibre ideals is 
one. A monomial x\textasciicircum{}a y\textasciicircum{}b belongs to I\_N exactly when 2a+b>=2N and a+2b>=2N. Summing gives a+b>=ceil(4N/3);
 balanced nonnegative exponents with that sum achieve both inequalities. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak m}(I_N)=\lceil4N/3\rceil,
\]
whose normalized limit is 4/3, not one. The two ideal profiles were not fibre constant. No general contraction-as-fibre-minimum formula is 
used in n4--n6.

The literal positive-gauge inequality in BdFFU Proposition 2.4(b) has the wrong sign. At a smooth surface take parameters x and b=x+y, and 
the monomial valuation v(x)=1, v(b)=2. On the first-blowup dual complex its retraction is ord\_m. For I=(x+y,x\textasciicircum{}3), v(I)=2 
whereas r(v)(I)=1. Hence the printed inequality r(v)(I)>=v(I) fails. The negative function -v(I) has the expected opposite inequality. 
Complete Definition 2.1--2.2 and Proposition 2.4 with proof were read from the bound BdFFU paper, solely for this diagnostic. Its own normal
 complex-variety hypotheses do not repair the sign. It supplies no premise of the construction.

The geometric boundary cone is not asserted to be the cone of literal CLD or classical logarithmic radial extensions. On a nodal curve 
R=k[x,y]\_(x,y)/(xy), its finite normalization has two DVR centres. The tuple (-1,0) is in C\_S and is fibre compatible: the conductor has 
finite positive value on both boundary points, so its restriction has no identified pair. N4 therefore puts (-1,0) in C\_R, and n8 puts it 
in C\_geom. For a classical analytic node with two normalized discs, a literal zero logarithmic slope on one disc forces the nodal value to 
be at least zero by upper semicontinuity. The other literal negative slope tends to minus infinity at its origin. If its nodal value is at 
least zero, the subharmonic maximum principle on that disc (the outer-circle value is zero and interior values are negative) forbids the 
resulting interior maximum. Thus this mixed-zero profile cannot be a literal classical psh radial extension. The original dossier's 
corresponding CLD closed-disc obstruction is kept as a scope constraint, not silently overridden or used as a theorem premise. We make no 
CLD comparison theorem for other singular germs. A boundary trace of a different kind is a separate question.

Artifacts: n11.md, exact\_checks.py, reports/exact-checks.json. Rerun: python exact\_checks.py; python build\_delivery.py. The monomial 
computation is proved for all N; finite enumeration only checks a specified range. The sign example is exact. This note rejects invalid 
approaches while retaining the independent geometric construction and its precise scope.

BEGIN ENTIRE exact-scope.md
# Exact scope

The construction is for every excellent local germ, after reduction, with a nonempty intrinsic centred ray boundary when the local reduction
 has positive dimension. Sections use arbitrary proper primary ideals. Nonminimal prime supports and infinite function values are retained. 
Zero-dimensional local reduction gives the empty boundary. For nonreduced germs this is a semivaluation theory of the reduction; nilpotent 
intersection multiplicities are not supplied.

The independent geometric core uses actual primary blowups of the reduced germ, actual negative effective finite real Cartier presentations,
 and degree >=0 on every contracted proper integral curve. Common product-ideal blowups identify presentations. There is no assertion that 
this system is cofinal in all proper birational models, no nonnormal Weil-coefficient substitute for Cartier effectivity, and no 
arbitrary-characteristic resolution assertion. The uniform and actual decreasing completions are justified by the proved comparison 
C_geom=C_ideal and D_geom=D_ideal; core positivity is geometric before that comparison.

P is the finite REAL positive ideal cone; Q=-P; C is its finite continuous uniform closure; D consists of actual decreasing C-nets with 
bottom allowed. N is the normalization-RAW compatible cone. Q subset N subset C, and both uniform closures equal C. The nonisolated cusp 
separates N and C from Q. No raw equality is asserted.

Primary-gauge changes are the exact homogeneous cocycle u_b(v/v(b))=u_a(v)/v(b), with bounded positive denominator. Completion is an 
all-semivaluation homeomorphism with exact primary contraction. Normalization branches are local normal centres above the marked point, not 
merely minimal components. Finite conductor value gives a singleton fibre; infinite value gives exactly the conductor quotient 
identification. The infinity stratum is closed and its finite complement open. Both C and D descend exactly iff constant on all fibres, 
including mixedzero and partialbottom. The same class-level pullback/descent result holds for every reduced finite injection over an 
excellent reduced local target. This supplies the cone rules asked in P12.2, not all geometric operators of P12.6.

Full BFJ specialization is proved on ALL semivaluations at a smooth affine closed germ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 
zero. C is exactly its finite continuous subclass; D is its full canonically retracted formal psh class with identically bottom adjoined. 
Smooth DVR and empty dimension zero are direct. Source domains are not enlarged to positive-characteristic singular SNC settings.

The cone is not identified with literal classical or CLD logarithmic radial extensions. The mixedzero nodal profile (-1,0) belongs to this 
boundary cone and remains excluded by the stated radial compatibility obstruction. Global projective trivially valued energy constructions 
are not claimed to solve this local target.

P12.3 obstacle envelopes, P12.4 bounded mixed Monge--Ampere products, P12.5 energy and P12.6 geometric envelope/product/operator 
functoriality are separate. They are not constructed here and their omission is not a P12.2 gap. This manuscript is a complete-solution 
candidate for ORIGINAL P12.2 only, requiring subsequent independent whole-original review.

END ENTIRE exact-scope.md
