===== ENTIRE QUALIFIED E350 COMPONENT: whole-proof.md =====
# Independent reconstruction of P12.5

This is a mathematical draft, relative only to the **entire qualified G331 and B341** reproduced in the accompanying TeX appendices. Their 
mandatory annotations, ledgers, scopes, acceptance records and the literal SH 17.4.7 qualification remain attached. G331 supplies the 
independently geometric function cones and their comparison, approximation and full conductor descent. B341 supplies the bounded 
**algebraic** mixed moment operator. Neither supplies the higher-dimensional Cartier bridge, locality, or energy results proved below. The 
native250 candidate and ROOT342/344/346 are data examined here, not premises. A successful computation, a hash, or an acceptance label is 
not a mathematical proof.

## 1. Domain, conventions, and theorem

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be excellent local. We use its reduction, still denoted $R$, and $n=\dim R$. Fix a proper $\mathfrak m$-primary ideal 
$\mathfrak a$. For $n>0$ let
$$X=X_{\mathfrak a}=\{v:v(\mathfrak a)=1\}.$$
These are centred real semivaluations with all prime supports retained; no minimal-support restriction is imposed. By qualified G331 this is
 compact Hausdorff. Primary values are positive finite continuous bounded functions. Units have value zero. The independently geometric core
 consists of evaluations of actual negative effective finite real Cartier presentations on actual primary blowups, with nonnegative degree 
on every contracted integral proper curve. Its uniform closure is $C$; its actual decreasing-$C$-net completion is $D$. The comparison 
$C=C_{\rm ideal}$, $D=D_{\rm ideal}$ and their full finite-injection/conductor descent are G331 grants. In particular $C,D$ are nonpositive 
cones, stable under addition, nonnegative scaling and finite maximum. No increasing closure or arbitrary infimum closure of $D$ is assumed. 
Write $D^{\rm bd}$ for its bounded finite-valued part.

Put $p=n-1$. Qualified B341 supplies a positive finite Radon moment measure $\mu(u_1,\ldots,u_p)$ for bounded $D$ inputs, characterized for 
rational primary profiles by
$$\int v(J)\,d\mu(-v(I_1)/k_1,\ldots,-v(I_p)/k_p)
=\frac{e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_p,J)}{\prod_i k_i}.$$
Unit entries give zero. The kernel is symmetric, additive and homogeneous in its negative input cone; scalar gauge moments are ordered. 
Uniform continuity and decreasing-net weak continuity apply with a common bound and a **specified limit in $D^{\rm bd}$**. Scalar moment 
order is not order of measures. B341 also gives the one-factor primary-gauge identity and residue-weighted degree-$n$ normalization identity
 in this bounded algebraic setting. Our proofs extend and geometrically identify this operator; they do not import those missing conclusions
 from B341.

All degree-$n$ operations use the maximal dimension of $R$. Lower-dimensional normalization centres remain in $X,C,D$ and in all fibre 
conditions, but have zero degree-$n$ contribution. Their separate-dimensional products would have another arity. Nilpotent generic lengths 
are not reconstructed from the reduced boundary. In dimension zero the boundary is empty and the unique energy and measure are zero. In 
dimension one the product has zero potential entries, treated directly in Section 9.

For $u\in D$ set $u^k=\max(u,-k)$, where the constant is $-k v(\mathfrak a)$ before choosing the section. Sections 2--5 construct a 
symmetric bounded $n$-form $F$ with
$$F(v,u_1,\ldots,u_p)=\int(-v)\,d\mu(u_1,\ldots,u_p)\quad(v\in D^{\rm bd}),$$
and identify its core restriction with minus an independently defined supported Cartier intersection. Define
$$F_\infty(u_1,\ldots,u_n)=\sup_{k_1,\ldots,k_n}F(u_1^{k_1},\ldots,u_n^{k_n}),\qquad
E(u)=-\frac1n F_\infty(u^{[n]}),\qquad
\mathcal E^1=\{u\in D:F_\infty(u^{[n]})<\infty\}.$$
Brackets indicate repeated slots, never ideal powers. We prove this class is a cone; it has canonical finite Radon mixed measures, extended 
test pairings, full decreasing-net continuity with specified $D$ limits, variation and reference formulas, and exact gauge and conductor 
rules. We also prove bounded Borel strict-maximum locality, nonpolar cutoff identities, total variation convergence for canonical integer 
truncations, comparison, capacity absolute continuity, decreasing-net convergence in capacity and quasicontinuity. These additional 
conclusions require Sections 10--13, not just weak approximation.

The polar class is specified precisely: poles of $z\in D$ with finite reference moment $\int(-z)\,d\mu((-1)^{[p]})$. Section 13 proves a 
branchwise Izumi reduction identifying that condition with exclusion of an entire bottom restriction on every top-dimensional normal centre.
 All finite-energy functions qualify. A globally nonbottom function which is bottom on one top-dimensional branch need not qualify. No whole
 bottom branch is called negligible. No general Choquet compact-above assertion, arbitrary-net total variation convergence, equation 
uniqueness, or complete P12.6 is claimed.

## 2. Supported Cartier intersection without a coefficient field

Let $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ be an actual primary blowup, and let $E$ be an effective exceptional **Cartier** divisor. All components of 
$Y$ dominate positive-dimensional reduced components of $R$ (G331); its primary ideal is locally generated by a regular element. Some power 
of $\mathfrak m$ kills $\mathcal O_E$: on finitely many affine charts the closed-fibre support gives this containment, and a common exponent
 works. Thus $E$ is proper over $R/\mathfrak m^N$. Every coherent cohomology group has finite $R$-length. Define $\chi_R$ as the alternating
 sum of those lengths.

For invertible bundles $L_1,\ldots,L_s$ on $E$, the full proper Euler-polynomial statement Stacks 0BEL gives that
$$\chi_R(E,\bigotimes_i L_i^{t_i})$$
is polynomial for all integer $t_i$, of degree at most $\dim E$. Here is the precise reduction to its field version: filter $\mathcal O_E$ 
by the finite powers of $\mathfrak m$. Each quotient is a coherent sheaf over the residue-field scheme $E_k$. Tensoring with invertible 
bundles preserves the filtration; cohomological Euler additivity applies. An $R$-length of a $k$-vector space equals its $k$-dimension. No 
coefficient-field embedding in $R/\mathfrak m^N$ is used. For every top-dimensional integral component $Z$ the multiplicity in the resulting
 leading coefficient is
$$\sum_j\ell_{\mathcal O_{E_k,\eta_Z}}((\mathfrak m^j\mathcal O_E/\mathfrak m^{j+1}\mathcal O_E)_{\eta_Z})
=\ell_{\mathcal O_{E,\eta_Z}}(\mathcal O_{E,\eta_Z}).$$
This is the full generic Artinian thickness, not the reduced fibre multiplicity. The equality is composition-series additivity in the 
generic Artinian local ring; the filtration quotients have its residue field as simple factors. The top coefficient is therefore the usual 
intersection on this cycle with these lengths, by the full 0BEL cycle/intersection theorem.

For integral exceptional Cartier divisors $D_1,\ldots,D_p$ define $Q_Y(D_1,\ldots,D_p,E)$ to be the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_p$ in
$$\chi_R(E,\mathcal O_Y(\sum_i t_iD_i)|_E).$$
Equivalently it is the $p$-fold finite difference; lower-degree terms vanish. It is additive in the first slots by polynomial substitution. 
Additivity in the last slot follows from
$$0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{E_1}(-E_2)\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{E_1+E_2}
\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{E_2}\longrightarrow0.$$
Tensoring by the variable invertible bundle and taking Euler characteristics shows the twist $-E_2$ changes only lower coefficients, so 
$Q(\boldsymbol D,E_1+E_2)=Q(\boldsymbol D,E_1)+Q(\boldsymbol D,E_2)$.

Symmetry with the last slot must also hold when two cuts have common components. Use the supported Koszul complexes $K_E=[\mathcal 
O(-E)\to\mathcal O]$, $K_H=[\mathcal O(-H)\to\mathcal O]$. Their derived tensor is supported on the closed fibre and is symmetric under 
exchanging its factors, even if the cuts are improper. Tensor with $L$; its Euler characteristic is computable from either two-term 
presentation, giving
$$\chi_R(E,L|_E)-\chi_R(E,L(-H)|_E)
=\chi_R(H,L|_H)-\chi_R(H,L(-E)|_H).$$
For clarity this does not subtract undefined infinite Euler characteristics on $Y$: compute the second Koszul differential on $L|_E$, whose 
two terms have proper Artinian support, or in the reverse order. Both compute the same bounded supported complex. Set $L=\mathcal 
O(tH+sE+\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}r_jG_j)$. Take the coefficient of $\prod r_j$ in the two differences at $t=s=0$. Only terms of total degree $n-1$ 
with one $H$, respectively one $E$, survive; powers at least two would exceed that degree. The signs of the two finite differences are the 
same. Hence $Q(H,\boldsymbol G,E)=Q(E,\boldsymbol G,H)$. For $n=1$ there is only one slot and no symmetry step.

Every integral exceptional Cartier divisor is a difference of effective exceptional Cartier divisors by the actual Cartier order-unit 
assertion in G331. Extend $Q$ by differences and finite real combinations. Additivity makes this extension independent of the choice of 
positive parts; the Koszul symmetry makes it a symmetric real $n$-form. This is an independent local intersection, not a definition using 
mixed-multiplicity moments.

### Actual cycle projection and nonpure dimensions

If $f:Y'\to Y$ is a common primary-model refinement, then for an effective exceptional $E$
$$f_*[f^*E]_{n-1}=[E]_{n-1}$$
as **actual cycles before quotienting by rational equivalence**. Stacks 0AYA, especially its componentwise divisor-cycle projection 
assertion, applies separately to each dominating integral component. All these component maps are birational, of generic degree one. 
Lower-dimensional components have no degree-$n$ cycle. Dimension comparisons use the catenary dimension convention of 02QL; excellence 
supplies universal catenarity. In particular a height-one point on a dimension-$d$ component has closure dimension $d-1$, so one does not 
promote a cut on a smaller component to dimension $n-1$.

One can check the multiplicities directly. At a relevant codimension-one point the reduced local ring $A$ is one-dimensional. It injects 
into the sum of its domain component quotients, with finite-length cokernel $T$. For a regular equation $g$, the multiplication snake 
sequence shows the discrepancy in the two quotient lengths is $\ell(T/gT)-\ell(T[g])=0$. These two lengths coincide by the multiplication 
sequence on the finite-length module $T$. On each component the divisor-cycle projection gives the order times its residue degree. Summing 
recovers exactly $\ell_A(A/gA)$. Thus embedded thickness of the cut and the genuine residue degrees are preserved; there is no nonnormal 
Weil-coefficient replacement for actual Cartier effectivity.

Apply the numerical projection formula on each proper integral component of the supported cycle. It proves
$$Q_{Y'}(f^*D_1,\ldots,f^*D_n)=Q_Y(D_1,\ldots,D_n).$$
Passing first to a global Chow class would be invalid here: a principal parameter on a DVR has supported degree one, whereas its class can 
be zero in the global affine Chow group. The supported cycle proof avoids this loss.

### Raw Rees sections and the ideal diagonal

Let $Y=\operatorname{Bl}_I R$, $E_I$ its actual exceptional Cartier divisor, $D_I=-E_I$, with $\mathcal O(D_I)$ the ample tautological 
bundle. Stacks 0AG7, applied to the **raw** finitely generated Rees algebra, gives
$$H^0(Y,\mathcal O(qD_I))=I^q\quad(q\gg0).$$
Stacks 0B5S gives Serre vanishing for this ample bundle. The exact sequence cutting $E_I$ consequently gives
$$\chi_R(E_I,\mathcal O((q-1)D_I)|_{E_I})=\ell_R(I^{q-1}/I^q)\quad(q\gg0).$$
Compare leading coefficients with the Samuel polynomial: the right side has leading coefficient $e_R(I)/(n-1)!$. The left has 
$Q_Y(D_I^{[p]},E_I)/(n-1)!$. Therefore
$$-Q_Y(D_I^{[n]})=e_R(I).$$
For several primary ideals use their common product blowup. For positive integers $t_i$, $\sum_i t_iD_{I_i}$ is the divisor of the product 
ideal $\prod_i I_i^{t_i}$ on that model, which maps to its blowup by 01OF's universal property. The diagonal identity and the mixed length 
polynomial imply polynomial equality in all $t_i$. The coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_n$ is $n!$ times the corresponding mixed coefficient on 
both sides. Hence
$$-Q(D_{I_1},\ldots,D_{I_n})=e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_n).$$
Unit slots are zero. This proves the ideal intersection comparison without using a normalized-Rees section formula or a finite-window guess 
for the polynomial's stabilization.

## 3. Positive real Cartier atoms, refinement, and the fixed-primary bridge

Normalize a primary model $Y$ componentwise; excellence makes this finite. Call it $N$. For each prime $Z$ of dimension $p$ in its closed 
fibre, the normal generic local ring is a DVR. Let $\nu_Z$ be its order, $b_Z=\nu_Z(\mathfrak a)>0$, and $v_Z=\nu_Z/b_Z\in X$. For negative 
real curve-nef core divisors $D_i$ set
$$\mu_Y(D_1,\ldots,D_p)=\sum_Z b_Z\,\deg_R(D_1|_Z\cdots D_p|_Z)\,\delta_{v_Z}.$$
The degree is the field intersection on the proper integral $R/\mathfrak m$-scheme $Z$, including its actual residue-field degree. 
Normalization plus the supported cycle projection in Section 2 proves, for every exceptional real Cartier test $H$,
$$\int H_H\,d\mu_Y=Q_Y(H,D_1,\ldots,D_p).$$
Indeed the pullback of $H$ has coefficient $\nu_Z(H)$ on $Z$, and $H_H(v_Z)=\nu_Z(H)/b_Z$. This accounts for the one normalization factor in
 the atom, and retains inseparable residue degrees.

These atoms are positive **before** comparison with ideal measures. The restrictions $D_i|_Z$ are real curve-nef. By the entire qualified 
G331 real ample-perturbation result, perturb each $D_i$ on the original $Y$ by $-\varepsilon E_I$ and approximate within its fixed finite 
coefficient span by rational ample classes, retaining actual negativity. Pullback by the finite normalization preserves ampleness (01VG) and
 restriction to proper $Z$ is ample. After clearing denominators the ample mixed degrees are positive, by full 0BEL. The degrees are finite 
polynomial functions of the finitely many coefficients, so their limits are nonnegative. This argument works on nonnormal/nonreduced fibres 
and arbitrary residue fields; no singular resolution or unstated normal-model positivity theorem is inserted. For $p=0$ the degree is the 
residue degree of a point.

Refinement independence is likewise prior to ideal comparison. Between normal component models, a prime on the new model whose image has 
dimension below $p$ contributes zero to the intersection of $p$ pulled-back bundles, by numerical projection. A prime dominating $Z$ has the
 same fraction field; the proper birational map over the normal DVR at $\eta_Z$ is an isomorphism there. Alternatively the divisor-cycle 
projection of a uniformizer gives a sum of positive integral orders times residue degrees equal to one, forcing a single order-one, 
residue-degree-one contributor. Its valuation, $b_Z$, and intersection weight are unchanged. Thus the atomic measure is unchanged. 
Componentwise normalization of a common product refinement provides a comparison model. Lower components are not deleted; they simply have 
no dimension-$p$ contribution.

Here is the missing uniform-function-to-intersection bridge. Fix **one** model $Y=\operatorname{Bl}_I R$. G331 gives finite 
$T=H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\subset Q(R)$ and an integer $h$ with $\mathfrak m^h(T/R)=0$. Fix once
$$\mathfrak c_0=\mathfrak m^{h+1},\qquad \mathfrak c_0T\subset\mathfrak m\subset R.$$
This is primary, not the possibly nonprimary normalization conductor. For a negative rational ample exceptional $L$ and sufficiently 
divisible large $q$, $\mathcal O(qL)$ is globally generated. Put
$$J_{q,L}=\mathfrak c_0 H^0(Y,\mathcal O(qL)).$$
This is an actual ideal of $R$, contained in $\mathfrak m$, and unit off $\mathfrak m$; hence proper primary. On the single refinement
$$Y'=\operatorname{Bl}_{I\mathfrak c_0}R,\qquad D_0=-E_{\mathfrak c_0},$$
the exact image of the pulled-back generating map gives
$$J_{q,L}\mathcal O_{Y'}=\mathcal O_{Y'}(qf^*L+D_0).$$
Right exactness suffices: the original evaluation map is surjective, its pulled-back image is the indicated invertible sheaf, and the 
primary correction is invertible on $Y'$. This equality concerns actual ideal sheaves with regular generic generators, not just numerical 
classes. Thus $Y'$ maps to $\operatorname{Bl}_{J_{q,L}}R$ by 01OF.

At every semivaluation support the pulled-back invertible module has a generating section with a unit coefficient at its valued centre. 
Consequently
$$-v(J_{q,L})/q=H_L(v)-v(\mathfrak c_0)/q.$$
This is uniform on all of $X$, since $\mathfrak c_0$ is primary. More importantly Section 2 and the exact image equality give
$$\frac{e_R(J_{q_1,L_1},\ldots,J_{q_n,L_n})}{\prod_iq_i}
=-Q_{Y'}(f^*L_1+D_0/q_1,\ldots,f^*L_n+D_0/q_n).$$
The right side converges by finite-coefficient polynomial continuity on this **fixed** refinement. Uniform functional approximation alone 
would not prove this identity or convergence.

Approximate real negative curve-nef $D_i$ on $Y$ by negative rational ample $L_{i,j}$ in their finite span, using G331, then take divisible 
$q_i$ large. The same $\mathfrak c_0,Y',D_0$ works for every $j$ and every slot. B341's uniform continuity, the displayed all-support 
profile identity and this finite-coefficient intersection convergence give
$$F(H_{D_1},\ldots,H_{D_n})=-Q_Y(D_1,\ldots,D_n).$$
In this formula $F$ on continuous inputs can equivalently be defined by the bounded polynomial kernel in Section 5. To identify the atomic 
measure it is enough to fix every primary ideal test $-v(J)$, which is another core divisor, and use the same comparison on a common fixed 
model. These ideal test differences are uniformly dense in all continuous tests by G331. The atom pairing and B341 moments are equal on that
 dense class, and both measures are finite. Thus the independent positive atomic operator equals the bounded algebraic operator on every 
real core tuple. Arbitrary Cartier tests follow by differences using the Cartier order unit. This is the geometric bridge, not an appeal to 
a provenance label.

## 4. Strict maximum identity and ordinary open locality

First take rational ideal profiles $u=-v(A)/q$, $v=-v(B)/q$, and core data in all other slots. Use a common primary model where $A,B,S=A+B$ 
are invertible. The ratios $L=A\mathcal O/S\mathcal O$ and $M=B\mathcal O/S\mathcal O$ are legitimate actual subideals, and $L+M=\mathcal 
O$. At a fibre prime $Z$ where $u(v_Z)>v(v_Z)$, $M|_Z\to\mathcal O_Z$ vanishes generically and hence identically on integral $Z$. The 
surjectivity of $L+M$ then makes $L|_Z\to\mathcal O_Z$ an isomorphism. The restrictions of the $A$ and $S$ divisor bundles therefore 
coincide on $Z$, as do their atomic weights with the other slots fixed. This proves the strict-max identity at the atom level. It does not 
divide a noninvertible ideal by a rational function on a nonnormal model.

Uniform rational approximation extends it to continuous $C$ inputs. Explicitly, take a continuous test with compact support 
$K\subset\{u>v\}$; the gap has a positive minimum on $K$, so uniform approximation preserves its sign there. Weak convergence then preserves
 the tested identity. On a compact Hausdorff space, equality on such legitimate continuous tests gives equality of the Radon restrictions to
 the open strict set. Approximate the other bounded $D$ slots by their actual bounded decreasing $C$ nets and use B341 weak continuity on 
the same fixed test. Thus strict-max locality holds when the compared entries are continuous and the other slots bounded $D$.

For ordinary open locality let bounded $u,v\in D$ agree on an open $U$, fix the other bounded slots, and fix a continuous test supported in 
compact $K\subset U$. Choose actual decreasing continuous representations $u_\alpha\downarrow u$, $v_\beta\downarrow v$. For fixed $\alpha$ 
and $\varepsilon>0$, the open sets
$$\{v_\beta-\varepsilon<u_\alpha\}$$
cover $K$, since their limits equal $u$ on $K$. A finite subcover and directedness give one $\beta$ and all its successors. Continuous 
strict-max locality makes the tested measure of $u_\alpha$ equal that of $\max(u_\alpha,v_\beta-\varepsilon)$. Let $\beta$ decrease to its 
specified bounded $D$ limit $\max(u_\alpha,v-\varepsilon)$, then let $\alpha$ decrease to $\max(u,v-\varepsilon)$. These maxima belong to 
$D$ by its finite-max rule. This gives the tested equality with $u$. Interchange $u,v$ and use the second compact cover to obtain the 
analogous equality with $v$. Finally both maxima are within $\varepsilon$ of $\max(u,v)$, globally; bounded uniform continuity lets 
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The tested measures of $u,v$ coincide. Radon regularity gives equality on $U$; replacing finitely many slots one 
at a time proves full bounded open locality. There is no measurable-net monotone-convergence step and no increasing-$D$ completion step 
here.

## 5. The full bounded symmetric form and discontinuous tests

On rational profiles define
$$F(-v(I_1)/k_1,\ldots,-v(I_n)/k_n)=e_R(I_1,\ldots,I_n)/\prod_i k_i.$$
B341 supplies its presentation independence, symmetry, cone multilinearity and order. For entries in $[-M,0]$, negative-constant shifts and 
expansion imply
$$|F(\boldsymbol u)-F(\boldsymbol w)|\le[(M+\varepsilon)^n-M^n]e_R(\mathfrak a)$$
if every coordinate differs uniformly by at most $\varepsilon$. Rational slightly larger bounds remove rationality restrictions. Uniform 
approximation defines the same form on $C$. For bounded $D$ tuples take the finite product of their actual decreasing $C$ representations. 
Form values increase and are bounded by $M^n e_R(\mathfrak a)$. Define $F$ as their supremum.

Representation independence follows from a compact **continuous** strict cover: for fixed majorants $h_i\in C$, $h_i\ge u_i$, the sets 
$\{g_{i,\alpha}<h_i+\varepsilon\}$ cover $X$. One index works in each of the finitely many slots. Thus $g_{i,\alpha}-\varepsilon\le h_i$; 
shift expansion bounds the discrepancy by the displayed vanishing error. Reversing two representations proves independence. It also proves 
the exact formula
$$F(\boldsymbol u)=\sup\{F(h_1,\ldots,h_n):h_i\in C,\ h_i\ge u_i\}.$$
Here all majorants inherit the common bound from the bounded target. The same compact cover for upper-semicontinuous bounded $D$ nets proves
 full decreasing-net continuity when the specified limit belongs to $D^{\rm bd}$ and all entries have a common bound. Addition is obtained 
by product nets of continuous summands; scaling and symmetry pass through the scalar limits. This proves the full $n$-form, not just an 
$(n-1)$-slot weak operator.

We need a Radon directed-integral lemma, not general measurable-net monotone convergence. If $f_\alpha\ge0$ is an increasing net of 
continuous functions on a compact Hausdorff space and $f=\sup f_\alpha$, then for a finite Radon measure $\sigma$
$$\int f\,d\sigma=\sup_\alpha\int f_\alpha\,d\sigma.$$
Indeed $f$ is lower semicontinuous. Inner regularity of its open superlevels, finitely many level steps and Urysohn cutoffs show that its 
integral is the supremum of integrals of continuous nonnegative minorants. For any such minorant $h$ and any $\varepsilon>0$, the open sets 
$\{f_\alpha>h-\varepsilon\}$ cover the compact space; directedness selects one index. This proves the formula, also for infinite integrals. 
A pointwise increasing net of arbitrary measurable functions would not justify the same argument.

For bounded $v\in D$ choose an actual continuous representation $g_\alpha\downarrow v$. Against fixed bounded $\mu(\boldsymbol u)$ the lemma
 applied to $-g_\alpha$ computes the integral of $-v$. For fixed continuous $g_\alpha$, B341 weak convergence in the other slots identifies 
its integral with the corresponding limit of $F$. All these nonnegative scalar suprema commute over the finite product of directed sets. It 
follows that
$$\int(-v)\,d\mu(\boldsymbol u)=F(v,\boldsymbol u)$$
for every bounded **discontinuous** $D$ test. In particular this pairing is symmetric in all $n$ entries. It is the additional 
test-continuity statement needed in the Borel and finite-energy arguments below.

## 6. Conditional Cauchy, full Hölder, and concavity

The required mixed inequality is
$$F(a,b,c_3,\ldots,c_n)^2\le F(a,a,c_3,\ldots,c_n)F(b,b,c_3,\ldots,c_n).\tag{6.1}$$
For ideals this is proved by reducing all three expressions over the **same** sequence of quotients, not by separately choosing reductions. 
If the residue field is finite, pass algebraically to $R(Z)=R[Z]_{\mathfrak mR[Z]}$. Full SH 8.4.1--2 gives faithful flatness and equal 
dimension. To check lengths exactly, tensor a finite composition series: each residue-field factor becomes $k(Z)$ and has length one over 
the new local ring. Thus all length polynomials and coefficients agree. No boundary identification under this transcendental extension is 
asserted.

Over the infinite residue field, in the slot $K_3$ choose a superficial element simultaneously for the three tuples $(I,I,K_3,\ldots)$, 
$(I,J,K_3,\ldots)$ and $(J,J,K_3,\ldots)$, avoiding every minimal prime of the current quotient. Full SH 17.2.1--4 supplies each allowed set
 as the complement of finitely many proper subspaces in $K_3/\mathfrak mK_3$. Their finite intersection still has a rational point. At each 
next slot repeat in the same quotient ring for the three remaining tuples. Avoiding the minimal primes makes its dimension drop exactly one:
 the upper bound follows from avoidance, and the lower bound from lifting a system of parameters and the height theorem. Nonreduced, 
embedded and nonpure quotient components are allowed.

For completeness the annihilator correction is finite. The eventual-colon assertion in SH 17.2.4 implies $(0:x)\cap AM=0$ for a sufficiently
 deep primary product $A$. Therefore $(0:x)$ injects into $M/AM$ and has finite length. In dimension greater than one its contribution is 
below the leading degree, so SH 17.4.6 reduces the mixed coefficient exactly. At the final dimension-one reduction its finite annihilator 
term must be kept. The literal SH 17.4.7 printed colon length must be read as
$$\ell\big(0:_{M/(x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1})M}x_d\big)
=\ell\big(((x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1})M:x_d)/(x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1})M\big).$$
The unquotiented printed colon can have infinite length. In a regular parameter sequence this finite quotient annihilator is zero; outside 
that case we do not discard it or assert a regular sequence.

After $n-2$ simultaneous cuts, full SH 17.7.1--3 applies in dimension two. Here is the essential inequality at its actual hypotheses. By SH 
8.3.7/9 replace $I$ by a two-generated minimal reduction $(a,b)$ without changing multiplicities. The length inequality used in 17.7.1, 
followed by the dimension-two parameter bound (SH 11.2.9--10), gives, for positive integers $r,s$,
$$e(I^rJ^s)\le2r^2e(I)+2s^2e(J).$$
Product linearity expands its left side as $r^2e(I)+2rs e(I,J)+s^2e(J)$. Hence
$$2rs e(I,J)\le r^2e(I)+s^2e(J).$$
Optimize over positive rational $r/s$ (dense in the positive reals) to get $e(I,J)^2\le e(I)e(J)$. The source proof applies to arbitrary 
Noetherian local dimension-two rings with infinite residue field; it does not assume Cohen--Macaulayness. The same quotient sequence in the 
preceding paragraph proves (6.1) for arbitrary fixed mixed slots. Power scaling gives rational profiles, and uniform and actual decreasing 
continuity give bounded $C,D$ inputs. Unit or zero entries follow directly, or by adding a vanishing negative primary constant before taking
 limits.

This conditional inequality implies the **full** Hölder bound
$$F(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\le\prod_{i=1}^n F(u_i^{[n]})^{1/n}.\tag{6.2}$$
Here is a finite proof, avoiding an unexplained invocation of generalized Alexandrov--Fenchel. First perturb each input by a positive 
multiple of $r=-1$, so all relevant form values are positive. On the finite integer simplex $\{\alpha\in\mathbb N^s:|\alpha|=n\}$ set
$$H(\alpha)=\log F(u_1^{[\alpha_1]},\ldots,u_s^{[\alpha_s]})-\sum_i\frac{\alpha_i}{n}\log F(u_i^{[n]}).$$
It is zero at the vertices. Whenever $\alpha_i,\alpha_j>0$, (6.1) gives $2H(\alpha)\le H(\alpha+e_i-e_j)+H(\alpha-e_i+e_j)$. If its maximum 
were positive, choose a maximizing point with the smallest number of nonzero coordinates. Both neighbours also maximize. Transfer one unit 
repeatedly from $j$ to $i$; as long as both remain positive the same maximum argument applies. Eventually $j=0$, giving a maximizing point 
of smaller support, a contradiction. Thus $H\le0$. Apply this to the tuple with each entry once, then let the perturbations vanish using 
bounded multilinearity. This proves (6.2), including zero diagonal values.

Set $A(u)=F(u^{[n]})^{1/n}$ for bounded inputs, and $\delta=e_R(\mathfrak a)^{1/n}$. Expand $F((u+v)^{[n]})$ and use (6.2) term by term. The
 binomial theorem gives $A(u+v)\le A(u)+A(v)$, and $A(tu)=tA(u)$ for $t\ge0$. This is a seminorm on the negative cone; nonpure null 
directions are possible.

For bounded $U,V$ and fixed bounded negative slots $K$, (6.1) shows
$$F(U-V,U-V,K)\ge(\sqrt{F(U,U,K)}-\sqrt{F(V,V,K)})^2\ge0.$$
The form here extends algebraically to differences; $F(U,V,K)$ is nonnegative and at most the geometric mean. For $u_t=(1-t)U+tV$, 
differentiating its finite polynomial energy gives
$$\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\big[-F(u_t^{[n]})/n\big]=-(n-1)F(V-U,V-U,u_t^{[n-2]})\le0.$$
For $n=1$ the energy is linear and this second derivative assertion is unnecessary. Concavity on unbounded finite-energy inputs follows 
later by decreasing bounded approximations. Positivity of this signed quadratic form does not imply uniqueness in null directions.

## 7. Truncations, all majorants, and the first unbounded approximation lemma

For arbitrary $D$ inputs the extended form in Section 1 is well defined as a nonnegative supremum. Its independent truncation levels are 
cofinal with a common integer level. Moreover
$$F_\infty(\boldsymbol u)=\sup\{F(h_1,\ldots,h_n):h_i\in C,\ h_i\ge u_i\}.\tag{7.1}$$
If $h_i\ge u_i$, then for $k_i\ge\|h_i\|_\infty$, $u_i^{k_i}\le h_i$ and bounded form order gives $F(\boldsymbol h)\le F(\boldsymbol 
u^{\boldsymbol k})$. Conversely each bounded truncation has the bounded all-majorant formula of Section 5; its continuous majorants are also
 majorants of $u_i$. Taking the suprema proves both directions. This argument does not create a new definition of $D$ or flatten nested 
nets.

Let $u_i\in\mathcal E^1$ and write $A_i=F_\infty(u_i^{[n]})^{1/n}$. Suppose **bounded** $D$ tuples $f_{i,\lambda}$ decrease to the specified
 $u_i$, with no common lower bound. Their individual diagonal sizes are at most $A_i$ by order, so bounded Hölder bounds every mixed form by
 $\prod A_i$. For fixed continuous majorants $h_i\ge u_i$, the open sets $\{f_{i,\lambda}<h_i+\varepsilon\}$ cover $X$. Upper semicontinuity
 of $f_{i,\lambda}$ and continuity of $h_i$ make these sets open; compactness and directedness select one common index for every slot. Thus 
$f_{i,\lambda}-\varepsilon\le h_i$. Expand the **bounded** form:
$$F(\boldsymbol h)\le F(\boldsymbol f_\lambda)+\prod_i(A_i+\varepsilon\delta)-\prod_i A_i.$$
For each nonempty subset of shifted slots, Hölder gives the corresponding product of $A_i$ and $\varepsilon\delta$. All constants are target
 diagonal sizes, independent of the growing sup norms. Send $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, then take (7.1). Together with order this proves
$$F(\boldsymbol f_\lambda)\uparrow F_\infty(\boldsymbol u).\tag{7.2}$$
This is the **first** finite-energy approximation theorem. It has been proved before assuming $\mathcal E^1$ is additive or that $F_\infty$ 
is multilinear. It also gives extended Hölder directly by taking truncations. In particular $F_\infty(\boldsymbol u)\le\prod A_i<\infty$ for
 finite-energy entries.

Now prove the cone property. If $u,v\in\mathcal E^1$, $s_k=u^k+v^k$ is bounded $D$, decreases to the already specified $D$ function $u+v$ 
(G331's addition rule), and bounded Minkowski gives $A(s_k)\le A(u)+A(v)$. Applying the compact-majorant estimate used above to every 
diagonal majorant of $u+v$, with this fixed bound, and then (7.1), proves $F_\infty((u+v)^{[n]})^{1/n}\le A(u)+A(v)$. Thus the sum is in 
$\mathcal E^1$. Positive scaling follows from cofinal rescaling of truncation levels; zero is separate and has energy zero.

Only **after** this cone proof use (7.2) for $u^k+v^k\downarrow u+v$ and the other truncated finite-energy slots. Bounded additivity passes 
to the limits and proves full cone multilinearity of $F_\infty$. Its symmetry, order, Hölder and Minkowski survive. Bounded concavity and 
pointwise convergence of the finite energies give concavity of $E$ on $\mathcal E^1$. Globally bottom has infinite energy whenever $n>0$, 
since $F((-k)^{[n]})=k^ne_R(\mathfrak a)$; bottom on a zero-degree lower component can instead be a null direction. Both facts are part of 
the convention, not a claim that all bottom sets are polar.

## 8. Canonical finite measures, extended tests, and full nets

For $\boldsymbol u\in(\mathcal E^1)^p$, the bounded measures $\mu(u_1^k,\ldots,u_p^k)$ have mass at most $\delta\prod_i A_i$, by (6.2) with 
the test $r=-1$. Each primary ideal gauge moment tends by (7.2) to
$$F_\infty(-v(J),u_1,\ldots,u_p).$$
Differences of these continuous gauges are uniformly dense in all continuous functions by G331. Their limiting functionals are positive, and
 the common mass bound extends them uniquely to a positive bounded functional on $C(X,\mathbb R)$. Compact-Hausdorff Riesz gives the 
canonical finite positive Radon measure $\mu(\boldsymbol u)$. Density also gives weak convergence. The same argument with any bounded 
decreasing approximations to the finite-energy targets, **without** a common bound, proves independence and weak convergence by (7.2).

For $v\in\mathcal E^1$ choose an actual decreasing $C$ representation $g_\alpha\downarrow v$. All terms lie in $\mathcal E^1$ and have size 
at most $A(v)$. Apply the directed Radon lemma of Section 5 against the fixed $\mu(\boldsymbol u)$. For fixed continuous $g_\alpha$, weak 
convergence of the truncation measures and (7.2) identify its integral with $F_\infty(g_\alpha,\boldsymbol u)$. Commuting nonnegative scalar
 suprema and (7.1), or the same compact-majorant argument, gives
$$\int(-v)\,d\mu(\boldsymbol u)=F_\infty(v,\boldsymbol u)\le A(v)\prod_iA_i.\tag{8.1}$$
Hence every finite-energy test is integrable against every finite-energy mixed measure. For arbitrary $v\in D$, use the integer sequence 
$v^k$ and ordinary sequential monotone convergence; (8.1) extends to an equality in $[0,\infty]$. In particular every finite-energy input 
pole has zero mixed measure, since its nonnegative integral is finite. No $\infty-\infty$ operation is made.

For decreasing finite-energy nets $u_{i,\lambda}\downarrow u_i\in\mathcal E^1$, their diagonal sizes are bounded by those of the specified 
limits. Repeat the continuous-majorant compact cover and use the now proved unbounded multilinearity and Hölder in the negative-shift 
expansion. This proves $F_\infty(\boldsymbol u_\lambda)\uparrow F_\infty(\boldsymbol u)$ and weak mixed-measure convergence on the dense 
gauge-difference tests, then all continuous tests. The net need not be sequential or commonly bounded in sup norm.

The exact uniform-energy criterion is: if $u_\lambda\in\mathcal E^1$ decreases to a **specified** $u\in D$, then
$$u\in\mathcal E^1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sup_\lambda F_\infty(u_\lambda^{[n]})<\infty.$$
The forward direction is order. For the reverse direction take any continuous majorant $h\ge u$, select $\lambda$ with 
$u_\lambda-\varepsilon\le h$ by the open compact cover, and use the proved finite-energy negative-shift expansion with the uniform diagonal 
bound. Then (7.1) gives finite diagonal size for $u$. The net continuity just proved applies afterwards. Limit membership in $D$ is an 
explicit hypothesis; this criterion does not assert infimum closure of the geometric class.

## 9. Variation, reference, primary gauge, normalization, and smooth convention

Fix a finite-energy reference $w$. Define the relative energy by the absolutely meaningful expression
$$E_w(u)=\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{p}\int(u-w)\,d\mu(u^{[j]},w^{[p-j]}).$$
Each of the two negative tests is separately integrable by (8.1), so the difference is defined almost everywhere and integrable; common 
poles are null for these measures. Cone multilinearity gives the telescoping identity
$$E_w(u)=E(u)-E(w),\qquad E_z(u)=E_w(u)+E_z(w).$$
On a finite-energy segment $u_t=(1-t)u+tv$, differentiation of the finite polynomial gives
$$\frac d{dt}E(u_t)=\int(v-u)\,d\mu(u_t^{[p]}).$$
This formula, endpoint versions included, follows by polynomial expansion of $F_\infty$, with integrability supplied before subtraction. 
Concavity is Section 7. Zero is the energy anchor; $r=-1$ is a primary reference with **nonzero curvature** and mass $e_R(\mathfrak a)$, not
 a locally flat additive constant.

For another proper primary gauge $\mathfrak b$, put $d(v)=v(\mathfrak b)$ on $X_{\mathfrak a}$ and $T(v)=v/d(v)$. Both $d$ and $1/d$ are 
bounded positive continuous. Homogeneous inputs obey $u_{\mathfrak b}(T(v))=u_{\mathfrak a}(v)/d(v)$. The bounded B341 identity is
$$\mu_{\mathfrak b}(\boldsymbol u_{\mathfrak b})=T_*[d\,\mu_{\mathfrak a}(\boldsymbol u_{\mathfrak a})].\tag{9.1}$$
Pair a transformed test with this measure: its $1/d$ cancels this **one** factor $d$, so the bounded $n$-form is gauge invariant. For 
unbounded inputs the transformed truncation pulls back to $\max(u_{\mathfrak a},-kd)/d$. The numerator $w_k=\max(u_{\mathfrak a},-kd)$ is 
bounded $D$ and decreases to $u_{\mathfrak a}$. It is squeezed between constant cuts with levels $k\inf d$ and $k\sup d$, which are cofinal.
 Consequently its diagonal supremum equals the constant-truncation diagonal supremum, also when infinite. This proves gauge invariance of 
$F_\infty,E,\mathcal E^1$. For finite-energy tuples the first bounded approximation theorem and the continuous weight $d$ pass (9.1) to the 
limit. The gauge cocycle is immediate from multiplying the ray denominators; there is neither $d^n$ nor an inverse-power factor.

Let $S$ be the finite normalization and $q$ its local normal centres, with $f_q=[\kappa(q):\kappa(\mathfrak m)]$, and restriction $\rho_q$. 
B341's bounded identity passes through finite sums and truncations to
$$F_{\infty,R}(\boldsymbol u)=\sum_{\dim S_q=n}f_q F_{\infty,S_q}(\rho_q^*\boldsymbol u),\qquad
\mu_R(\boldsymbol u)=\sum_{\dim S_q=n}f_q\rho_{q,*}\mu_{S_q}(\rho_q^*\boldsymbol u).\tag{9.2}$$
All terms are nonnegative before forming the energy, so infinite suprema commute with the finite sum. These are actual residue degrees, 
including inseparable ones; normalization has generic degree one on each reduced component. Finite energy downstairs is equivalent to finite
 energy on every top-dimensional normal centre. The $D$-class condition still requires constancy on the **full** restriction fibres: 
singleton fibres at finite conductor value, exact conductor-quotient fibres at infinite value. Lower-dimensional centres remain constrained 
by this class descent and are not discarded. Arbitrary fibre-constant upstairs data must first descend in $D$ by G331; (9.2) then supplies 
their energy criterion. This does not define a general finite-map energy pushforward or solve all P12.6.

For a reduced excellent curve, the entire boundary is the finite set $v_q=\operatorname{ord}_q/a_q$ where 
$a_q=\operatorname{ord}_q(\mathfrak a)>0$. The geometric zero-potential reference measure from B341 is
$$\mu=\sum_q f_q a_q\delta_{v_q},\qquad E(u)=\sum_qf_qa_qu(v_q).$$
Thus $\mathcal E^1$ consists exactly of finite nonpositive branch vectors. All residue degrees, units, zeros and mixed-zero vectors are 
retained. A branch bottom is infinite energy and has positive reference mass. A smooth DVR with maximal-ideal gauge has reference mass one. 
Dimension zero has the empty measure and energy zero, without negative arity. For nonreduced rings these formulas use the reduction: 
$k[[t]]$ and $k[[t]][\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ have identical reduced boundary and gauge but lengths $N$ and $2N$ for their parameter 
quotients. Unreduced intersection multiplicity needs additional generic-length data.

### Direct comparison with exact BFJ Definition 4.3

Here, and only here, the germ is a smooth affine **closed** point over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, $n\ge2$. G331 
identifies $C,D$ with the full BFJ formal psh class on all semivaluations, with global bottom adjoined. The complete BFJ Setting, 1.14, 
2.3--2.8 and Section 4 give its Cartier evaluation, closed-simplex/all-retraction extension, and canonical nef intersection
$$\langle Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\rangle=\inf\{\langle W_1,\ldots,W_n\rangle:W_i\text{ nef Cartier},\ W_i\ge Z_i\}.\tag{BFJ4.3}$$
The value may be $-\infty$. BFJ itself does **not** name an $\mathcal E^1$ space here. Define the canonical finite-self-intersection 
convention directly as those formal psh $g$ for which $\langle Z_g^{[n]}\rangle> -\infty$, with energy $\langle Z_g^{[n]}\rangle/n$.

We prove equality with our class, rather than attaching a smooth name. The coefficient order $W\ge Z_g$ is equivalent to $H_W\ge g$ on all 
semivaluations. Divisorial order gives order on each closed simplex by the actual BFJ continuity and dense divisorial points; all-retraction
 infima then preserve it on every support. Conversely divisorial values are part of the full boundary. BFJ 1.14/2.2 makes a nef Cartier 
evaluation finite continuous formal psh, hence in $C$ by G331. For an arbitrary BFJ nef Cartier tuple, B341's exact bounded BFJ operator 
comparison together with the full BFJ 4.6 test pairing gives $F(H_{W_1},\ldots,H_{W_n})=-\langle W_1,\ldots,W_n\rangle$. All these 
evaluations are bounded, so this use of B341 remains inside its grant. It does not assert that every BFJ model is dominated by a primary 
model. On primary ideal tuples the coefficient/generic-length convention agrees by repeated SH 17.4.6 and the corrected zero annihilator in 
the regular ring, as in B341's qualification. Thus Cartier majorants give a subset of the all-$C$ majorants in (7.1), with exactly the same 
bounded form values.

For the reverse equality, take any nonzero $C$ majorant $h\ge u$. On this normal branch G331's zero dichotomy makes $h$ uniformly negative, 
say $h\le-c<0$. For small $\eta>0$, approximate $(1-\eta)h$ uniformly by a rational primary profile with error $<\eta c/2$. The profile is 
at least $h+\eta c/2\ge u$, is a nef Cartier majorant, and tends uniformly to $h$ as $\eta\downarrow0$. For a tuple do this in each slot; 
bounded form continuity proves equality of the suprema. A zero majorant gives zero form and needs no approximation, and an input $u=0$ has 
only the zero nonpositive majorant in that slot. Global bottom is excluded by infinite diagonal size. Therefore
$$F_\infty(\boldsymbol u)=-\langle Z_{u_1},\ldots,Z_{u_n}\rangle,$$
and our $\mathcal E^1,E$ equal **exactly** the BFJ finite-self-intersection convention just stated. This proves the requested smooth 
specialization without inventing a named BFJ energy space.

For finite-energy tuples Hölder gives finite reference mass, so BFJ 4.6's unique measure exists and its ideal moments identify it with ours.
 BFJ 4.4 gives decreasing-family continuity: coefficientwise decreasing nets converge in the weak coefficient topology, and upper 
semicontinuity together with monotonicity gives the limit. BFJ 4.8 alone is sequential and is not used as a net theorem. The DVR and empty 
cases above are direct; no singular or positive-characteristic resolution assertion is inferred.

## 10. Bounded test algebra and full Borel strict-max locality

The real span of $D^{\rm bd}$ is a product algebra. To prove this from the actual class, fix $u\in[-M,0]\cap D$ and set $q_M(t)=t^2+2Mt$. On
 $[-M,0]$ it is convex, increasing and nonpositive. Its tangent at $s\in[-M,0]$ is
$$2(s+M)t-s^2,$$
with nonnegative slope and nonpositive constant. Finite maxima of these tangents evaluated at a bounded $g\in C$ belong to $C$ and converge 
uniformly to $q_M(g)$, so $q_M(g)\in C$. If $g_\alpha\downarrow u$ is its actual $C$ representation, all terms are in $[-M,0]$ and 
monotonicity gives $q_M(g_\alpha)\downarrow q_M(u)$. Thus $q_M(u)\in D^{\rm bd}$ by an actual representation. Hence
$$u^2=q_M(u)-2Mu\in\operatorname{span}D^{\rm bd},\qquad
uv=((u+v)^2-u^2-v^2)/2\in\operatorname{span}D^{\rm bd}.$$
Constants belong to this span; distributivity gives a real product algebra. No increasing closure or arbitrary continuous functional 
calculus of $D$ is assumed.

This construction also justifies **moving product tests**. For example, with actual bounded continuous representations $u_\alpha\downarrow 
u$, $v_\beta\downarrow v$, the identity expressing products as sums of $q_M$ applied to their sums yields finite linear combinations of 
bounded $D$ entries with actual decreasing $C$ representations and specified limits. Section 5's full symmetric $n$-form continuity 
therefore passes their pairings to the limit when the measure inputs also move. This is stronger than weak convergence tested against a 
fixed continuous function; weak convergence alone would not justify these moving tests.

For bounded $u,v$ let $w=\max(u,v)$ and $\Delta=w-v\ge0$, and fix the other bounded slots $\boldsymbol t$. We claim
$$\Delta\,[\mu(u,\boldsymbol t)-\mu(w,\boldsymbol t)]=0.\tag{10.1}$$
For continuous compared inputs this follows from Section 4 on $\{u>v\}$; elsewhere $\Delta=0$. Approximate compared inputs by their actual 
bounded continuous nets, and the other slots similarly. For any fixed ideal-difference continuous test $h$, the moving $\Delta_\alpha h$ is 
in the product algebra just proved, with the explicit decreasing representations for its constituent terms. Full form continuity in **all** 
slots passes the weighted identity to the limits. Thus (10.1) holds tested against every such $h$. Uniform density and the finite 
mass/bounded weight bounds extend it to every continuous $h$. Multiplication of a finite Radon measure by a bounded Borel function is again 
Radon: approximate that function in measure by finite simple functions and use the regularity of the original finite measure. Riesz 
uniqueness now proves (10.1) as a signed Radon measure identity.

On $\{\Delta\ge1/m\}$ divide the zero signed weighted measure by its bounded measurable reciprocal. Taking the countable union over $m$ 
gives
$$\mu(u,\boldsymbol t)|_{\{u>v\}}=\mu(\max(u,v),\boldsymbol t)|_{\{u>v\}}.\tag{10.2}$$
The strict set is Borel because the inputs are Borel; it need not be open for two upper-semicontinuous functions. This is full Borel 
strict-max locality, independently proved. It is not an attempted use of ordinary open locality on a nonopen set. For $p=0$ both measures 
are the same reference measure and this identity is automatic.

## 11. Finite-energy nonpolar cutoffs and canonical total variation

Let $u_1,\ldots,u_p\in\mathcal E^1$ and
$$U_k=\bigcap_i\{u_i>-k\},\qquad \mu_k=\mu(u_1^k,\ldots,u_p^k).$$
We prove the setwise cutoff identity
$$\mathbf1_{U_k}\mu_k=\mathbf1_{U_k}\mu(\boldsymbol u).\tag{11.1}$$
Fix one slot $u$, put $w=\max(u,-k)$ and $\Delta=w+k$. This nonnegative bounded span test is positive exactly on $\{u>-k\}$. For every 
integer $\ell\ge k$, bounded strict-max locality gives
$$\Delta[\mu(u^\ell,\boldsymbol t^\ell)-\mu(w,\boldsymbol t^\ell)]=0.$$
Test it with fixed $h$ in the ideal-difference lattice. The fixed $\Delta h$ is a finite linear combination of bounded $D$ tests by Section 
10, hence finite-energy tests. Section 8's full form continuity and extended pairing pass every measure slot to its finite-energy limit. 
Density then gives the weighted signed measure identity with $u$ and the finite-energy other slots. Divide on the slices where 
$\Delta\ge1/m$ as before. This replaces $u$ by $u^k$ on $\{u>-k\}$. Repeat the finitely many slots and intersect the strict sets to get 
(11.1). This proof uses a **fixed bounded $D$ test** during the all-slot limit, not a discontinuous moving indicator in a weak limit.

The union of $U_k$ is the complement of the input poles. Each pole has zero target mixed measure by (8.1). Therefore the measures 
$\mathbf1_{U_k}\mu_k$ are increasing setwise restrictions of the target and converge setwise to it. This is the nonpolar construction and 
proves its agreement with the canonical finite-energy measure.

There is also **total variation for these canonical truncations**. In the diagonal case put $A=A(u)$. The two measures agree on $\{u>-k\}$. 
On its complement,
$$\mu(u^{k[p]})\{u\le-k\}\le F((u^k)^{[n]})/k\le A^n/k,$$
because $-u^k=k$ there. Likewise $\mu(u^{[p]})\{u\le-k\}\le F_\infty(u^{[n]})/k$. Consequently
$$\|\mu(u^{k[p]})-\mu(u^{[p]})\|_{\rm TV}\le2A^n/k.\tag{11.2}$$
For mixed inputs put $P=\prod_{j=1}^p A_j$. On $X\setminus U_k$ use the union bound and (8.1), for both the target and truncated tuple, with
 test $u_i$. Hölder bounds each such test integral by $A_iP$. Thus
$$\|\mu_k-\mu(\boldsymbol u)\|_{\rm TV}\le\frac2k\sum_{i=1}^p A_iP.\tag{11.3}$$
These estimates remain valid when a size is zero, by the same Hölder bound; if $p=0$ the operator is constant and its total variation 
difference is zero. No total variation statement for arbitrary decreasing nets follows from this argument. Weak convergence for those nets 
was Section 8, and is distinct.

## 12. Capacity, comparison, convergence in capacity, and quasicontinuity

For a Borel $B\subset X$ define the mixed-degree reference capacity
$$\operatorname{Cap}(B)=\sup\{\mu(\phi^{[p]})(B):\phi\in D,\ -1\le\phi\le0\}.$$
Every measure in this supremum has mass at most $m=e_R(\mathfrak a)$, so the capacity is finite. It is monotone and countably subadditive, 
since each measure is. For increasing Borel sets it is continuous from below: the suprema over the set index and $\phi$ commute. We do 
**not** deduce compact continuity from above or the full Choquet axioms from these facts. For $n=1$ this is simply the fixed finite branch 
measure.

For diagonal finite energy, (11.1) and a tail bound give
$$\mu(u^{[p]})(B)\le k^p\operatorname{Cap}(B)+A(u)^n/k.$$
Here $u^k/k$ is an admissible capacity input. The proof of Section 11 works unchanged with any fixed positive real cut level $k$, taking 
integer $\ell\ge k$ for its approximations. Optimizing at $k=A(u)/\operatorname{Cap}(B)^{1/n}$ yields
$$\mu(u^{[p]})(B)\le2A(u)^p\operatorname{Cap}(B)^{1/n}\quad(A(u)>0,\ \operatorname{Cap}(B)>0).\tag{12.1}$$
Zero capacity follows by sending $k\to\infty$; zero size gives a zero measure if $p>0$. For $p=0$ the capacity is the reference measure and 
the corresponding assertion is its tautological absolute continuity, including a zero-size test. For mixed tuples, positivity and 
multilinearity give an **actual measure** expansion
$$p!\,\mu(u_1,\ldots,u_p)\le\mu((u_1+\cdots+u_p)^{[p]}).$$
All expansion terms are positive measures. Apply (12.1) and Minkowski to the sum. Thus every finite-energy mixed measure is uniformly 
absolutely continuous with respect to this capacity. This measure inequality comes from positive expansion, not from ordering scalar gauge 
moments.

### The precise polar class

Put $r=-1$ and $L_z=\int(-z)\,d\mu(r^{[p]})$ for $z\in D$. If $L_z<\infty$, then, by the extended pairing and **scalar form order** $\phi\ge
 r$,
$$\int(-z)\,d\mu(\phi^{[p]})\le L_z\qquad(-1\le\phi\le0).$$
For an arbitrary $z$ take its truncations first, then use sequential monotone convergence. Therefore
$$\operatorname{Cap}\{z<-t\}\le L_z/t,\qquad \operatorname{Cap}\{z=-\infty\}=0.\tag{12.2}$$
Every $\mathcal E^1$ input has $L_z\le A(z)\delta^p$ by Hölder. A broader branch-admissible reduction is proved in Section 13; no 
unrestricted global nonbottom-pole claim is made here.

### Comparison, with equality-locus and reference curvature

For bounded $u,v$, set $w_\varepsilon=\max(u,v-\varepsilon)$, with $v-\varepsilon=v+\varepsilon r$. On the Borel set $\{u<v-\varepsilon\}$, 
(10.2) identifies $\mu(w_\varepsilon^{[p]})$ with $\mu((v-\varepsilon)^{[p]})$; on $\{u>v-\varepsilon\}$ it identifies it with 
$\mu(u^{[p]})$. Scalar mass order, tested by $-1$, says $\mu(w_\varepsilon^{[p]})(X)\le\mu(u^{[p]})(X)$. Decompose into these two strict 
sets and the equality locus. Cancel the identical contribution on the second strict set and discard the nonnegative left equality-locus 
contribution, obtaining
$$\mu((v-\varepsilon)^{[p]})\{u<v-\varepsilon\}\le\mu(u^{[p]})\{u\le v-\varepsilon\}.$$
The positive reference-curvature expansion gives $\mu(v^{[p]})\le\mu((v+\varepsilon r)^{[p]})$ as measures, because every added mixed term 
is positive. The right set is contained in $\{u<v\}$. The left strict sets increase to $\{u<v\}$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Hence
$$\mu(v^{[p]})\{u<v\}\le\mu(u^{[p]})\{u<v\}.\tag{12.3}$$
With fixed other slots the same proof gives the one-slot mixed comparison. The equality-locus term has been retained until it can 
legitimately be discarded; it is not silently assumed zero.

For finite-energy inputs apply the bounded comparison to $u^k,v^k$. The changing strict set is exactly
$$\{u^k<v^k\}=\{u<v\}\cap\{v>-k\},$$
which increases to the full strict set; input poles are null. Canonical total variation convergence (11.2/11.3), and then setwise continuity
 of the limiting finite measures, justify the passage despite the moving Borel sets. This proves finite-energy comparison. Ordinary weak 
convergence would not suffice.

### Decreasing-net capacity convergence

Let $u_\lambda\downarrow u\in\mathcal E^1$ with specified limit. Define the nonnegative integrable gap to be zero on their common poles; its
 ambiguity is on a capacity-zero set by (12.2). By Section 8
$$I_\lambda=\int(u_\lambda-u)\,d\mu(u^{[p]})
=F_\infty(u,u^{[p]})-F_\infty(u_\lambda,u^{[p]})\downarrow0.$$
For any capacity input $\phi$ and $\varepsilon>0$ put $v_\lambda=u_\lambda+\varepsilon\phi-\varepsilon/2$. This is finite energy by the cone
 result; its positive measure expansion gives $\mu(v_\lambda^{[p]})\ge\varepsilon^p\mu(\phi^{[p]})$. Outside the null poles,
$$\{u_\lambda-u>2\varepsilon\}\subset\{u<v_\lambda\}\subset\{u_\lambda-u>\varepsilon/2\}.$$
Use comparison and Markov's inequality against $\mu(u^{[p]})$, then take the supremum in $\phi$:
$$\operatorname{Cap}\{u_\lambda-u>2\varepsilon\}\le2I_\lambda/\varepsilon^{p+1}=2I_\lambda/\varepsilon^n\longrightarrow0.\tag{12.4}$$
For $p=0$ the expansion is the identity of the fixed reference measure and the same argument works. No subtraction of infinities occurs on 
the ignored pole set.

### Actual open exceptional sets and quasicontinuity

For bounded $u\in D$, take an actual $C$ representation $g_\alpha\downarrow u$. It is also a finite-energy net to $u$, so (12.4) applies. 
The sets $O_j=\{g_{\alpha_j}-u>2^{-j}\}$ are **open**: $g_{\alpha_j}$ is continuous and $u$ is upper semicontinuous. Choose increasing 
indices $\alpha_j$ with $\operatorname{Cap}(O_j)<\eta2^{-j-1}$; directedness and capacity convergence allow this, without requiring a 
countable cofinal representation. Outside the open union $O$, $g_{\alpha_j}$ converges uniformly to $u$. Thus $u|_{X\setminus O}$ is 
continuous and $\operatorname{Cap}(O)<\eta$. For unbounded finite energy, choose $k$ with the open set $\{u<-k\}$ of small capacity by 
(12.2), and apply bounded quasicontinuity to $u^k$. Outside the union of the two open exceptional sets, $u=u^k$ is finite and continuous. 
This proves quasicontinuity using genuine open sets and countable subadditivity; no Choquet regularity is assumed.

## 13. Branch-admissible Izumi reduction and necessary polar qualifications

We now discharge the remaining reduction rather than infer a broad polar theorem from a name. On an excellent normal local domain $A$, the 
**qualified G331 n6 result** says that for each centred divisorial valuation $\nu$, normalized by a fixed primary ideal, there is a finite 
$C_\nu>0$ with
$$g(\nu)\ge C_\nu g(v_0)\quad(g\in C_A,\ v_0\in X_A).\tag{13.1}$$
This came from the nonunit Izumi bound, normal excellent analytic irreducibility, and primary order comparison; units were handled 
separately in that grant. Its exact source restrictions remain attached. Passing an actual decreasing $C_A$ representation to its pointwise 
infimum proves (13.1) for $z\in D_A$. If $z$ is not identically bottom, choose $v_0$ where $z(v_0)$ is finite. It follows that $z(\nu)$ is 
finite at **every** centred divisorial valuation. This is a direct use of the granted inequality; a merely nonzero value, or a source label,
 would not imply it.

The reference measure $\mu((-1)^{[p]})$ on $A$ is supported on the finitely many prime divisorial atoms of a primary model by Section 3. 
Each weight is finite and nonnegative, and their sum is $e_A(\mathfrak a)>0$. Thus $L_z$ is finite if $z$ is not identically bottom on this 
branch; if it is bottom, the positive total reference mass makes $L_z=\infty$. On a general reduced germ, apply the exact residue-weighted 
normalization identity (9.2) to this reference measure and its nonnegative test integral. There are finitely many centres. We obtain the 
equivalence
$$L_z<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\rho_q^*z\not\equiv-\infty\ \text{for every top-dimensional normal centre }q.\tag{13.2}$$
Lower-dimensional centres contribute zero to $L_z$ in this degree convention but retain their full conductor compatibility. Their individual
 image points are **not** automatically capacity zero: an identified point can also have top-dimensional preimages. Capacity is a downstairs
 measure supremum, and normalization adds all top-dimensional contributions in the fibre.

Equation (13.2) proves the polar assertion for every branch-admissible $D$ function, whether or not its self-intersection is finite. It is 
stronger than the finite-energy consequence and supplies the requested actual Izumi reduction at the available hypotheses. It also specifies
 the maximal claim justified by this reference moment argument.

The exclusion of whole bottom branches is necessary. For the reduced node curve with two normalized DVR centres and maximal-ideal gauge, 
$z=(-\infty,0)$ belongs to $D$ by G331 and is globally nonbottom. Its pole is the first branch point, and the reference measure gives it 
positive mass; in the split rational node its capacity is one. Thus the implication “globally nonbottom $D$ pole is negligible” is false on 
the prescribed boundary. No polar assertion here makes that mistake. On a nonpure ring a lower-dimensional null branch may carry bottom 
values in $\mathcal E^1$; the assertion is only the explicitly defined top-degree capacity statement, not a deletion of that boundary or its
 conductor identifications.

## ENTIRE independently ROOT-authored standalone proof

\title{A continuous obstacle with no greatest geometric envelope\\
Normal crossing germs, conductor fibres, and an exact canonical filtration}
\author{Independent ROOT working paper; ORIGINAL P12.3 remains open}
\date{9 October 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Over any field and in every dimension at least two, we construct a continuous
signed obstacle on the normalized semivaluation boundary of a normal crossing
germ whose geometric continuous and decreasing classes have no greatest
minorant. The raw supremum is explicitly discontinuous and is not upper
semicontinuous. Its upper semicontinuous regularization is not geometrically
positive. We compute every canonical ideal and every canonical profile; their
pointwise convergence has an exact nonvanishing uniform error. On the
normalization, the same obstacle has a continuous geometric envelope, which
fails constancy on the infinite-conductor fibres. The only incoming theorem
is the entire qualified geometric comparison grant G331. This is a complete
scoped negative result, subject to independent review, rather than closure
of the general normal-germ part of ORIGINAL P12.3.
\end{abstract}

\section{Precise geometric input and statement}

We use the entire qualified G331 construction and comparison theorem, with
all its source, model, support, and historical-reading qualifications.
For an excellent reduced local ring and a proper primary gauge, its
independently geometric core consists of evaluations of actual negative
effective finite real Cartier divisors on actual primary blowups, with
nonnegative degree on \emph{every} contracted proper integral curve.
Its finite continuous uniform completion is \(\C_R\), and its actual
decreasing-net completion, with bottom included, is \(\D_R\).
The comparison in G331, not a new definition of positivity here, gives
\[
 \C_R=\overline{Q_R}^{\|\cdot\|_\infty},\qquad
 Q_R=\left\{-\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_jv(I_j):
              \lambda_j\geq0,\ I_j\text{ unit or proper primary}\right\},
 \qquad \D_R=\{\inf_i g_i:g_i\in\C_R\text{ decrease}\}.
\]
Raw geometric and ideal cores need not be equal. We use only their proved
equality after uniform and decreasing completion. In particular, a numerical
inequality valid for every member of \(Q_R\) passes to \(\C_R\) and then
to \(\D_R\). Every member of \(\D_R\) is upper semicontinuous, being an
actual infimum of continuous functions. No increasing-limit closure is used.

Fix any field \(k\), an integer \(d\geq2\), and real numbers \(0<a<b\).
Put \(\mathbf z=(z_1,\ldots,z_{d-1})\) and
\[
 R=k[x,y,\mathbf z]_{(x,y,\mathbf z)}/(xy),\qquad
 \m=(x,y,\mathbf z),\qquad X=V_{\m}(R).
\]
Every prime support is retained. Coordinates may have value \(+\infty\).
Set
\[
 X_1=\{v:v(y)=+\infty\},\quad X_2=\{v:v(x)=+\infty\},
 \quad Z=X_1\cap X_2.
\]
Define, with \(1/(+\infty)=0\),
\[
 f(v)=\begin{cases}
       -a,&v\in X_1,\\
       -a-(b-a)/v(y),&v\in X_2.
       \end{cases}
\]

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
The function \(f\) is finite continuous. Both raw suprema
\[
 p_{\C}(f)(v)=\sup\{g(v):g\in\C_R,\ g\leq f\},\qquad
 p_{\D}(f)(v)=\sup\{g(v):g\in\D_R,\ g\leq f\}
\]
equal the function
\[
 p(v)=\begin{cases}-a,&v(x)<+\infty,\\-b,&v(x)=+\infty.\end{cases}
\]
It is not upper semicontinuous. There is no greatest \(\C_R\)-minorant
and no greatest \(\D_R\)-minorant of \(f\).

For every integer \(m\geq1\), put \(A_m=\lceil ma\rceil\) and
\(B_m=\lceil mb\rceil\). The canonical ideal of the obstacle is exactly
\[
 \mathfrak a_m(f)=\{g\in R:v(g)+mf(v)\geq0\ \forall v\in X\}
       =\m^{B_m}+x\m^{A_m-1}.
\]
It is proper primary. Its actual geometric profile satisfies on every support
\[
 h_m=-\frac1m v(\mathfrak a_m(f))
    =\max\left\{-\frac{B_m}{m},-\frac{v(x)+A_m-1}{m}\right\},
 \qquad h_m\longrightarrow p\quad\text{pointwise},
\]
and has the exact error
\[
 \|p-h_m\|_\infty=\frac{\lceil mb\rceil}{m}-a\geq b-a.
\]
For \(a=1/2,b=1\), this error is \(1/2\) in every degree.
\end{theorem}

\section{All supports and the infinite-conductor fibres}

Since \(xy=0\), multiplicativity forces every semivaluation to kill
\(x\) or \(y\). Hence \(X=X_1\cup X_2\), a finite closed cover.
The first piece is the entire boundary of
\(T_1=k[x,\mathbf z]_{(x,\mathbf z)}\); the second is that of
\(T_2=k[y,\mathbf z]_{(y,\mathbf z)}\).
They are identified along the entire boundary of
\(B=k[\mathbf z]_{(\mathbf z)}\). These descriptions follow directly
by factoring a semivaluation through its killed coordinate, and preserve
every further prime support.

The normalization is \(S=T_1\times T_2\).
Indeed the natural embedding is a fibre product
\(R=T_1\times_B T_2\): pairs have equal restrictions at \(x=0,y=0\).
The polynomial fibre-product identity survives localization; common unit
denominators can be lifted from the two component polynomial rings.
The idempotent \((1,0)=x/(x+y)\) lies in the total quotient ring, since
\(x+y\) is a nonzerodivisor, and is integral over \(R\).
The component projections are surjective, so \(S=R+R(1,0)\) is finite.
Both component rings are normal, proving the asserted normalization.
Its conductor is
\[
 \mathfrak c=(x,y),\qquad R/\mathfrak c=B,
 \qquad S/\mathfrak c=B\times B.
\]
To check the conductor, multiply a pair by each component idempotent:
both resulting pairs descend precisely when their common restriction to
\(B\) is zero. This is the displayed ideal.

If \(v(x)\) is finite, only the first component can lift \(v\); if
\(v(y)\) is finite, only the second can. If both are infinite, there
are exactly two component lifts, with the same arbitrary semivaluation
on \(B\). Thus \(Z\), which is nonempty because \(d\geq2\), is
exactly the infinite-conductor stratum, and its fibres have two points.
No such support is deleted.

On \(X_2\), normalization gives
\(\min\{v(y),v(z_1),\ldots,v(z_{d-1})\}=1\), so \(v(y)\geq1\).
The reciprocal is continuous on the compact interval \([1,+\infty]\).
Consequently the second formula for \(f\) is continuous and takes values
in \([-b,-a]\); on \(Z\) it equals \(-a\).
The first formula is continuous and has the same value there.
The finite closed-cover pasting lemma proves continuity on \(X\).
This also proves full-fibre compatibility on the normalization.

\section{A geometric inequality on the second component}

Let \(o_i\) be the generic monomial valuation on \(T_i\) which assigns
value one to every regular coordinate. Its pullback to \(R\) kills
the other component coordinate, and belongs to \(X_i\).
For any normalized centred semivaluation \(w\) on \(T_i\), every
regular coordinate has value at least one. Therefore
\[
 w(g)\geq o_i(g)\quad\text{for every }g\in T_i.
\]
For completeness, represent \(g=P/Q\), where \(Q\) has nonzero
constant coefficient and hence value zero. Every monomial of \(P\)
has value at least its total degree, including monomials containing
killed coordinates. The ultrametric inequality proves the claim.
Generic monomial evaluation of \(P\) is its least total degree, so
no residue cancellation is assumed away for \(w\).

For every unit-or-primary \(R\)-ideal \(I\) this gives
\(w(I)\geq o_2(I)\) on \(X_2\); primary values are finite.
Taking negative finite nonnegative real combinations gives
\(q(w)\leq q(o_2)\) for \(q\in Q_R\).
Uniform limits preserve this inequality, as do pointwise infima of
actual decreasing nets. By the entire geometric comparison input,
\[
 g(w)\leq g(o_2)\qquad(w\in X_2,\ g\in\C_R\text{ or }\D_R).
\]
Since \(f(o_2)=-b\), every geometric minorant of \(f\) is at most
\(-b\) on the \emph{entire} second component, including \(Z\).
This is a statement about the original independently geometric classes,
not about a substitute ideal-order class.

\section{Exact canonical ideals and their positivity}

For \(g\in R\), write its component images as \(g_1,g_2\).
The first obstacle is constant, so its defining inequalities are equivalent to
\(g_1\in\m_1^{A_m}\). Necessity follows by testing \(o_1\);
sufficiency follows from the order bound on every semivaluation.
On the second component, testing \(o_2\) forces
\(g_2\in\m_2^{B_m}\). Conversely this condition implies, on every support,
\[
 w(g_2)\geq B_m\geq mb\geq
     m\left(a+\frac{b-a}{w(y)}\right),
\]
including \(w(y)=+\infty\). These are exactly all the obstacle tests.
The two conditions agree on the common quotient only for pairs whose
common restriction has order at least \(B_m\) in \(B\).

We verify that their inverse image is \(\m^{B_m}+x\m^{A_m-1}\).
This ideal has the required orders on both components, so one inclusion
is immediate. For the other, lift \(g_2\in\m_2^{B_m}\) from
the localized \(k[y,\mathbf z]\) subring of \(R\); this lift lies
in \(\m^{B_m}\) and has first component \(g_2(0,\mathbf z)\).
Subtract it from \(g\). The remaining second component is zero;
its first component is divisible by \(x\) and still belongs to
\(\m_1^{A_m}\), because \(B_m\geq A_m\).
Dividing by \(x\) in the regular polynomial local ring gives an
element of \(\m_1^{A_m-1}\), which lifts to
\(\m^{A_m-1}\) in \(R\). Multiplication by \(x\) kills its
second component. This proves the identity, with unit denominators
handled by the same localized subrings.

The ideal contains \(\m^{B_m}\) and is contained in \(\m\),
so it is proper primary. Ideal product and sum evaluations give the
formula for \(h_m\) in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, with infinity retained.
Positivity is established before any limit is identified: on the actual
blowup \(Y_m=\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathfrak a_m(f)}\Spec R\), the pulled-back
ideal is \(\mathcal O_{Y_m}(-E_m)\), for an actual effective Cartier
divisor supported on the closed fibre, and this line bundle is relatively
ample. The Rees algebra is reduced as a subalgebra of \(R[t]\);
each generator chart embeds in its localization, where its ideal
generator is a nonzerodivisor. This proves actual Cartier effectivity
even though \(R\) is nonnormal and reducible.
The rational divisor \(-E_m/m\) is negative effective and its bundle
has positive degree on every contracted proper integral curve, by
ampleness restricted to that curve. It therefore belongs to the independently
geometric core and evaluates to \(h_m\). No arbitrary-model cofinality,
resolution, finite generation, or matrix positivity premise is used.

\section{Raw supremum, nonexistence, and exact uniform loss}

The constant \(-b=-b\,v(\m)\) is itself geometric and lies below \(f\).
The second-component inequality therefore makes either raw supremum
equal \(-b\) on \(X_2\).
On the remaining points \(v(x)<+\infty\), the obstacle is \(-a\)
and \(h_m(v)\to-a\). Since all \(h_m\) are geometric minorants,
both suprema equal \(-a\) there. This proves the asserted formula
and pointwise convergence on every support.

For each fixed degree the profiles lie between \(-B_m/m\) and \(p\).
On \(X_2\) the gap is \(B_m/m-b\), and on its complement it is
at most \(B_m/m-a\). A generic monomial point of the first component
with \(v(x)=r\geq B_m-A_m+1\) and \(v(z_j)=1\) attains the latter
gap. Thus the exact sup norm is \(B_m/m-a\), as claimed.

Let \(v_r\) be these first-component monomial points with integer
\(r\to+\infty\). They converge to \(v_\infty\), which kills
\(x,y\) and has generic monomial values one on all the \(z_j\).
Indeed for a polynomial \(F(x,\mathbf z)=\sum_i x^iF_i(\mathbf z)\),
\[
 v_r(F)=\min_i\{ri+\ord_{(\mathbf z)}F_i\}.
\]
If \(F_0\neq0\), this eventually equals its order; otherwise it tends
to infinity. Unit denominators have value zero. This proves convergence
on every element of \(R\), which is the boundary topology, and gives
\[
 \limsup_r p(v_r)=-a>-b=p(v_\infty).
\]
Hence \(p\) is not upper semicontinuous.

Any greatest \(\C_R\)- or \(\D_R\)-minorant would dominate
the constant \(-b\) and every \(h_m\), so the preceding pointwise
calculation would force it to equal \(p\). Both classes consist of
upper semicontinuous functions. This contradiction proves nonexistence.

Even ordinary upper semicontinuous regularization does not repair positivity.
Define \(p^*(v)=\inf_{U\ni v}\sup_U p\), over open neighbourhoods.
It is bounded upper semicontinuous, and \(p\leq p^*\leq f\) because
\(f\) is continuous. The sequence gives \(p^*(v_\infty)=-a\).
The open neighbourhood \(\{v:v(y)<2\}\) of \(o_2\) lies wholly in
\(X_2\), where \(p=-b\), so \(p^*(o_2)=-b\).
These values violate the mandatory geometric inequality
\(g(v_\infty)\leq g(o_2)\). Thus \(p^*\notin\C_R\cup\D_R\).

\section{Normalization and arbitrary primary gauges}

On the normalization, the first obstacle has envelope \(-a\), its
own constant geometric minorant. On the second component the same order
comparison makes its envelope the constant \(-b\).
Consequently the source envelope is the continuous geometric tuple
\((-a,-b)\), and it is not constant on any infinite-conductor fibre.
This proves failure of envelope preservation by normalization for this
continuous full-fibre-compatible obstacle. Exact class-level positive
descent in G331 is consistent: it requires the function being descended,
not merely its obstacle, to be constant on every fibre.
For this particular obstacle both normal components have continuous
geometric envelopes by the preceding elementary proof; no general normal
continuous-envelope theorem is needed.

For another proper primary gauge \(\mathfrak b\), set
\(d(v)=v(\mathfrak b)>0\) on \(X\) and \(T(v)=v/d(v)\).
The G331 homogeneous cocycle is an order bijection of both geometric
classes, with bounded positive continuous denominator. Transport the
obstacle by \(f_{\mathfrak b}(T(v))=f(v)/d(v)\).
Every canonical defining inequality is divided by the same \(d(v)\),
so the ideals are unchanged; profiles and the raw supremum divide by it.
The sequence \(T(v_r)\to T(v_\infty)\) retains the strict gap
\((b-a)/d(v_\infty)>0\). No greatest minorant exists in that gauge
either. Its uniform canonical error is bounded below by
\((b-a)/\max_X d\), by evaluating the same degree-dependent points.
This proves gauge-invariant failure without discarding supports.

\section{Source and scope record}

The sole incoming theorem is ENTIRE qualified G331, physically reread
here in bounded untruncated ranges 1--140, 141--270, 271--400, 401--530,
and 531--607, including all source and exact-scope annotations.
Its geometric comparison (n3 and n7--n8) is applied at this excellent
reduced polynomial local germ, with the actual primary-model and all-curve
conditions retained. Its primary-gauge cocycle is used only in the last
paragraph. This is fresh reading of the qualified grant, not fresh
recursive reading of its published primary sources.
Polynomial local rings being regular, normal and excellent, and their
ordinary monomial orders, are conventional algebraic background;
all normalization, conductor, support, obstacle, filtration and limit
computations needed here are proved above.

The proof is valid over every field, including imperfect and positive
characteristic fields; no integer coefficient is divided in the field.
It applies in every dimension at least two. It gives a nonnormal reduced
example, not a normal counterexample. In dimension one this conductor
quotient is zero dimensional and the centred quotient boundary is empty;
the construction then has no point \(v_\infty\), consistently with
geometric reduced-curve clipping. The boundary cone remains distinct
from literal classical or CLD logarithmic radial extensions.

General normal excellent higher-dimensional envelope regularity and
the full appropriate-existence classification remain open.
P12.4 products, P12.5 energy and P12.6 full operators remain separate.
Historical recursive/whole-book audits retain all G331 qualifications.
This complete scoped working proof is UNREVIEWED, with no original
closure or new accepted-paper claim. It was developed without inspection
of active native291 or native292 mathematics or hot feedback.
Compilation is separately unverified until an actual successful native
